periopRules.summary: Withhold before surgery or procedures with prolonged fasting, if possible.
periopRules.why: The labels list surgery and reduced caloric intake among the conditions that precipitate ketoacidosis.

drugs.name: Empagliflozin (Jardiance)

timings.text: Withhold for at least 3 days, if possible, prior to surgery or procedures associated with prolonged fasting.

drugs.restart: Resume when the patient is clinically stable and has resumed oral intake.

drugs.name: Dapagliflozin (Farxiga)

timings.text: Withhold for at least 3 days, if possible, prior to surgery or procedures associated with prolonged fasting.

drugs.restart: Resume when the patient is clinically stable and has resumed oral intake.

drugs.name: Canagliflozin (Invokana)

timings.text: Withhold for at least 3 days, if possible, prior to surgery or procedures associated with prolonged fasting.

drugs.restart: Resume when the patient is clinically stable and has resumed oral intake.

drugs.name: Ertugliflozin (Steglatro)

timings.text: Withhold for at least 4 days, if possible, prior to surgery or procedures associated with prolonged fasting.

drugs.restart: Resume when the patient is clinically stable and has resumed oral intake.

periopRules.summary: Stop before surgery or invasive procedures. The interval depends on the drug, and for dabigatran on creatinine clearance.
periopRules.why: The labels ask for interruption before procedures because of the risk of bleeding.
cautions: These are the manufacturers' timings for surgery and procedures. They are not the ASRA intervals for placing a spinal, epidural or deep block: tick 'DOACs: spinal, epidural or deep block (ASRA)' for those.

drugs.name: Apixaban (Eliquis)

timings.when: Moderate or high risk of unacceptable or clinically significant bleeding
timings.text: Discontinue at least 48 hours prior to elective surgery or invasive procedures.

timings.when: Low risk of bleeding, or bleeding that would be non-critical in location and easily controlled
timings.text: Discontinue at least 24 hours prior to elective surgery or invasive procedures.

catheter: Indwelling epidural or intrathecal catheters should not be removed earlier than 24 hours after the last administration.
The next dose should not be administered earlier than 5 hours after the removal of the catheter.
drugs.restart: Restart after the surgical or other procedures as soon as adequate hemostasis has been established.

drugs.name: Rivaroxaban (Xarelto)

timings.text: If anticoagulation must be discontinued to reduce the risk of bleeding with surgical or other procedures, stop at least 24 hours before the procedure.

catheter: Placement or removal of an epidural catheter or lumbar puncture is best performed when the anticoagulant effect is low; however, the exact timing to reach a sufficiently low anticoagulant effect in each patient is not known.

An indwelling epidural or intrathecal catheter should not be removed before at least 2 half-lives have elapsed (i.e., 18 hours in young patients aged 20 to 45 years and 26 hours in elderly patients aged 60 to 76 years), after the last administration.
The next dose should not be administered earlier than 6 hours after the removal of the catheter.
drugs.restart: Restart after the surgical or other procedures as soon as adequate hemostasis has been established, noting that the time to onset of therapeutic effect is short.

drugs.name: Edoxaban (Savaysa)

timings.text: Discontinue at least 24 hours before invasive or surgical procedures because of the risk of bleeding.

catheter: Indwelling epidural or intrathecal catheters should not be removed earlier than 12 hours after the last administration.
The next dose should not be administered earlier than 2 hours after the removal of the catheter.
drugs.restart: Can be restarted after the surgical or other procedure as soon as adequate hemostasis has been established, noting that the time to onset of pharmacodynamic effect is 1-2 hours.

drugs.name: Dabigatran (Pradaxa capsules, adults)

timings.text: If possible, discontinue 1 to 2 days before invasive or surgical procedures because of the increased risk of bleeding.
If possible, discontinue 3 to 5 days before invasive or surgical procedures because of the increased risk of bleeding.
Consider longer times for patients undergoing major surgery, spinal puncture, or placement of a spinal or epidural catheter or port.

drugs.restart: Temporarily discontinue before invasive or surgical procedures when possible, then restart promptly.

periopRules.summary: Published perioperative protocols conflict on both the drug instruction and the fasting instruction, so this app does not pick one. See "GLP-1 perioperative protocols" in References (the book icon) for the side-by-side comparison.

periopRules.drugClass: Warfarin: spinal, epidural or deep block (ASRA)
periopRules.section: ASRA: spinal, epidural and deep blocks
periopRules.summary: Stop 5 days before the block, and check that the INR is normal before needle placement.
periopRules.why: ASRA bases this on warfarin pharmacology, the clinical relevance of vitamin K coagulation factor levels, case series and case reports of spinal hematoma.
cautions: These are ASRA's recommendations for placing a spinal, epidural or deep plexus/peripheral block and for removing catheters. Deviation may be acceptable in the judgment of the responsible anesthesiologist, and a bloody or difficult needle placement needs a case-by-case decision.

drugs.name: Warfarin

timings.text: We recommend that the anticoagulant therapy be stopped 5 days prior to the planned procedure, and the INR be measured and normalized (normal range of the local laboratory) prior to needle placement (grade IB)

In patients receiving an initial dose of warfarin prior to surgery, we suggest the INR should be checked prior to needle placement if the first dose was given >24 hours earlier, or if a second dose of oral anticoagulant has been administered (grade IIC)

catheter: In patients receiving low-dose warfarin therapy during epidural analgesia, we suggest that their INR be monitored daily (grade IIC)
We suggest that neuraxial catheters be removed when the INR is <1.5 (grade IIC)

In patients with INR >1.5 but <3, the increased risk of maintaining a neuraxial catheter remains unknown. We suggest indwelling catheters may be maintained or removed with caution, closely following the INR and duration of warfarin therapy (grade IIC)
In patients with an INR >3, we recommend that the warfarin dose be held or reduced in patients with indwelling neuraxial catheters (grade IA)
We suggest that neurological assessment be continued for at least 48 hours following catheter removal (grade IIC)

Neurological testing of sensory and motor function should be performed routinely during epidural analgesia for patients on warfarin therapy. To facilitate neurological evaluation, we recommend that the type of analgesic solution be tailored to minimize the degree of sensory and motor blockade (grade IC)

periopRules.drugClass: Unfractionated heparin: spinal, epidural or deep block (ASRA)
periopRules.section: ASRA: spinal, epidural and deep blocks
periopRules.summary: Intravenous: stop the infusion 4 to 6 hours before, with coagulation assessed. Subcutaneous: the interval depends on the dose.
periopRules.why: ASRA bases the subcutaneous intervals on the pharmacology of a 5000-unit dose, which starts to act 1 hour after administration and persists for 4 to 6 hours.
cautions: These are ASRA's recommendations for placing a spinal, epidural or deep plexus/peripheral block and for removing catheters. Deviation may be acceptable in the judgment of the responsible anesthesiologist, and a bloody or difficult needle placement needs a case-by-case decision.

drugs.name: Unfractionated heparin, intravenous

timings.text: Discontinue heparin infusion for a minimum of 4–6 hours and coagulation status be assessed and normal prior to neuraxial block or deep plexus/peripheral block (grade IA)
Delay intravenous heparin administration for a minimum of 1 hour after needle placement (grade IA)

Since heparin-induced thrombocytopenia may occur during heparin administration, we recommend that patients receiving intravenous or subcutaneous UFH for >4 days have a platelet count assessed (grade IC)

catheter: Remove indwelling neuraxial catheters 4 to 6 hours after the last heparin dose (and after assessment of the patient's coagulation status); reheparinize 1 hour after catheter removal (grade 1A).

Monitor the patient postoperatively to provide early detection of motor blockade and consider use of minimal concentration of local anesthetics to enhance the early detection of a spinal hematoma (grade 1A).

Although the occurrence of a bloody or difficult neuraxial needle placement may increase the risk of hematoma, there are no data to support mandatory cancellation of a case. Direct communication with the surgeon and a specific risk-benefit decision about proceeding in each case is recommended (grade IA)

It is not suggested to maintain neuraxial or deep plexus/peripheral catheters in the setting of full anticoagulation during cardiac surgery. If unanticipated heparinization occurs, we suggest postoperative monitoring of neurological status and consider use of minimal concentration of local anesthetics to enhance early detection of neuraxial hematoma (grade IIC)

drugs.name: Unfractionated heparin, subcutaneous

timings.text: Preoperative low-dose UFH for thromboprophylaxis (5000 U two times per day or three times per day). We suggest needle placement occur a minimum of 4–6 hours after heparin administration or coagulation status be assessed and normal (grade IIC)

timings.when: 7500–10 000 U two times per day or a daily dose of ≤20 000 U
timings.text: We suggest neuraxial block occur a minimum of 12 hours after subcutaneous heparin administration and confirmation of normal coagulation status (grade IIC)

timings.when: >10 000 U subcutaneously per dose, or >20 000 U total daily dose
timings.text: We suggest neuraxial block occur a minimum of 24 hours after subcutaneous heparin administration and confirmation of normal coagulation status (grade IIC)

catheter: There is no contraindication to maintaining neuraxial catheters in the presence of low-dose UFH. We suggest catheter removal occurs a minimum of 4–6 hours after heparin administration. Subsequent heparin administration may occur immediately after catheter removal (grade IIC)

The safety of indwelling neuraxial catheters in patients receiving doses >5000 U at a time or >15 000 U of UFH daily has not been established. We suggest that the risk and benefits be assessed on an individual basis and that techniques to facilitate detection of new/progressive neurological deficits (eg, enhanced neurological monitoring occur and neuraxial solutions to minimize sensory and motor block) be applied (grade IIC)

periopRules.drugClass: Low molecular weight heparin: spinal, epidural or deep block (ASRA)
periopRules.section: ASRA: spinal, epidural and deep blocks
periopRules.summary: Low dose: at least 12 hours before needle placement. High (therapeutic) dose: at least 24 hours.
periopRules.why: In a small study cited by ASRA, almost 60% of patients on high-dose enoxaparin still had higher than expected anti-Xa levels at least 24 hours after the last dose.
cautions: These are ASRA's recommendations for placing a spinal, epidural or deep plexus/peripheral block and for removing catheters. Deviation may be acceptable in the judgment of the responsible anesthesiologist, and a bloody or difficult needle placement needs a case-by-case decision.

drugs.name: Low molecular weight heparin (enoxaparin, dalteparin, tinzaparin)

timings.text: Low-dose LMWH regimens administered for prophylaxis include enoxaparin 40 mg/day, enoxaparin 30 mg every 12 hours, dalteparin 5000 IU daily. The target aXa level for prophylaxis (measured 4 hours after a dose) is regarded to be 0.2–0.5 IU/mL.

High-dose LMWH regimens for treatment of VTE or bridging therapy involves administering a much higher dose that is typically weight based, such as enoxaparin 1 mg/kg every 12 hours, enoxaparin 1.5 mg/kg daily, dalteparin 120 IU/kg every 12 hours, dalteparin 200 IU/kg daily, or tinzaparin 175 IU/kg daily. It is advisable to maintain peak aXa levels between 0.5 U/mL and 1 U/mL (measured 3–4 hours after the LMWH dose). With high-dose LMWH, it is recommended that the last dose should occur at least 24 hours preoperatively and the last dose should be halved in patients with moderate (CrCl 30–49 mL/min) to severe (CrCl <30 mL/min) renal insufficiency to avoid an exaggerated or prolonged response.
We recommend that needle placement should occur at least 12 hours after low-dose LMWH (grade IC)
Consider checking aXa activity level if <12 hours (grade 2C). An acceptable level of residual aXa activity remains undetermined, therefore we suggest aXa value of ≤0.1 IU/mL (grade IIC)
In patients receiving high (therapeutic) doses of LMWH, we recommend delay of at least 24 hours prior to needle/catheter placement (grade IC)

Consider checking aXa activity level if <24 hours particularly in elderly patients (age >75 years) and patients with renal insufficiency (CrCl ≤30 mL/min). An acceptable level of residual aXa activity remains undetermined, therefore we suggest aXa value of ≤0.1 IU/mL (grade IIC)

Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia may occur during LMWH administration; therefore, we recommend that patients receiving LMWH for >4 days have a platelet count assessed prior to needle placement (grade IC)

timings.when: Blood during needle or catheter placement
timings.text: The presence of blood during needle and catheter placement does not necessitate postponement of surgery. We suggest that initiation of LMWH therapy in this setting should be delayed for 24 hours postoperatively and that this consideration be discussed with the surgeon (grade IIC)

catheter: Antiplatelet or oral anticoagulant medications administered in combination with LMWH increases the risk of neuraxial hematoma. We recommend against concomitant administration of medications affecting hemostasis, such as antiplatelet drugs, standard heparin, or dextran, regardless of LMWH dosing regimen when there is an indwelling neuraxial catheter (grade IA)

Twice-daily low dose. We recommend the first dose of LMWH be administered the following day and at least 12 hours after needle/catheter placement. Indwelling catheters should be removed prior to initiation of LMWH. Administration of LMWH should be delayed for 4 hours after catheter removal (grade IC)

Single daily low dose. We recommend the first postoperative LMWH dose should be administered at least 12 hours after needle/catheter placement. The second postoperative dose should occur no sooner than 24 hours after the first dose. Indwelling neuraxial catheters do not appear to represent increased risk and may be maintained. However, no additional hemostasis altering medications should be administered due to the additive effects. The catheter should be removed 12 hours after the last dose of LMWH. Subsequent LMWH dosing should occur at least 4 hours after catheter removal (grade IC)

Single or twice-daily high (therapeutic) dosing. High-dose LMWH may be resumed 24 hours after non-high-bleeding-risk surgery and 48–72 hours after high-bleeding-risk surgery. We recommend that indwelling neuraxial catheters be removed 4 hours prior to the first postoperative dose and the first postoperative dose should be at least 24 hours after needle/catheter placement, whichever is greater (grade IC)

periopRules.drugClass: Fondaparinux: spinal, epidural or deep block (ASRA)
periopRules.section: ASRA: spinal, epidural and deep blocks
periopRules.summary: Long intervals that depend on the dose and on renal function.
periopRules.why: ASRA notes that fondaparinux has a long half-life and direct renal excretion, and that protamine would not be an effective reversal strategy.
cautions: These are ASRA's recommendations for placing a spinal, epidural or deep plexus/peripheral block and for removing catheters. Deviation may be acceptable in the judgment of the responsible anesthesiologist, and a bloody or difficult needle placement needs a case-by-case decision.

drugs.name: Fondaparinux (Arixtra)

timings.when: Low dose (2.5 mg once per day)
timings.text: We suggest holding low-dose fondaparinux (2.5 mg once per day) for 36 hours (young patients) to 42 hours (elderly patients) in healthy patients with normal renal function (grade IIC)
We suggest holding fondaparinux for a minimum of 58 hours in patients with moderate renal insufficiency (CrCl 30–50 mL/min) (grade 2C)
We suggest not performing neuraxial or deep plexus/peripheral blocks in patients with severe renal impairment (CrCl <30 mL/min) due to the 72 hours half-life (grade IIC)
We suggest testing aXa activity calibrated to fondaparinux if placing the needle prior to these recommended times is considered (aXa ≤0.1 IU/mL) (grade IIC)

timings.when: High-dose fondaparinux (5–10 mg once per day)
timings.text: We suggest holding fondaparinux for a minimum of 70 hours in young patients with normal renal function (grade IIC)
We suggest holding fondaparinux for a minimum of 105 hours in elderly patients with normal renal function (grade IIC)
We suggest testing aXa activity calibrated to fondaparinux if placing needle prior to the recommended times is considered (aXa ≤0.1 IU/mL) (grade IIC)

catheter: We suggest that neuraxial catheters be removed at least 6 hours prior to the first postoperative dose (grade IIC)

periopRules.drugClass: DOACs: spinal, epidural or deep block (ASRA)
periopRules.section: ASRA: spinal, epidural and deep blocks
periopRules.summary: High dose of apixaban, edoxaban or rivaroxaban: at least 72 hours. Low-dose intervals are shorter. Dabigatran depends on creatinine clearance.
periopRules.why: ASRA bases its intervals on pharmacology, with the intent of near-complete resolution of the antithrombotic effect at the time of the block.
cautions: These are ASRA's recommendations for placing a spinal, epidural or deep plexus/peripheral block and for removing catheters. Deviation may be acceptable in the judgment of the responsible anesthesiologist, and a bloody or difficult needle placement needs a case-by-case decision.

ASRA's high and low doses decide which line applies, and this app cannot tell which dose the patient takes. The part of the guideline that this app could read does not state the doses behind 'high' and 'low'; check the guideline's tables.

The manufacturers recommend that in case of a traumatic neuraxial puncture the administration of the next dose of apixaban and rivaroxaban should be delayed for 48 hours and 24 hours, respectively. There is no such recommendation for dabigatran and edoxaban.

If a DOAC were to be inadvertently administered in the presence of an indwelling neuraxial catheter, a therapy-free interval identical to the ones recommended prior to a neuraxial intervention should be observed, or the absence of any residual anticoagulant activity should be documented using an appropriate hemostatic assay.

drugs.name: Apixaban

timings.text: We suggest that a high dose of apixaban be discontinued at least 72 hours prior to neuraxial block or deep plexus/peripheral block. Consider checking apixaban or aXa plasma level if <72 hours (grade IIC)

We suggest that a low dose of apixaban be discontinued for at least 36 hours prior to neuraxial block or deep plexus/peripheral block. Consider checking apixaban or aXa plasma level if <36 hours (grade IIC)
We suggest that a residual apixaban plasma level <30 ng/mL or a residual aXa activity plasma level ≤0.1 IU/mL is acceptable prior to neuraxial block or deep plexus/peripheral block (grade IIC)

catheter: With the unanticipated administration of high dose of apixaban with a neuraxial catheter in situ, we suggest that apixaban dosing be withheld for at least 72 hours, or a residual apixaban plasma level <30 ng/mL or a residual aXa activity plasma level ≤0.1 IU/mL before the catheter is removed (grade IIC)

With the unanticipated administration of low dose of apixaban with a neuraxial catheter in situ, we suggest that apixaban dosing be withheld for at least 36 hours, or a residual apixaban plasma level <30 ng/mL or a residual aXa activity plasma level ≤0.1 IU/mL before the catheter is removed (grade IIC)
drugs.restart: High dose: We suggest that needle placement/catheter removal occurs at least 24 hours prior to the first postoperative dose (grade IIC) Low dose: We suggest that needle placement/catheter removal occurs at least 6 hours prior to the first postoperative dose (grade IIC)

drugs.name: Edoxaban

timings.text: We suggest that a high dose of edoxaban be discontinued for at least 72 hours prior to neuraxial block or deep plexus/peripheral block. Consider checking edoxaban or aXa activity plasma level if <72 hours (grade IIC)
There is no FDA-approved medical indication for low-dose edoxaban.
We suggest that a residual edoxaban plasma level <30 ng/mL or a residual aXa activity plasma level ≤0.1 IU/mL is acceptable prior to neuraxial block or deep plexus/peripheral block (grade IIC)

catheter: With the unanticipated administration of high dose of edoxaban with a neuraxial catheter in situ, we suggest that edoxaban dosing be withheld for at least 72 hours, or a residual edoxaban plasma level <30 ng/mL or a residual aXa activity plasma level ≤0.1 IU/mL before the catheter is removed (grade IIC)
drugs.restart: High dose: We suggest that needle placement/catheter removal occurs at least 24 hours prior to the first (postoperative) dose (grade IIC)

drugs.name: Rivaroxaban

timings.text: We suggest that a high dose of rivaroxaban be discontinued for at least 72 hours prior to neuraxial block or deep plexus/peripheral block. Consider checking rivaroxaban or aXa activity plasma level if <72 hours (grade IIC)

We suggest that a low dose of rivaroxaban be discontinued for at least 24 hours (30 hours if CrCl <30 mL/min) prior to neuraxial block or deep plexus/peripheral block. Consider checking rivaroxaban or aXa activity plasma level if <24 hours (grade IIC)
We suggest that a residual rivaroxaban plasma level <30 ng/mL or a residual aXa activity plasma level ≤0.1 IU/mL is acceptable prior to neuraxial block or deep plexus/peripheral block (grade IIC)

catheter: With the unanticipated administration of high dose of rivaroxaban with a neuraxial catheter in situ, we suggest that rivaroxaban dosing be withheld for at least 72 hours, or a residual rivaroxaban plasma level <30 ng/mL or a residual aXa activity plasma level ≤0.1 IU/mL before the catheter is removed (grade IIC)

With the unanticipated administration of low dose of rivaroxaban with a neuraxial catheter in situ, we suggest that rivaroxaban dosing be withheld for at least 24 hours (30 hours if CrCl <30 mL/min), or a residual rivaroxaban plasma level <30 ng/mL or a residual aXa activity plasma level ≤0.1 IU/mL before the catheter is removed (grade IIC)
drugs.restart: High dose: We suggest that needle placement/catheter removal occurs at least 24 hours prior to the first postoperative dose (grade IIC) Low dose: We suggest that needle placement/catheter removal occurs at least 6 hours prior to the first postoperative dose (grade IIC)

drugs.name: Dabigatran

timings.when: High dose, CrCl 50 mL/min or more
timings.text: We suggest that a high dose of dabigatran be discontinued for at least 72 hours in patients with a CrCl ≥50 mL/min prior to neuraxial block or deep plexus/peripheral block. Consider checking dabigatran plasma level if <72 hours (grade IIC)

We suggest that a high dose of dabigatran be discontinued for 120 hours in patients with a CrCl 30–49 mL/min prior to neuraxial block or deep plexus/peripheral block. Consider checking dabigatran plasma level if <120 hours (grade IIC)
We suggest against the performance of neuraxial or deep plexus/peripheral blocks in patients with a CrCl <30 mL/min unless a dabigatran plasma level is obtained and <30 ng/mL (grade IIC)

We suggest that a low dose of dabigatran be discontinued for at least 48 hours prior to neuraxial block or deep plexus/peripheral block. Consider checking dabigatran plasma level if <48 hours (grade IIC)
Prior to neuraxial block or deep plexus/peripheral block we suggest that a residual dabigatran plasma level <30 ng/mL is acceptable (grade IIC)

catheter: With the unanticipated administration of high-dose dabigatran with a neuraxial catheter in situ, we suggest that dabigatran dosing be withheld for at least 72 hours (120 hours if CrCl 30–49 mL/min) or a residual dabigatran plasma level <30 ng/mL before the catheter is removed (grade IIC)

With the unanticipated administration of low dose of dabigatran with a neuraxial catheter in situ, we suggest that dabigatran dosing be withheld for at least 48 hours, or a residual dabigatran plasma level <30 ng/mL before the catheter is removed (grade IIC)
drugs.restart: High dose: We suggest that needle placement/catheter removal occurs at least 24 hours prior to the first postoperative dose (grade IIC) Low dose: We suggest that needle placement/catheter removal occurs at least 6 hours prior to the first postoperative dose (grade IIC)

periopRules.drugClass: Antiplatelet drugs: spinal, epidural or deep block (ASRA)
periopRules.section: ASRA: spinal, epidural and deep blocks
periopRules.summary: Aspirin and NSAIDs: no added risk. Clopidogrel 5 to 7 days, prasugrel 7 to 10 days, ticagrelor 5 days.
periopRules.why: ASRA notes that aspirin affects platelet function for the life of the platelet, while other NSAIDs produce a short-term defect that normalizes within 3 days.
cautions: These are ASRA's recommendations for placing a spinal, epidural or deep plexus/peripheral block and for removing catheters. Deviation may be acceptable in the judgment of the responsible anesthesiologist, and a bloody or difficult needle placement needs a case-by-case decision.

NSAIDs alone do not significantly increase the risk of spinal hematoma. However, combination therapy with UFH, LMWH, oral anticoagulants, and thrombolytics have been demonstrated to increase the frequency of spontaneous hemorrhagic complications, bleeding at puncture sites, and spinal hematoma.

timings.text: NSAIDs appear to represent no added risk for the development of major bleeding after regional anesthetic techniques. NSAIDs (including aspirin) do not create a level of risk that will interfere with the performance of neuraxial or deep plexus/peripheral blocks. In patients receiving these medications, we do not identify specific concerns as to the timing of single-injection or catheter techniques, postoperative monitoring, or the timing of neuraxial catheter removal (grade IC)

drugs.name: Clopidogrel and prasugrel

timings.text: Based on labeling and surgical/procedural experience, the suggested time interval between discontinuation of thienopyridine therapy and needle placement is 5–7 days for clopidogrel, and 7–10 days for prasugrel (grade IIC)

catheter: Neuraxial and deep plexus/peripheral catheters should not be maintained with prasugrel due to the rapid onset. However, since the antiplatelet effect is not immediate with clopidogrel, they may be maintained for 1–2 days, provided a loading dose of the antiplatelet agent is not administered (grade IIC)
drugs.restart: Thienopyridine therapy may be resumed immediately after needle placement/catheter removal, provided a loading dose of the drugs is not administered. If a loading dose is administered, we suggest a time interval of 6 hours between catheter removal and administration (grade IIC)

drugs.name: Ticagrelor

timings.text: Based on labeling and surgical/procedural experience, the recommended time interval between discontinuation of ticagrelor therapy and needle placement is 5 days (grade 2C)

catheter: Neuraxial catheters should not be maintained with ticagrelor due to the rapid onset (grade IIC)
drugs.restart: Ticagrelor therapy may be resumed immediately after needle placement/catheter removal, provided a loading dose of the drug is not administered. If a loading dose is administered, we suggest a time interval of 6 hours between catheter removal and administration (grade IIC)

drugs.name: Cilostazol

timings.text: The risk of serious bleeding in the presence of residual cilostazol effect is unknown. Based on the elimination half-life, we suggest that needle placement be avoided for 2 days after discontinuation of cilostazol (grade IIC)

catheter: We suggest that neuraxial and deep plexus/peripheral catheters be removed prior to reinstitution of cilostazol therapy postoperatively (grade IIC)
drugs.restart: We suggest that the first postoperative dose of cilostazol be administered 6 hours after neuraxial or deep plexus/peripheral catheter removal (grade IIC)

drugs.name: Cangrelor

timings.text: The risk of serious bleeding in the presence of residual cangrelor effect is unknown. Based on the elimination half-life, we suggest that needle placement be avoided for 3 hours after discontinuation of cangrelor (grade IIC)

catheter: We suggest that neuraxial and deep plexus/peripheral catheters be removed prior to reinstitution of cangrelor therapy postoperatively (grade IIC)
drugs.restart: We suggest that the first postoperative dose of cangrelor be administered 8 hours after neuraxial or deep plexus/peripheral catheter removal (grade IIC)

drugs.name: Platelet GP IIb/IIIa inhibitors (abciximab, eptifibatide, tirofiban)

timings.text: The platelet GP IIb/IIIa inhibitors exert a profound effect on platelet aggregation. Following administration, the time to normal platelet aggregation is 24–48 hours for abciximab and 4–8 hours for eptifibatide and tirofiban. We recommend that needle placement should be avoided until platelet function—as impacted by the GP IIb/IIIa inhibitor—has recovered. Caution in patients on dual therapy who may still have residual NSAID effect (grade IC)

catheter: Postoperative. Although GP IIb/IIIa antagonists are contraindicated within 4 weeks of surgery, should one be emergently administered in the postoperative period following a neuraxial or deep plexus/peripheral technique, we recommend the neuraxial infusion should be limited to drugs minimizing sensory and motor block to facilitate assessment of neurological function and that the patient be carefully monitored neurologically (grade IC)

Timing of catheter removal is based on ongoing risk of thromboembolism and need for continued antithrombotic therapy and the potential for spinal bleeding during catheter maintenance and removal (grade IIC)

periopRules.drugClass: Thrombolytic drugs: spinal, epidural or deep block (ASRA)
periopRules.section: ASRA: spinal, epidural and deep blocks
periopRules.summary: No needle placement for at least 48 hours after thrombolytic therapy.
periopRules.why: ASRA bases these on the profound effect on hemostasis, the use of concomitant heparin and/or antiplatelet agents, and the potential for neuraxial bleeding.
cautions: These are ASRA's recommendations for placing a spinal, epidural or deep plexus/peripheral block and for removing catheters. Deviation may be acceptable in the judgment of the responsible anesthesiologist, and a bloody or difficult needle placement needs a case-by-case decision.

drugs.name: Fibrinolytic and thrombolytic drugs

timings.text: In patients scheduled to receive thrombolytic therapy, we recommend that the patient be queried, and the medical record reviewed for a recent history of lumbar puncture, spinal or epidural anesthesia, or epidural steroid injection to allow appropriate monitoring. Guidelines detailing original contraindications for thrombolytic drugs suggest avoidance of these drugs for 10 days following puncture of non-compressible vessels (grade IA)

In patients who have received fibrinolytic and thrombolytic drugs, we recommend against needle placement for at least 48 hours. Documentation of normalization of clotting studies (including fibrinogen) is suggested (grade IA)

catheter: In those patients who have received neuraxial blocks at or near the time of fibrinolytic and thrombolytic therapy, we recommend that frequent neurological monitoring (eg, every 2 hours) should be continued for at least 48 hours after the last dose. If neuraxial blocks have been combined with fibrinolytic and thrombolytic therapy and ongoing epidural catheter infusion, we recommend the infusion should be limited to drugs minimizing sensory and motor block to facilitate assessment of neurological function (grade IC)

There is no definitive recommendation for removal of neuraxial catheters in patients who unexpectedly receive fibrinolytic and thrombolytic therapy during a neuraxial catheter infusion. We suggest the measurement of fibrinogen level (one of the last clotting factors to recover) to evaluate the presence of residual thrombolytic effect and appropriate timing of catheter removal. Patients should have frequent neurological monitoring for at least 48 hours following catheter removal (grade IIC)

periopRules.summary: Continue chronic therapy through surgery; do not start one routinely, or on the day of surgery.
periopRules.why: AHA/ACC: acutely discontinuing beta blockers for long-term indications is harmful, and initiating them on the day of surgery is harmful, particularly at higher doses.

timings.text: In patients on stable doses of beta blockers undergoing NCS, beta blockers should be continued through the perioperative period as appropriate based on the clinical circumstances.

In patients scheduled for elective NCS who have a new indication for beta blockade, beta blockers may be initiated far enough before surgery (optimally >7 days) to permit assessments of tolerability and drug titration if needed.
In patients undergoing NCS and with no immediate need for beta blockers, beta blockers should not be initiated on the day of surgery due to increased risk for postoperative mortality.
Peri-operative continuation of beta-blockers is recommended in patients currently receiving this medication. (Class I, level B)
Routine initiation of beta-blocker peri-operatively is not recommended. (Class III, level A)

periopRules.why: ESC: the long-term use of statins in patients with cardiovascular disease or high risk of it is well established, while trials of starting a statin in the perioperative period are scarce.

timings.text: In patients currently on statins and scheduled for NCS, continuation of statin therapy is recommended to reduce the risk of MACE.

In statin-naïve adult patients who meet criteria for statin use based on ASCVD history or 10-year risk assessment and are scheduled for NCS, perioperative initiation of statin is recommended with intention of long-term use.
In patients already on statins, it is recommended to continue statins during the peri-operative period. (Class I, level B)

periopRules.drugClass: ACE inhibitors, ARBs and other RAAS inhibitors
periopRules.summary: The two guidelines differ by indication: continue for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction; consider withholding in hypertension or without heart failure.

timings.text: In patients on chronic RAASi for HFrEF, perioperative continuation is reasonable.
Transient discontinuation of ACEIs or ARBs before NCS in hypertensive patients should be considered. (Class IIa)
In patients without HF, withholding RAAS inhibitors on the day of NCS should be considered to prevent peri-operative hypotension. (Class IIa)

periopRules.drugClass: Antiplatelet drugs after a coronary stent (aspirin, clopidogrel, prasugrel, ticagrelor)
periopRules.summary: Keep aspirin if the bleeding risk allows; the timing of surgery and any P2Y12 interruption depend on the stent and are decided by the surgeon, anaesthesiologist and cardiologist together.
cautions: These statements are about cardiac and thrombotic risk. For the timing of a spinal, epidural or deep block, use the ASRA cards.
periopRules.why: AHA/ACC: the risk of perioperative stent thrombosis is greatest in the first 4 to 6 weeks after PCI, with excess risks that decline over time but persist to 6 months.

timings.text: In patients with prior PCI undergoing NCS, it is recommended to continue aspirin∗ (75-100 mg), if possible, to reduce the risk of cardiac events.
∗ Platelet adenosine diphosphate receptor (P2Y12) monotherapy may be considered if surgical bleeding risks are acceptable or if aspirin is not tolerated.
In patients with recent coronary artery balloon angioplasty without stent placement, elective NCS should be delayed for a minimum of 14 days to minimize perioperative MACE.
In patients with DES-PCI placed for CCD who require elective NCS with interruption of ≥1 antiplatelet agents, it is reasonable to delay surgery for ≥6 months after PCI to minimize perioperative MACE.

In patients with DES-PCI who require time-sensitive NCS with interruption of ≥1 antiplatelet agents, NCS may be considered ≥3 months after PCI if the risk of delaying surgery outweighs the risk of MACE.

In patients with CAD who require time-sensitive NCS within 30 days of PCI with BMS or <3 months of PCI with DES, DAPT should be continued unless the risk of bleeding outweighs the benefit of the prevention of stent thrombosis.
In patients with prior PCI in whom OAC monotherapy must be discontinued before NCS, aspirin should be substituted when feasible in the perioperative period until OAC can be safely reinitiated.

In select patients after PCI who have a high thrombotic risk, perioperative bridging with intravenous antiplatelet therapy may be considered <6 months after DES or <30 days after BMS if NCS cannot be deferred.

drugs.name: ESC 2022

timings.text: It is recommended to delay elective NCS until 6 months after elective PCI and 12 months after an ACS. (Class I, level A)
After elective PCI, it is recommended to delay time-sensitive NCS until a minimum of 1 month of DAPT treatment has been given. (Class I, level B)
In patients with a recent PCI scheduled for NCS, it is recommended that management of antiplatelet therapy is discussed between the surgeon, anaesthesiologist, and cardiologist. (Class I, level C)
In patients with a previous PCI, it is recommended to continue aspirin peri-operatively if the bleeding risk allows. (Class I, level B)
If interruption of P2Y12 inhibitor is indicated, it is recommended to withhold ticagrelor for 3–5 days, clopidogrel for 5 days, and prasugrel for 7 days prior to NCS. (Class I, level B)

For patients undergoing high bleeding risk surgery (e.g. intracranial, spinal neurosurgery, or vitroretinal eye surgery), it is recommended to interrupt aspirin for at least 7 days pre-operatively. (Class I, level C)

drugs.restart: If antiplatelet therapy has been interrupted before a surgical procedure, it is recommended to restart therapy as soon as possible (within 48 h) post-surgery, according to interdisciplinary risk assessment. (Class I, level C)

periopRules.summary: Routine bridging is not recommended. ESC: for minor-bleeding-risk procedures, do not interrupt the anticoagulant.
cautions: These statements are about cardiac and thrombotic risk. For the timing of a spinal, epidural or deep block, use the ASRA cards.

timings.text: In most patients with CVD who are undergoing elective NCS where OAC interruption is warranted, routine periprocedural bridging is not recommended due to increased bleeding risk.
When an urgent surgical intervention is required, it is recommended that NOAC therapy is immediately interrupted. (Class I, level C)
In minor bleeding risk surgery and other procedures where bleeding can easily be controlled, it is recommended to perform surgery without interruption of OAC therapy. (Class I, level B)
In non-minor bleeding risk procedures in patients using a NOAC, it is recommended to use an interruption regimen based on the NOAC compound, renal function, and bleeding risk. (Class I, level B)
In patients using NOACs, it is recommended that minor bleeding risk procedures are performed at trough levels (typically 12–24 h after last intake). (Class I, level C)
LMWH is recommended, as an alternative to UFH, for bridging in patients with MHVs and high surgical risk. (Class I, level B)
Bridging of OAC therapy is not recommended in patients with low/moderate thrombotic risk undergoing NCS. (Class III, level B)
Use of reduced-dose NOAC to attenuate the risk of post-operative bleeding is not recommended. (Class III, level C)

glp1Protocols.label: ASA 2023
glp1Protocols.drugRule: Consider holding daily GLP-1 on the day of the procedure and weekly GLP-1 for 1 week before, regardless of indication, dose or procedure.
glp1Protocols.fastingRule: No GLP-1-specific interval. Follow standard ASA fasting; treat urgent or emergent cases as full stomach.
glp1Protocols.distinction: Superseded: the ASA page now points to the 2024 multisociety guidance, which ASA co-authored. Precautionary withholding; the source notes there is no evidence for an optimal GLP-1 fasting duration.

glp1Protocols.label: Multisociety 2024
glp1Protocols.drugRule: Most patients continue. Defer elective care during dose escalation or until significant GI symptoms resolve; document a team decision.
glp1Protocols.fastingRule: Low risk: standard fasting. Higher risk: consider a 24 h liquid-only diet, aspiration-plan changes and trained gastric ultrasound; selected cases may be delayed.
glp1Protocols.distinction: Risk-stratified: no universal 24 h diet for every patient on a GLP-1.

glp1Protocols.label: SPAQI 2025
glp1Protocols.drugRule: Continue if there are no significant GI symptoms. Severe nausea, vomiting or inability to tolerate oral intake needs prescriber review before elective care.
glp1Protocols.fastingRule: Solids 24 h (clear liquids only); clear liquids <10% glucose 4 h and ≥10% glucose 8 h.
glp1Protocols.distinction: A distinct fixed fasting protocol for all GLP-1 patients without significant GI symptoms.

glp1Protocols.label: UK 2025
glp1Protocols.drugRule: Continue GLP-1 and dual GIP/GLP-1 therapy throughout the perioperative period.
glp1Protocols.fastingRule: Follow standard recommended fasting; no GLP-1-specific extended fast. Use individualized aspiration-risk mitigation and consider gastric ultrasound.
glp1Protocols.distinction: Most permissive fasting; rejects extra fasting for the drug alone.

glp1Protocols.label: ADS / ANZCA / GESA / NACOS 2025
glp1Protocols.drugRule: Do not routinely stop GLP-1 or dual GIP/GLP-1 therapy before the procedure.
glp1Protocols.fastingRule: 24 h clear-fluid diet, then a standard 6 h fast before the procedure, for all patients on these drugs.
glp1Protocols.distinction: A universal 24 h clear-fluid day for every patient on these drugs.

preop: Assess baseline pulmonary function (FEV1, FVC), baseline room-air oxygen saturation, sputum microbiology (colonization with Pseudomonas aeruginosa or Burkholderia cepacia), and chest physiotherapy regimen.
Coordinate preop chest physiotherapy and nebulized bronchodilators or mucolytics to clear viscous endobronchial secretions.

Screen for CF-related comorbidities: CF-related diabetes (check blood glucose and plan insulin management), cirrhosis with portal hypertension, and coagulopathy from malabsorption of fat-soluble vitamins (check PT/INR).
Continue maintenance antibiotic and pulmonary therapies without interruption.
intraop: Maintain active humidification and warming of inspired gases throughout anesthesia to prevent inspissation of mucus.
Perform thorough tracheal and bronchial suctioning under direct vision prior to extubation.
Maintain lung-protective ventilation: cautious tidal volumes with adequate expiratory time to prevent dynamic hyperinflation and auto-PEEP.
Invasive arterial line monitoring is indicated for major procedures with moderate-to-severe pulmonary impairment or blood gas monitoring.
Strict infection control and barrier precautions to prevent cross-contamination (especially with Burkholderia cepacia).
avoid: Anticholinergic drying agents (atropine, glycopyrrolate) that desiccate airway secretions and create intractable mucus plugs.
Dry, unhumidified anesthetic gas mixtures.
Heavy sedative premedication without continuous monitoring due to high risk of hypoventilation and mucus retention.
postop: Aim for early extubation in the operating room to restore spontaneous coughing and deep breathing.
Resume aggressive chest physiotherapy, postural drainage, and nebulized bronchodilators immediately in the recovery period.
Provide multimodal, opioid-sparing analgesia (regional blocks, acetaminophen) to facilitate deep breathing and prevent splinting.

preop: Assess impaired mucociliary clearance, chronic purulent sputum production, baseline bronchodilator therapy, and extent of bronchiectasis.
Evaluate for Kartagener syndrome triad (situs inversus totalis, chronic sinusitis, bronchiectasis): review chest imaging and confirm organ laterality.
In patients with dextrocardia, plan lead placement: invert left and right arm ECG leads and place precordial leads V1-V6 on the right hemithorax.
Preoperative chest physiotherapy and nebulized saline or bronchodilators to optimize airway clearance before surgery.
intraop: Utilize active warming and humidification of all inspired anesthetic gases to facilitate mucus clearance.
Be mindful of reversed vascular and cardiac anatomy if central venous cannulation or emergency thoracostomy is required.
Perform deep endotracheal suctioning prior to emergence to remove secretions accumulated during positive-pressure ventilation.
Maintain lung-protective ventilation with positive end-expiratory pressure to prevent atelectasis in dependent lung segments.
avoid: Anticholinergic medications (glycopyrrolate, atropine) that increase secretion viscosity and defeat residual cough clearance.
Prolonged periods of unhumidified mechanical ventilation.
postop: Prioritize early extubation once awake and generating adequate cough mechanics.
Resume chest physiotherapy, flutter valve therapy, and pulmonary toilet early in the recovery room.
Multimodal analgesia with regional techniques to facilitate effective coughing and deep inspiration.

preop: Multisystem granulomatous disorder: evaluate restrictive lung defect, diffusion capacity (DLCO), and baseline arterial blood gases.
Evaluate for cardiac sarcoidosis: 12-lead ECG, troponin, and echocardiogram to detect complete heart block, bundle branch blocks, malignant ventricular arrhythmias, or cardiomyopathy.
Assess airway involvement: examine for supraglottic, vocal cord, or subglottic granulomatous lesions and laryngeal stenosis that complicate tracheal intubation.
Screen for hypercalcemia (calcitriol production by granulomas) and evaluate chronic corticosteroid therapy (plan stress-dose steroids).
intraop: Prepare for potentially difficult airway: have video laryngoscopy and flexible fiberoptic intubation equipment readily available.
Continuous ST-segment and rhythm monitoring: high risk for intraoperative conduction disturbances and ventricular arrhythmias if cardiac involvement exists.
Employ lung-protective ventilation with lower tidal volumes and cautious plateau pressures to prevent barotrauma in stiff, low-compliance lungs.
Maintain normocarbia and avoid acute increases in pulmonary vascular resistance, especially in patients with associated pulmonary hypertension.
avoid: Aggressive blind or forceful airway instrumentation that could provoke bleeding from fragile granulomatous mucosal lesions.
Acidosis, hypercarbia, and hypoxemia, which precipitate acute pulmonary vasoconstriction and right ventricular strain.
postop: Continuous ECG telemetry monitoring in recovery or step-down unit if cardiac sarcoidosis is suspected.
Observe closely for post-extubation laryngeal edema or stridor when laryngeal granulomas are present.
Administer scheduled perioperative stress-dose corticosteroids as planned.

preop: Rare disease of women of childbearing age characterized by smooth muscle cell proliferation and thin-walled pulmonary cysts: evaluate baseline dyspnea, SpO2, and DLCO.
Obtain detailed history of recurrent spontaneous pneumothoraces, chylothorax, or prior pleurodesis; review recent high-resolution chest CT.
Screen for extrapulmonary manifestations, particularly renal angiomyolipomas (bleeding risk) and retroperitoneal lymphangioleiomyomas.
Continue mTOR inhibitor therapy (sirolimus) per institutional perioperative protocol.
intraop: Extremely high risk of intraoperative cyst rupture and tension pneumothorax under positive-pressure ventilation; maintain low tidal volumes, minimal peak inspiratory pressures, and low PEEP.
Nitrous oxide is strictly contraindicated: N2O diffuses rapidly into air-filled thin-walled pulmonary cysts and closed pleural spaces, causing rapid expansion and tension pneumothorax.
Have a dedicated chest thoracostomy tray and pleural drainage system immediately in the operating room.
Maintain vigilance for sudden unexplained hypotension, rising peak airway pressures, or acute hypoxemia, which signals tension pneumothorax.
avoid: Nitrous oxide (N2O) in all circumstances.
High peak inspiratory pressures, large tidal volumes, and vigorous manual bag-mask ventilation.
postop: Obtain immediate post-procedure chest radiography in PACU to rule out occult or developing pneumothorax.
Monitor for signs of chylothorax or increasing pleural effusion.
Provide regional analgesia (thoracic epidural or paravertebral block) for thoracic or upper abdominal procedures to minimize splinting without depressing respiratory drive.

preop: Assess degree of right ventricular outflow tract (RVOT) obstruction, baseline oxygen saturation, functional class, and history of hypercyanotic (tet) spells.
Maintain hydration and minimize preoperative fasting; chronic cyanosis causes secondary erythrocytosis, hyperviscosity, and coagulopathy, increasing thrombosis risk.
Continue beta-adrenergic blockers through morning of surgery to prevent infundibular spasm.
Infective endocarditis prophylaxis indicated for unrepaired cyanotic disease, residual defects adjacent to prosthetic patches, or first 6 months post-repair.
intraop: Maintain systemic vascular resistance (SVR) and avoid tachycardia or hypovolemia; maintain Qp:Qs balance.
Ketamine is preferred for IV induction as it preserves SVR and maintains pulmonary blood flow.
Avoid increases in pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR): maintain high inspired oxygen, normocarbia or mild hypocarbia, normothermia, and avoid high mean airway pressures or excessive PEEP.
Meticulous air bubble precautions on all intravenous lines: right-to-left shunting risks paradoxical systemic embolization and stroke.

Treat acute hypercyanotic spell: 100% inspired oxygen, knee-chest positioning (increases SVR), IV fluid bolus, phenylephrine to raise SVR, and beta blockade (esmolol) or morphine to relieve infundibular spasm.
avoid: Decreases in SVR (systemic vasodilation), which aggravate right-to-left shunting and precipitate profound hypoxemia.
Factors increasing PVR: hypoxia, hypercarbia, acidosis, hypothermia, high peak inspiratory pressures.
Sympathomimetics with strong beta-1 agonist activity (isoproterenol, epinephrine) that increase inotropy and worsen infundibular muscular spasm.
Air bubbles in all intravenous lines.
postop: Admit to monitored telemetry or ICU setting for observation of right ventricular dysfunction, dysrhythmias, and bleeding.
Ensure adequate analgesia to prevent agitation-induced catecholamine surges and infundibular spasm.
Right bundle branch block (RBBB) is nearly universal following surgical repair; monitor for heart blocks and ventricular ectopy.

preop: Evaluate pulmonary artery pressures, resting cyanosis and oxygen saturation, right ventricular function on echocardiogram, and baseline hematocrit.
High perioperative mortality (10% to 25%); elective noncardiac surgery should be performed at an adult congenital heart disease center.
Avoid dehydration: secondary erythrocytosis and hyperviscosity severely predispose to microvascular thrombosis.
Continue pulmonary vasodilator therapy (endothelin receptor antagonists, phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors, prostacyclins) up to surgery.
intraop: Goal is strict preservation of SVR: any drop in SVR increases right-to-left shunting across the fixed pulmonary vascular bed and worsens critical hypoxemia.
Invasive arterial pressure monitoring is mandatory before induction; place with de-airing filters.
Maintain intravascular volume and RV preload while avoiding acute volume overload that precipitates acute RV failure.
General anesthesia with slow, titrated high-opioid or ketamine-based technique is preferred over neuraxial sympathectomy.
Avoid systemic vasodilation: treat hypotension immediately with phenylephrine or vasopressin to maintain SVR greater than PVR.
avoid: Drops in systemic vascular resistance (SVR) or sudden systemic hypotension.
Spinal anesthesia or dense bilateral epidural sympathectomy due to precipitous afterload reduction.
Elevations in PVR: hypoxia, hypercapnia, acidosis, atelectasis, hypothermia, or high PEEP.
Air bubbles in any IV line: fatal paradoxical systemic or cerebral embolization.
postop: Maintain mandatory ICU monitoring for at least 48 to 72 hours; hemodynamic instability and sudden death most commonly occur in the early postoperative period.
Provide multimodal analgesia: untreated pain increases sympathetic PVR, while excessive sedation causes hypoventilation, hypercarbia, and pulmonary vasoconstriction.
Early ambulation and pneumatic compression devices to prevent deep vein thrombosis.

preop: Differentiate surgical history: arterial switch operation (anatomic repair) versus older atrial switch (Mustard or Senning atrial inversion) or congenitally corrected (L-TGA).
In atrial switch, the morphologic right ventricle serves as the systemic pump and is prone to systemic RV failure, tricuspid regurgitation, and sinus node dysfunction.
Review recent echocardiography to evaluate systemic ventricular ejection fraction, outflow tract obstruction, and baffle leaks or stenosis.
Endocarditis prophylaxis required if residual defects or prosthetic materials are present.
intraop: Maintain sinus rhythm and AV synchrony: loss of atrial kick in systemic RV failure causes significant cardiac output reduction.
In arterial switch patients, monitor for myocardial ischemia: coronary arteries were reimplanted and may develop stenosis or kinking.
Maintain adequate systemic preload and contractility; support systemic right ventricle with inotropes (milrinone, dobutamine) and cautious vasoconstrictors if indicated.
Meticulous de-airing of all intravenous lines if residual shunts or baffle leaks exist.
avoid: Tachyarrhythmias or loss of sinus rhythm, which severely compromise systemic ventricular filling.
Excessive afterload or severe hypertension when a systemic right ventricle is present.
Hypovolemia and sudden myocardial depressant anesthetic doses.
postop: Postoperative ICU or step-down telemetry monitoring for bradyarrhythmias, junctional rhythms, or heart block.
Maintain cautious fluid balance to prevent systemic RV volume overload and congestive heart failure.

preop: Identify stage of surgical palliation: Stage 1 (Norwood), Stage 2 (Glenn / bidirectional cavopulmonary shunt), or Stage 3 (completed Fontan).
In single-ventricle Fontan physiology, pulmonary blood flow is completely passive and depends entirely on low PVR, adequate transpulmonary pressure gradient, and central venous pressure.
Assess for single RV dysfunction, protein-losing enteropathy, plastic bronchitis, and hepatic congestion or fibrosis.
Maintain adequate hydration during fasting to preserve preload required for passive pulmonary flow.
intraop: Maintain sinus rhythm, euvolemia, and adequate systemic preload: single ventricle cannot compensate for hypovolemia.
Avoid high positive-pressure ventilation, high mean airway pressures, and excessive PEEP, which obstruct passive non-pulsatile pulmonary blood flow in Fontan circulation.
Extubate early or maintain spontaneous or pressure-supported ventilation when feasible to facilitate negative intrathoracic pressure.
Invasive arterial monitoring is recommended; central venous pressure (CVP) reflects pulmonary perfusion pressure in Fontan patients.
avoid: Elevated mean airway pressures, excessive PEEP, and prolonged positive-pressure inspiration.
Dehydration or acute decreases in venous return.
Hypercarbia, acidosis, and hypoxia, which increase PVR and halt passive pulmonary blood flow.
Air bubbles in all intravenous lines (risk of direct cerebral paradoxical embolus).
postop: ICU or HDU admission with continuous hemodynamic and pulse oximetry monitoring.
Early extubation to restore negative-pressure breathing and optimize cardiac output.
Maintain meticulous fluid balance; avoid fluid overload causing ascites or pleural effusions.

preop: Obtain 12-lead ECG and calculate corrected QT interval (QTc = QT / sqrt(RR)); QTc > 470 ms in men or > 480 ms in women is prolonged, with > 500 ms conferring high risk of Torsades de Pointes.
Identify LQT subtype if known: LQT1 (triggered by exercise/sympathetic surge), LQT2 (triggered by auditory stimuli/startle), LQT3 (triggered by bradycardia/sleep).
Continue beta-blocker therapy without interruption up to the time of surgery; have IV beta-blocker (esmolol) available.
Check and aggressively correct serum potassium (target at or above 4.0 mEq/L) and magnesium (target at or above 2.0 mg/dL).
Interrogate implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) if present: disable antitachycardia therapy before surgery and ensure external defibrillator pads are placed.
intraop: Attach external defibrillation pads and ensure IV magnesium sulfate is immediately at hand in the operating room.
Provide smooth induction with adequate anesthetic depth and analgesia to prevent sympathetic catecholamine surges.
Maintain normothermia, normal electrolyte balance, and normal acid-base status.

If Torsades de Pointes occurs: administer IV magnesium sulfate, initiate overdrive pacing (or isoproterenol in bradycardia-dependent LQT3), and perform unsynchronized defibrillation if hemodynamically unstable.
avoid: QTc-prolonging drugs: ondansetron, droperidol, haloperidol, metoclopramide, amiodarone, sotalol, procainamide.
Volatile anesthetics that significantly prolong QTc (sevoflurane and isoflurane prolong QTc; propofol TIVA is preferred).
Ketamine and ephedrine (sympathetic stimulation triggers arrhythmias in LQT1 and LQT2).
Sudden acoustic or sensory stimulation during induction and emergence.
Hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, hypocalcemia, and hypothermia.
postop: Continuous ECG telemetry monitoring until full recovery and resumption of oral beta-blocker therapy.
Reactivate ICD antitachycardia/shock therapy in the recovery room before discharge from PACU.
Maintain multimodal, opioid-sparing analgesia with smooth awakening to prevent emergence sympathetic surges.

preop: Assess for history of syncope, nocturnal agonal respiration, aborted sudden cardiac death, or family history of sudden death.
Review 12-lead ECG for characteristic coved-type ST-segment elevation at or above 2 mm in V1-V2 followed by negative T wave (Type 1 Brugada pattern).
Identify and discontinue any Brugada-triggering home medications (BrugadaDrugs.org database).
Ensure strict normothermia: fever is the most potent trigger for unmasking Brugada ECG changes and ventricular fibrillation.
Place external defibrillation pads before induction in all symptomatic or high-risk patients.
intraop: Aggressively treat and prevent hypothermia and hyperthermia; maintain normothermia with active warming.
Ensure immediate availability of isoproterenol and an external biphasic defibrillator.
Use continuous ST-segment monitoring in leads V1 to V3.
Short-duration propofol for induction is acceptable, but prolonged propofol infusions must be avoided.
If ventricular tachycardia or fibrillation develops: prompt defibrillation and infusion of isoproterenol (increases L-type calcium current) or quinidine.
avoid: Class IC antiarrhythmics (flecainide, propafenone) and Class IA agents (procainamide).
High-dose or prolonged propofol infusions (Brugada-like ECG and fatal arrhythmias reported in propofol infusion syndrome).
Local anesthetics in excessive doses: bupivacaine, levobupivacaine, ropivacaine, and lidocaine (potent sodium channel blockers).
Ketamine and tramadol.
Alpha-adrenergic agonists, beta-blockers, and vagotonic drugs that unmask the ST elevation.
Hyperthermia (fever) and electrolyte shifts (hypokalemia, hyperkalemia).
postop: Continuous 12-lead telemetry monitoring in PACU or ICU for at least 24 hours.
Aggressive antipyretic therapy (acetaminophen) immediately at the earliest sign of temperature elevation.
Re-interrogate and reactivate ICD before discharge from monitored environment.

preop: Assess history of palpitations, syncope, prior catheter ablation, and presence of antegrade accessory pathway conduction.
Review ECG for short PR interval (<120 ms), widened QRS, and delta wave.
Continue antiarrhythmic therapy (Class IC such as flecainide, or Class III such as amiodarone) through morning of surgery.
Place defibrillator/cardioversion pads prior to induction in patients with history of pre-excited atrial fibrillation.
intraop: Maintain hemodynamic stability and avoid sympathetic stimulation (light anesthesia, pain, hypovolemia) that enhances accessory pathway conduction.
Maintain normothermia and normal electrolyte concentrations.
If orthodromic AVRT (narrow complex) occurs: vagal maneuvers, adenosine, or synchronized cardioversion.

If pre-excited atrial fibrillation (wide, irregular QRS tachycardia) occurs: immediate synchronized DC cardioversion is the treatment of choice; IV procainamide is the drug of choice for stable patients.
avoid: AV nodal blocking agents in pre-excited atrial fibrillation: digoxin, diltiazem, verapamil, beta-blockers, and adenosine. Blocking the AV node diverts all conduction down the accessory pathway, causing ventricular fibrillation and cardiac arrest.
Sympathomimetic agents that increase adrenergic tone: ketamine, pancuronium, ephedrine, epinephrine.
Histamine-releasing drugs and hypovolemia that provoke reflex tachycardia.
postop: Continuous telemetry monitoring in PACU until fully awake and stable.
Smooth emergence and effective postoperative pain control to prevent catecholamine-triggered tachyarrhythmias.

preop: Recognize clinical presentation: acute chest pain or dyspnea mimicking acute myocardial infarction, typically preceded by severe emotional or physical stress.
Echocardiogram typically shows transient apical ballooning with basilar hypercontractility; coronary angiography demonstrates absence of obstructive coronary disease.
Assess for left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT) obstruction and moderate-to-severe mitral regurgitation (from systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve).
Delay elective surgery until left ventricular systolic function recovers (typically 4 to 8 weeks).
intraop: Minimize emotional and physical stress with adequate preoperative anxiolysis and smooth induction.
Invasive arterial monitoring and intraoperative echocardiography (TEE) are recommended for major surgery.
If dynamic LVOT obstruction is present: treat hypotension with volume expansion and pure alpha-1 agonists (phenylephrine); avoid inotropes.
Maintain normovolemia, normothermia, and deep surgical anesthesia.
If cardiogenic shock without LVOT obstruction occurs: cautious inotropic support or mechanical circulatory support (intra-aortic balloon pump / Impella).
avoid: Exogenous catecholamines (epinephrine, norepinephrine, dopamine, dobutamine, isoproterenol), which worsen myocardial toxicity and apical ballooning.
Inotropes in the presence of dynamic LVOT obstruction (increases obstruction and worsens hypotension).
Hypovolemia and vasodilators (reduce LV filling and aggravate systolic anterior motion).
Light anesthesia, inadequate analgesia, and emergence tachycardia.
postop: ICU or step-down telemetry monitoring until hemodynamic stability is verified.
Monitor for heart failure, pulmonary edema, mural thrombus formation, and ventricular arrhythmias.
Provide smooth extubation and excellent multimodal analgesia to prevent postoperative catecholamine surges.

preop: Assess onset of heart failure in late pregnancy or within 5 months postpartum in the absence of other identifiable causes.
Review echocardiogram for left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF < 45%), LV chamber dilation, and mural thrombi.
Evaluate functional NYHA class, signs of fluid overload, and orthopnea.
High risk of thromboembolism due to ventricular akinesis combined with the hypercoagulable postpartum state; assess anticoagulation status.
Continue heart failure medications (beta-blockers, hydralazine/nitrates, diuretics); avoid ACE inhibitors and ARBs before delivery due to fetotoxicity.
intraop: Goals are optimization of myocardial contractility, afterload reduction, and careful preload maintenance.
For cesarean delivery, carefully titrated incremental epidural or combined spinal-epidural (CSE) anesthesia provides beneficial afterload reduction while preventing sudden hypotension.
Invasive arterial monitoring is recommended for severe ventricular dysfunction (LVEF < 35%).
Have inotropes (milrinone, dobutamine) and vasopressors ready for immediate hemodynamic support.
avoid: Myocardial depressant drugs in high concentrations.
Single-shot high-dose spinal anesthesia due to sudden, uncompensated venodilation and profound hypotension.
Fluid overload: postpartum auto-transfusion from uterine involution can precipitate acute flash pulmonary edema.
Ergometrine and methylergonovine for uterine atony (induce severe coronary vasoconstriction and hypertension); oxytocin must be given as a slow dilute infusion.
postop: Mandatory ICU monitoring for at least 24 to 48 hours postpartum; autotransfusion during this window is the peak danger period for acute decompensation.
Restart anticoagulation postpartum once hemostasis is secure.
Advise on long-term follow-up; persistent LV dysfunction carries high maternal mortality in subsequent pregnancies.

preop: Systemic necrotizing vasculitis of medium and small arteries: evaluate multiorgan involvement including kidneys (renal failure, renovascular hypertension), heart (coronary arteritis, myocarditis), nervous system (mononeuritis multiplex), and GI tract.
Assess baseline renal function, blood urea nitrogen, creatinine, electrolytes, and urinalysis (proteinuria/hematuria).
Assess cardiac status: 12-lead ECG, troponin, and echocardiogram to detect subclinical coronary arteritis or myocardial ischemia.
Document preexisting peripheral motor and sensory neuropathies before regional anesthesia.
Evaluate chronic corticosteroid and immunosuppressive therapy (cyclophosphamide, azathioprine); plan stress-dose steroids.
intraop: Maintain tight blood pressure control: labile hypertension and renovascular stenosis predispose to end-organ ischemia and intracranial hemorrhage.
Invasive arterial pressure monitoring is indicated for major procedures; assess collateral circulation (Allen test) prior to radial cannulation.
Maintain normovolemia and avoid renal hypoperfusion.
Protective padding of all pressure points and careful patient positioning to protect vulnerable nerves from compression neuropathies.
avoid: Hypotension, which precipitates visceral, coronary, and renal microvascular infarction.
Severe hypertension, which risks rupture of microaneurysms and tissue hemorrhage.
Nephrotoxic medications (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides) in patients with existing renal vasculitis.
postop: Monitor renal output, creatinine, and electrolytes closely in recovery.
Maintain stress-dose corticosteroid coverage as planned.
Carefully assess neurologic status to detect new-onset mononeuritis multiplex.

preop: Progressive stenosis of terminal internal carotid arteries with fragile basal collateral vessels: review stroke and TIA history.
Identify triggers for transient ischemia: crying, hyperventilation, dehydration, hypotension, and pain.
Maintain liberal hydration before surgery; continue antiplatelet therapy unless surgical bleeding risk strictly prohibits.
intraop: Maintain strict normocarbia (EtCO2 35 to 40 mmHg): avoid hyperventilation (causes cerebral vasoconstriction and infarction) and severe hypoventilation (causes intracerebral steal).
Maintain baseline or slightly elevated mean arterial pressure to sustain flow through high-resistance collaterals.
Ensure deep surgical anesthesia and aggressive analgesia to prevent sympathetic surges and hyperventilation.
Maintain normothermia and normal hematocrit (target 30% to 35% for optimal cerebral oxygen delivery without hyperviscosity).
avoid: Hyperventilation and hypocapnia (potent cerebral vasoconstrictors).
Systemic hypotension and hypovolemia.
Agitation, pain, or crying during induction and emergence.
postop: Admit to neuro-ICU for continuous neurological checks and tight blood pressure titration.
Maintain aggressive multimodal analgesia to prevent postoperative hyperventilation and crying.
Continue generous IV hydration through the recovery period.

preop: Herniation of cerebellar tonsils through foramen magnum: evaluate for signs of brainstem compression, syringomyelia, and elevated intracranial pressure.
Screen for lower cranial nerve dysfunction: dysphagia, depressed gag reflex, vocal cord weakness, and central sleep apnea.
Review cervical spine and posterior fossa neuroimaging for extent of tonsillar descent.
intraop: Avoid extreme neck flexion or extension during laryngoscopy and positioning: cervical manipulation can cause acute brainstem or cervicomedullary compression.
Employ smooth induction with adequate depth and muscle relaxation to prevent coughing, bucking, or straining that raises intracranial pressure.
Use video laryngoscopy or flexible fiberoptic intubation to minimize cervical spine motion.
Neurophysiologic monitoring (somatosensory and motor evoked potentials) is commonly indicated for posterior fossa decompression.
avoid: Neck hyperflexion or hyperextension during airway management and prone or sitting positioning.
Coughing, straining, or sudden increases in intrathoracic pressure on induction and emergence.
High positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) or hypercapnia that elevates ICP.
postop: Observe closely in ICU for central respiratory depression, apneas, and vocal cord dysfunction.
Assess swallowing function and gag reflex before initiating oral intake (high aspiration risk).

preop: Autosomal dominant neurocutaneous disorder: evaluate for central nervous system tubers (refractory epilepsy, cognitive impairment, subependymal giant cell astrocytomas).
Screen for cardiac rhabdomyomas with echocardiogram (may cause outflow tract obstruction, pre-excitation, or ventricular arrhythmias; typically regress with age).
Assess for renal angiomyolipomas (bleeding risk) and pulmonary lymphangioleiomyomatosis in adult females.
Continue home antiepileptic medications up to the morning of surgery.
intraop: Maintain anticonvulsant coverage and avoid anesthetic agents that precipitate seizure activity.
Prepare for sudden intraoperative arrhythmias or ventricular outflow obstruction if cardiac rhabdomyomas are present.
Employ lung-protective low-pressure ventilation if cystic pulmonary lesions exist.
avoid: Anesthetic agents that lower seizure threshold (enflurane, meperidine).
Ketamine in patients with intracranial lesions or elevated ICP.
Excessive peak airway pressures in patients with cystic pulmonary disease.
postop: Continuous ECG telemetry in recovery if cardiac rhabdomyomas or conduction defects exist.
Resume oral antiepileptic medications as early as feasible.

preop: Evaluate for neurofibromas involving the upper airway (tongue, posterior pharyngeal wall, larynx) causing difficult airway anatomy.
Screen for associated undiagnosed pheochromocytoma (1% to 2% prevalence in NF-1): check blood pressure and history of headaches/palpitations.
Assess for spinal deformities (severe kyphoscoliosis) and cervical spine neurofibromas prior to positioning or neuraxial procedures.
intraop: Prepare for difficult endotracheal intubation: have video laryngoscopy and fiberoptic equipment available.

Expect unpredictable responses to neuromuscular blockers: patients may demonstrate normal response or sensitivity to succinylcholine, and either marked sensitivity or resistance to nondepolarizing agents.
Use quantitative neuromuscular monitoring throughout.
Place arterial line if severe kyphoscoliosis or suspected pheochromocytoma is present.
avoid: Blind or forceful airway instrumentation that could traumatize vascular neurofibromas.
Unmonitored muscle relaxant dosing without train-of-four monitoring.
Overlooking hypertension that could signify an occult pheochromocytoma.
postop: Observe closely in PACU for airway edema or stridor following extubation.
Perform detailed documentation of neurological status.

preop: Progressive autosomal dominant neurodegenerative disorder: assess degree of choreiform movements, dysphagia, and chronic malnutrition.
High risk of pulmonary aspiration due to pharyngeal muscle incoordination and impaired protective airway reflexes.
Review psychiatric medications and continue neuroleptics if indicated.
intraop: Rapid sequence induction or aspiration prophylaxis is recommended.
Altered response to neuromuscular blockers: sensitivity to both succinylcholine (prolonged apnea reported) and nondepolarizing relaxants (delayed recovery).
Increased sensitivity to IV induction agents: titrate propofol slowly to prevent profound hypotension.
Employ quantitative neuromuscular monitoring to confirm complete reversal.
avoid: Dopamine receptor antagonists (metoclopramide, droperidol, haloperidol, phenothiazines) that aggravate chorea and extrapyramidal symptoms.
Full doses of neuromuscular blocking agents without objective twitch monitoring.
postop: Observe closely for post-extubation aspiration; nurse with head-of-bed elevation.
Ensure complete reversal of neuromuscular blockade before extubation.

preop: Document all preexisting motor, sensory, visual, and autonomic deficits thoroughly before surgery.
Screen for autonomic dysfunction (labile blood pressure, resting tachycardia, gastroparesis) and respiratory muscle weakness.
Evaluate chronic baclofen, corticosteroid, or immunosuppressive therapy.
Inform the patient that perioperative relapses can occur regardless of the anesthetic technique chosen.
intraop: Maintain strict normothermia: an increase in core body temperature as small as 0.5 degrees C can block conduction across demyelinated axons (Uhthoff phenomenon) and trigger clinical relapse.
Succinylcholine is strictly contraindicated: causes life-threatening hyperkalemia due to denervation-induced proliferation of extrajunctional acetylcholine receptors.
Response to nondepolarizing muscle relaxants is variable: patients may exhibit resistance or prolonged weakness; monitor quantitatively.
Spinal anesthesia has been associated with disease exacerbation due to local anesthetic neurotoxicity on demyelinated fibers; epidural and peripheral nerve blocks are considered safe.
avoid: Hyperthermia (even mild core temperature elevation).
Succinylcholine in all stages of disease (risk of lethal hyperkalemia).
Spinal (intrathecal) anesthesia when alternatives (general, epidural, peripheral block) are available.
postop: Active temperature management: treat any postoperative fever or shivering promptly with antipyretics and active cooling.
Monitor for respiratory weakness and bulbar insufficiency in advanced disease.
Continue perioperative corticosteroid coverage if chronically administered.

preop: Mitochondrial myopathy triad: progressive external ophthalmoplegia, pigmentary retinopathy, and progressive cardiac conduction block before age 20.
Review 12-lead ECG and echocardiogram: high risk of sudden progression to complete atrioventricular heart block and syncope.
Assess pacemaker status if present; ensure external pacing capability is ready in the operating room.
Check baseline serum lactate and glucose.
intraop: Have transcutaneous or transvenous cardiac pacing immediately available in the room.
Extreme sensitivity to volatile anesthetics, IV induction agents, and nondepolarizing muscle relaxants.
Avoid prolonged infusions of propofol, which impairs mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation.
Avoid lactate-containing IV solutions (Lactated Ringer) to prevent worsening metabolic lactic acidosis.
Maintain normothermia: shivering dramatically increases oxygen consumption and precipitates metabolic decompensation.
avoid: Lactated Ringer solution and lactate-containing fluids.
Succinylcholine (risk of hyperkalemia).
Prolonged propofol infusions.
Hypothermia, shivering, and prolonged fasting.
postop: Continuous ECG telemetry monitoring in recovery or step-down unit for progressive heart block.
Monitor arterial blood gases and serum lactate levels.

preop: Massive uninhibited sympathetic response in spinal cord injury at or above T6 triggered by cutaneous or visceral stimulation below the lesion (bladder distension, bowel dilation, surgical stimulation).
Review history of autonomic crises (severe headache, facial flushing, profuse sweating above lesion, cutis anserina).
Check baseline blood pressure; patients typically run low resting blood pressure (systolic 90 to 100 mmHg).
intraop: Establish deep general anesthesia or dense spinal anesthesia: both reliably block the afferent sensory pathway that initiates the reflex arc.
Invasive arterial pressure monitoring is essential for real-time detection and treatment of severe paroxysmal hypertension.
Have rapid-acting vasodilators immediately drawn up and connected to IV line: sodium nitroprusside, nicardipine, nitroglycerin, or phentolamine.
Expect compensatory reflex bradycardia from intact baroreceptor vagal stimulation during hypertensive surges.
avoid: Light general anesthesia during bladder, pelvic, or lower extremity manipulation.
Succinylcholine after the first 24 to 48 hours post-injury through at least 6 to 12 months or indefinitely (causes lethal hyperkalemia).
Obstructed or full urinary bladder: confirm urinary catheter is draining freely throughout.
postop: Ensure urinary catheter patency before leaving the OR; bladder distension is the most common postoperative trigger.
Maintain arterial blood pressure monitoring in PACU, as wound pain, vaginal packing, or surgical drains can provoke delayed episodes.

preop: Progressive degeneration of upper and lower motor neurons: evaluate bulbar involvement (dysphagia, dysarthria, high aspiration risk).
Assess pulmonary function: forced vital capacity (FVC < 50% predicts nocturnal hypoventilation and high risk of postop respiratory failure).
Discuss postoperative ventilatory expectations and advanced directives regarding noninvasive ventilation or intubation.
intraop: Succinylcholine is strictly contraindicated: causes massive, potentially fatal hyperkalemia from widespread lower motor neuron denervation.
Marked sensitivity to nondepolarizing muscle relaxants: small doses produce profound and prolonged paralysis; titrate with quantitative monitoring.
Whenever possible, avoid neuromuscular blockers entirely by using volatile agents or remifentanil for intubation and maintenance.
Maintain aspiration precautions with cuffed tube.
avoid: Succinylcholine under all circumstances.
Standard doses of nondepolarizing muscle relaxants.
High doses of long-acting opioids or sedatives that precipitate respiratory failure.
postop: Plan for early noninvasive ventilation (BiPAP) or prolonged mechanical ventilation if FVC is severely compromised.
