High risk of postoperative atelectasis and pulmonary aspiration; nurse with head elevated.

preop: Autosomal recessive spinocerebellar degeneration: assess for prominent hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (present in up to 90% of patients).
Review echocardiogram for symmetric or asymmetric ventricular hypertrophy and outflow tract obstruction.
Review 12-lead ECG for T-wave inversions, ST abnormalities, and bundle branch blocks.
Evaluate restrictive pulmonary disease secondary to thoracic kyphoscoliosis.
intraop: Manage hemodynamics according to hypertrophic cardiomyopathy principles: maintain adequate preload, afterload, and normal sinus rhythm.
Avoid drops in systemic vascular resistance or hypovolemia that worsen dynamic left ventricular outflow tract obstruction.
Succinylcholine is contraindicated due to risk of hyperkalemia from muscle degeneration.
Titrate nondepolarizing muscle relaxants carefully with objective twitch monitoring.
avoid: Succinylcholine.
Sympathomimetics with strong inotropic activity (epinephrine, isoproterenol) and vasodilators that worsen dynamic LVOT obstruction.
Hypovolemia and tachycardia.
postop: Continuous ECG telemetry monitoring for atrial and ventricular arrhythmias.
Monitor respiratory mechanics and pulmonary function in patients with severe scoliosis.

preop: Neurodegenerative disorder combining parkinsonism, cerebellar ataxia, and severe central autonomic failure (Shy-Drager syndrome).
Assess for profound orthostatic hypotension, laryngeal stridor (from vocal cord abductor paralysis), and central sleep apnea.
Review medications: continue antiparkinsonian agents and fludrocortisone or midodrine.
intraop: Invasive arterial pressure monitoring is essential: expect profound hypotension upon induction, positive-pressure ventilation, and position changes.
Denervation supersensitivity: direct-acting vasopressors (phenylephrine, norepinephrine) produce an exaggerated hypertensive response; dilute and titrate carefully.
Loss of baroreceptor reflexes blunts compensatory tachycardia.
Inspect vocal cords during direct laryngoscopy: bilateral abductor paralysis can present as laryngeal stridor or difficult airway.
avoid: Indirect-acting vasopressors (ephedrine) due to depleted endogenous norepinephrine stores.
Spinal or dense epidural anesthesia (causes severe, refractory hypotension).
Rapid postural changes and hypovolemia.
postop: Observe closely in PACU for post-extubation laryngeal stridor and upper airway obstruction.
High risk of postoperative aspiration and orthostatic syncope; continue invasive arterial monitoring.

preop: Excessive heart rate increase (at least 30 bpm) upon standing in the absence of orthostatic hypotension: evaluate resting volume status and heart rate.
Patients are frequently chronically hypovolemic: administer liberal intravenous crystalloid hydration prior to surgery.
Continue home medications (fludrocortisone, midodrine, beta-blockers, ivabradine) as planned.
intraop: Maintain generous intravascular volume expansion to preserve venous return and ventricular preload.
Avoid light anesthesia, inadequate analgesia, or rapid emergence that provokes severe sinus tachycardia.
Use phenylephrine rather than ephedrine if vasopressor support is needed, to avoid exacerbating tachycardia.
avoid: Hypovolemia and prolonged preoperative fasting without IV hydration.
Vagolytic drugs (atropine, pancuronium) and beta-agonists.
Histamine-releasing drugs that cause peripheral vasodilation and reflex tachycardia.
postop: Maintain intravenous fluid hydration until oral fluid intake is fully established.
Apply lower-extremity compression stockings and avoid sudden head-up posture changes.
Multimodal analgesia to prevent pain-induced sympathetic tachycardia.

preop: Extra-adrenal chromaffin cell tumor (carotid body, glomus jugulare, or retroperitoneal sympathetic chain): determine whether tumor is catecholamine-secreting.
If secretory, manage identically to pheochromocytoma with alpha-adrenergic blockade for at least 1 to 2 weeks followed by beta-blockade if tachycardic.
For carotid body tumors, evaluate cranial nerve function (cranial nerves IX, X, XII) and collateral cerebral blood flow.
intraop: For functional tumors, place an arterial line before induction and have sodium nitroprusside, phentolamine, and esmolol ready for hypertensive surges during manipulation.
Manipulation of the carotid bifurcation can trigger profound bradycardia or hypotension from the carotid sinus reflex: infiltrate with local anesthetic.
Expect sudden hypotension after tumor vein ligation or resection: volume expand and titrate norepinephrine or vasopressin.
avoid: Beta-adrenergic blockade before adequate alpha-adrenergic blockade in secretory tumors.
Vigorous uncoordinated tumor palpation before vascular control.
Histamine-releasing drugs in catecholamine-secreting tumors.
postop: Monitor for neck hematoma and airway compromise following head and neck paraganglioma resection.
Assess cranial nerve function (swallowing, vocal cord movement, tongue deviation).
Monitor blood glucose closely if secretory (rebound hypoglycemia from acute catecholamine withdrawal).

preop: Autosomal recessive disorder affecting autonomic and sensory neurons: history of episodic autonomic crises (hypertension, tachycardia, diaphoresis, vomiting).
Assess for chronic dehydration, recurrent aspiration pneumonias, and thoracic kyphoscoliosis.
Corneal anesthesia and absent tearing: requires vigilant eye protection.
intraop: Marked hemodynamic lability: profound hypotension with induction agents and blunted response to surgical stimulation.
Blunted ventilatory response to hypoxia and hypercapnia.
Direct-acting vasopressors should be titrated in small dilute doses due to receptor denervation hypersensitivity.
Apply generous ophthalmic lubricating ointment and tape eyes closed securely to prevent corneal ulceration.
avoid: Hypovolemia and sudden position changes.
Indirect-acting sympathomimetics (ephedrine).
Corneal abrasion (absent lacrimation and corneal reflex).
postop: Admit to ICU for hemodynamic monitoring and control of autonomic crises (treated with diazepam, clonidine).
High risk of postoperative hypoventilation, aspiration, and hypothermia.

preop: Hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy: assess degree of distal muscle weakness, foot deformities, and loss of deep tendon reflexes.
Evaluate for associated thoracic kyphoscoliosis and restrictive pulmonary impairment in advanced cases.
Document baseline peripheral neuropathies thoroughly before regional anesthesia.
intraop: Succinylcholine is contraindicated due to the risk of hyperkalemia from chronic denervation.
Response to nondepolarizing muscle relaxants is variable: patients may exhibit prolonged blockade or heightened sensitivity; quantitative twitch monitoring is mandatory.
Ensure meticulous protective padding of all bony prominences and peripheral nerve pathways.
Neuraxial and peripheral nerve blocks have been performed safely, but require careful documentation of preexisting deficits.
avoid: Succinylcholine (risk of hyperkalemia).
Unmonitored muscle relaxant administration.
Excessive pressure or stretch on peripheral nerves during positioning.
postop: Ensure complete reversal of neuromuscular blockade before extubation.
Reassess and document postoperative motor and sensory examination.

preop: Acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy: assess ascending motor weakness, cranial nerve involvement, and forced vital capacity.
Evaluate for severe autonomic instability (cardiac arrhythmias, wide swings between severe hypertension and profound hypotension).
Review recent treatment: intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) or plasma exchange.
intraop: Succinylcholine is strictly contraindicated: causes massive, potentially fatal hyperkalemic cardiac arrest due to widespread denervation-induced receptor upregulation; contraindication lasts for months to years.
Expect extreme hemodynamic instability: exaggerated hypotensive response to anesthetic agents, positive-pressure ventilation, and position changes.
Denervation supersensitivity: direct vasopressors (phenylephrine, norepinephrine) produce exaggerated pressor responses; titrate cautiously.
Place an arterial line for continuous blood pressure monitoring in active or severe disease.
avoid: Succinylcholine under all circumstances.
High doses of direct-acting vasopressors or vasodilators.
Volatile anesthetic overdose causing refractory hypotension.
postop: High incidence of postoperative mechanical ventilation: extubate only after objective criteria for respiratory strength are fulfilled.
Continuous ECG telemetry in ICU for life-threatening arrhythmias and autonomic instability.

preop: X-linked recessive dystrophin deficiency: assess for progressive dilated cardiomyopathy (present in virtually all patients over age 18) with echocardiogram and 12-lead ECG.
Evaluate restrictive pulmonary disease: progressive scoliosis and diaphragm weakness lead to nocturnal hypoventilation and reduced cough clearance.
High risk of chronic aspiration due to pharyngeal weakness and delayed gastric emptying.
intraop: Succinylcholine is strictly contraindicated: causes massive rhabdomyolysis, hyperkalemic cardiac arrest, and intractable ventricular fibrillation.

Avoid volatile halogenated anesthetics: can trigger anesthesia-induced rhabdomyolysis (AIR), which clinically mimics malignant hyperthermia with hyperkalemia, elevated creatine kinase, and cardiac arrest.
Total intravenous anesthesia (TIVA) with propofol, opioids, and remifentanil is the technique of choice.
Marked sensitivity to nondepolarizing muscle relaxants: duration of action is significantly prolonged; titrate with quantitative twitch monitoring.
avoid: Succinylcholine under all circumstances.
Volatile halogenated anesthetics (risk of anesthesia-induced rhabdomyolysis and hyperkalemic arrest).
Standard doses of nondepolarizing neuromuscular blockers.
postop: Admit to ICU or monitored step-down unit for respiratory monitoring and serial evaluation of cardiac function and urine for myoglobinuria.
High incidence of postoperative pulmonary atelectasis and acute gastric dilatation.
Use multimodal, opioid-sparing analgesia to prevent respiratory depression.

preop: Milder allelic form of dystrophinopathy: skeletal muscle weakness is slower, but severe dilated cardiomyopathy can occur early and disproportionately.
Review echocardiogram for left ventricular ejection fraction and regional wall motion abnormalities.
Review 12-lead ECG and evaluate baseline pulmonary function.
intraop: Succinylcholine is strictly contraindicated: precipitates massive rhabdomyolysis, acute hyperkalemia, and cardiac arrest.
Avoid volatile halogenated anesthetics due to risk of rhabdomyolysis; total intravenous anesthesia is strongly preferred.
Careful titration of fluid and anesthetic depth in the presence of dilated cardiomyopathy.
Nondepolarizing muscle relaxants exhibit prolonged action; monitor quantitatively.
avoid: Succinylcholine.
Volatile halogenated anesthetics.
Myocardial depressant drugs in high concentrations.
postop: Continuous ECG telemetry in recovery/step-down unit.
Monitor serum potassium and check urine for myoglobinuria if rhabdomyolysis is suspected.

preop: Heterogeneous group of muscular dystrophies primarily affecting shoulder and pelvic girdles: evaluate for associated cardiomyopathy (frequent in LGMD1B, LGMD2C-F).
Assess for restrictive pulmonary defect from diaphragm and intercostal muscle involvement.
Review 12-lead ECG and echocardiogram.
intraop: Succinylcholine is contraindicated due to risk of rhabdomyolysis and hyperkalemic cardiac arrest.
Increased sensitivity and prolonged recovery with nondepolarizing muscle relaxants; use quantitative twitch monitoring.
Consider total intravenous anesthesia (TIVA) to minimize myocardial depression.
Position carefully with padding to protect weak, atrophic muscle groups.
avoid: Succinylcholine.
Unmonitored muscle relaxant dosing.
Prolonged periods of unmonitored respiratory depression.
postop: Observe respiratory rate and tidal volume closely before extubation.
Monitor for delayed emergence and residual muscle weakness in PACU.

preop: Autosomal dominant dystrophy with progressive weakness of facial, scapular, and upper arm musculature.
Assess for respiratory muscle involvement and thoracic kyphoscoliosis; check baseline PFTs if dyspneic.
Evaluate for cardiac arrhythmias and retinal telangiectasias (Coat syndrome).
intraop: Succinylcholine is avoided due to potential risk of hyperkalemia.
Heightened sensitivity to nondepolarizing muscle relaxants; monitor train-of-four quantitatively.
Vigilant eye protection: weakness of orbicularis oculi causes incomplete eyelid closure, predisposing to corneal exposure and ulceration.
avoid: Succinylcholine.
Inadequate eye taping and corneal exposure.
Excessive muscle relaxant dosing.
postop: Ensure complete reversal of neuromuscular blockade before tracheal extubation.
Apply ophthalmic lubrication to prevent dry eye and exposure keratopathy.

preop: Late-onset progressive dystrophy characterized by ptosis, dysphagia, and proximal limb weakness.
Severe dysphagia leads to chronic aspiration risk, frequent pulmonary infections, and malnutrition.
Evaluate swallowing mechanics, pulmonary history, and baseline nutritional status.
intraop: Rapid sequence induction or awake intubation is indicated for aspiration protection.
Increased sensitivity to nondepolarizing muscle relaxants; titrate cautiously with twitch monitor.
Use short-acting anesthetic agents to ensure rapid return of protective airway reflexes at emergence.
avoid: Full doses of nondepolarizing muscle relaxants without twitch monitoring.
Extubation before full return of consciousness and intact airway reflexes.
postop: Maintain head-of-bed elevation in the postoperative period.
Keep aspiration precautions active until oral intake is evaluated.

preop: Triad of early contractures (elbows, Achilles tendons, posterior cervical spine), slowly progressive muscle weakness, and cardiac disease.
High incidence of life-threatening cardiac conduction defects (complete heart block, atrial standstill, ventricular arrhythmias) and dilated cardiomyopathy.
Interrogate pacemaker or ICD if implanted; ensure external pacing capability is immediately ready.
Assess cervical spine mobility: posterior neck contractures frequently cause severe restriction of neck extension and difficult intubation.
intraop: Prepare for difficult airway management (video laryngoscopy, flexible bronchoscope) due to rigid cervical spine.
Succinylcholine is strictly contraindicated (risk of hyperkalemia and rhabdomyolysis).
Continuous cardiac rhythm monitoring: have transcutaneous pacing pads placed and external defibrillator in the room.
Titrate anesthetic agents cautiously to avoid depressing an already compromised myocardium.
avoid: Succinylcholine.
Forceful cervical spine extension during airway manipulation.
High concentrations of negative inotropic anesthetic agents.
postop: Continuous ECG telemetry in ICU or cardiac step-down unit.
Verify pacemaker function and monitor for delayed cardiac conduction blocks.

preop: Look for cardiomyopathy and conduction disease: first-degree heart block is common, and complete heart block can cause sudden death.
Assess respiratory muscle weakness. Pharyngeal and chest wall weakness raise aspiration risk; central sleep apnea and hypersomnolence add to sensitivity to sedatives.
Many patients reach surgery with the myotonia unrecognized.
intraop: Keep the patient warm and prevent shivering: cold and shivering trigger myotonia.
TIVA may be preferable to volatile agents, which can aggravate cardiomyopathy and conduction problems. Expect increased sensitivity to propofol, opioids and benzodiazepines.
The response to nondepolarizing relaxants is normal, but existing weakness may make them unnecessary, which also avoids neostigmine.

Myotonic contraction from surgical handling or diathermy is not relieved by relaxants or general or regional anesthesia; local anesthetic infiltration of the muscle, phenytoin, quinine or procainamide may help (quinine and procainamide can worsen conduction).
Epidural anesthesia is considered safe.
avoid: Succinylcholine: it can cause prolonged myotonia that relaxants and anesthesia cannot reverse.
Other myotonia triggers: methohexital, etomidate, neostigmine, hypothermia, and mechanical or electrical stimulation.
postop: Watch breathing closely: weak respiratory muscles add to any residual opioid, benzodiazepine or propofol effect. Perioperative complications are mainly cardiopulmonary.

preop: Congenital myopathy with characteristic rod-like structures in skeletal muscle: evaluate for dysmorphic facial features (micrognathia, high-arched palate) that predict difficult intubation.
Assess for disproportionate weakness of respiratory and bulbar muscles; obtain baseline PFTs and room-air saturation.
Screen for cardiomyopathy and skeletal deformities (scoliosis, pectus excavatum).
intraop: Prepare for difficult airway management with video laryngoscopy or fiberoptic intubation.
Succinylcholine is contraindicated due to reports of abnormal contractures and hyperkalemia.
Marked sensitivity to nondepolarizing muscle relaxants: prolonged paralysis is common; monitor quantitatively.
Volatile anesthetics can induce profound myocardial depression in affected patients.
avoid: Succinylcholine.
Blind or traumatic airway instrumentation.
Standard doses of nondepolarizing neuromuscular blockers.
postop: High rate of postoperative ventilatory failure: extubate only after full recovery of airway reflexes and respiratory mechanics.
Plan for monitored ICU care with access to noninvasive or invasive ventilatory support.

preop: Skeletal muscle chloride channel (CLCN1) mutation causing muscle stiffness after voluntary contraction that improves with repetition (warm-up phenomenon); absence of cardiomyopathy.
Assess severity of stiffness; continue home antimyotonic therapy (mexiletine, carbamazepine).
Check serum electrolytes and confirm absence of baseline weakness.
intraop: Maintain strict normothermia throughout: cold exposure and shivering are potent triggers for generalized, sustained myotonic contracture.
Succinylcholine is strictly contraindicated: produces severe, generalized contracture that can prevent mask ventilation and endotracheal intubation.

Nondepolarizing muscle relaxants do not abolish myotonic spasms induced by direct mechanical stimulation or electrocautery; local anesthetic infiltration at the surgical site can help relax the muscle.
Regional anesthesia (epidural, spinal, peripheral blocks) is safe and effective.
avoid: Succinylcholine under all circumstances.
Hypothermia, cold irrigation fluids, and post-extubation shivering.
Neostigmine: anticholinesterases increase acetylcholine concentration at the motor endplate and can provoke severe myotonia.
postop: Ensure active warming continues in PACU until normothermia is verified.
Provide effective analgesia to prevent shivering and muscle contracture.

preop: Skeletal muscle sodium channel (SCN4A) mutation characterized by cold-induced myotonia that paradoxically worsens with exercise (paradoxical myotonia), followed by flaccid muscle weakness.
Identify history of temperature sensitivity and episodes of potassium-induced weakness; continue mexiletine.
Check baseline serum potassium and electrolytes.
intraop: Maintain active patient warming, warmed IV fluids, and warm operating room ambient temperature.
Succinylcholine is strictly contraindicated: triggers massive myotonic contracture and hyperkalemia.
Nondepolarizing relaxants do not relieve paramyotonic spasms; neostigmine can exacerbate myotonia.
Avoid potassium-containing IV fluids.
avoid: Cold operating room environment, unheated IV fluids, and hypothermia.
Succinylcholine.
Neostigmine for reversal; use sugammadex if rocuronium or vecuronium was administered.
Potassium-containing intravenous solutions.
postop: Maintain diligent active warming in recovery room until normal core temperature is sustained.
Monitor serum potassium and muscle strength closely.

preop: Identify disease subtype: hypokalemic (CACNA1S mutation; triggered by carbohydrate meals, rest after exercise, cold, and stress) versus hyperkalemic (SCN4A mutation; triggered by fasting, cold, stress, and potassium intake).
Check baseline serum potassium, sodium, and magnesium.
Continue home medications (acetazolamide, potassium supplements or potassium-sparing diuretics) as indicated.
intraop: Maintain strict normothermia: hypothermia and shivering trigger paralytic attacks in both types.
In hypokalemic periodic paralysis: avoid glucose-containing IV fluids and beta-2 adrenergic agonists (which drive potassium intracellularly); monitor potassium closely.
In hyperkalemic periodic paralysis: avoid potassium-containing fluids (Lactated Ringer) and prolonged fasting; maintain a mild glucose infusion to stimulate insulin-mediated potassium uptake.
Succinylcholine is contraindicated in both types: can trigger profound hyperkalemia or sustained contracture.
Titrate nondepolarizing muscle relaxants cautiously with quantitative twitch monitoring.
avoid: Succinylcholine in all forms of periodic paralysis.
Hypothermia and post-anesthetic shivering.
In hypokalemic: large glucose infusions, beta-2 agonists, and potassium-wasting diuretics.
In hyperkalemic: potassium-containing IV fluids, prolonged fasting, and metabolic acidosis.
postop: Serial monitoring of serum potassium levels in PACU.
Maintain active patient warming and aggressive pain management to prevent stress-induced attacks.

preop: Congenital myopathy linked to ryanodine receptor (RYR1) gene mutations: strongly associated with malignant hyperthermia susceptibility.
Must be managed under strict Malignant Hyperthermia Susceptible precautions: prepare clean machine, trigger-free anesthetic, and verify dantrolene availability.
Evaluate for musculoskeletal deformities: progressive kyphoscoliosis, congenital hip dislocation, and joint laxity.
intraop: Trigger-free anesthetic technique: total intravenous anesthesia (propofol, opioids) or regional anesthesia.
Prepare anesthesia workstation: flush machine per protocol, remove vaporizers, change carbon dioxide absorbent, and install activated charcoal filters.
Monitor continuously for signs of acute MH crisis: unexplained tachycardia, rising end-tidal CO2, mixed acidosis, and hyperthermia.
Nondepolarizing muscle relaxants may show increased sensitivity; monitor quantitatively.
avoid: All volatile halogenated anesthetics: sevoflurane, desflurane, isoflurane.
Succinylcholine.
postop: Observe in PACU or ICU for at least 12 to 24 hours for signs of delayed-onset malignant hyperthermia or rhabdomyolysis.
Ensure crisis protocol and dantrolene remain accessible.

preop: Congenital myopathy characterized by centrally located nuclei in muscle fibers: evaluate for severe generalized weakness, ptosis, and ophthalmoplegia.
High prevalence of severe restrictive respiratory disease and diaphragmatic weakness; assess baseline nocturnal ventilatory dependence.
Review pulmonary function and history of chronic aspiration.
intraop: Prepare for potentially difficult airway management.
Succinylcholine is contraindicated due to risk of rhabdomyolysis and hyperkalemic response.
Extreme sensitivity to nondepolarizing muscle relaxants: marked prolongation of paralysis; avoid relaxants if feasible or use minimal doses with sugammadex reversal.
Volatile anesthetics can cause significant myocardial depression in severe cases.
avoid: Succinylcholine.
Standard doses of nondepolarizing muscle relaxants.
Heavy sedative premedication without ventilatory support.
postop: High incidence of postoperative ventilatory failure: plan for postoperative mechanical ventilation in ICU.
Extubate only when objective criteria for respiratory muscle strength and gas exchange are met.

preop: Defects in mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation: evaluate multiorgan involvement including cardiomyopathy, cardiac conduction blocks, epilepsy, and diabetes mellitus.
Assess baseline serum lactate and blood glucose; avoid prolonged preoperative fasting.
Continue anticonvulsants and cofactors (coenzyme Q10, carnitine) as prescribed.
intraop: Increased sensitivity to volatile anesthetics, IV induction agents, and muscle relaxants.
Avoid prolonged or high-dose propofol infusions: propofol inhibits mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation and can trigger propofol infusion syndrome or severe lactic acidosis.
Avoid lactate-containing IV solutions (Lactated Ringer) to prevent worsening metabolic acidosis; use normal saline or balanced non-lactate solutions with glucose.
Maintain strict normothermia: shivering dramatically elevates cellular metabolic demand.
avoid: Prolonged propofol infusions.
Lactated Ringer solution and lactate-containing fluids.
Succinylcholine (risk of hyperkalemia).
Hypothermia, shivering, and prolonged fasting.
postop: Monitor serial arterial blood gases, serum lactate, and blood glucose in PACU.
Continuous ECG telemetry monitoring for cardiac conduction abnormalities.

preop: Tell the patient they may stay intubated and ventilated after surgery.
After transsternal thymectomy, the need for ventilation correlated with disease longer than 6 years, pyridostigmine above 750 mg a day, vital capacity below 2.9 L and COPD unrelated to myasthenia.
Bulbar weakness brings a high aspiration risk. Look for associated thyroid and other autoimmune disease.
Infection, electrolyte disturbance, stress, surgery and some antibiotics (especially aminoglycosides) can worsen weakness.
intraop: Patients are very sensitive to nondepolarizing relaxants: if one is needed, reduce the initial dose by one-half to two-thirds and titrate with a nerve stimulator.
Patients are resistant to succinylcholine (ED95 about 2.6 times normal), but usual doses still usually give adequate intubating conditions.
Intubation is often possible without a relaxant, and volatile agents can reduce or remove the need for one.
After rocuronium, sugammadex may reverse more reliably than neostigmine with glycopyrrolate.
avoid: Nondepolarizing relaxants in usual doses or without neuromuscular monitoring.
Opioids for maintenance where possible: their respiratory effects can last into recovery.
postop: Delay extubation until respiratory function is clearly good: strength can seem adequate early and fall again a few hours later.
Plan postoperative ventilation for patients who meet the risk criteria.

preop: Presynaptic disorder with autoantibodies against P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channels: proximal muscle weakness that transiently improves with exercise.
Strongly associated with small cell lung cancer (up to 60% of cases): evaluate for underlying malignancy.
Assess autonomic symptoms (orthostatic hypotension, dry mouth, impaired sweating); continue 3,4-diaminopyridine (amifampridine) or pyridostigmine.
intraop: Extreme, life-threatening sensitivity to BOTH succinylcholine AND nondepolarizing muscle relaxants.

A small dose of nondepolarizing relaxant can produce profound paralysis lasting for hours; attempt tracheal intubation without muscle relaxants (using propofol/remifentanil or volatile agent) whenever possible.
Quantitative neuromuscular monitoring (train-of-four) is mandatory.
Expect autonomic lability with exaggerated hypotension on induction.
avoid: Succinylcholine and standard doses of nondepolarizing muscle relaxants.
Aminoglycoside and polymyxin antibiotics (block presynaptic calcium channels and precipitate severe neuromuscular block).
Calcium channel blockers and magnesium infusions unless strictly indicated.
postop: High incidence of postoperative ventilatory failure and delayed extubation: monitor in ICU or step-down setting.
Reverse with sugammadex if rocuronium was used, but continue close observation as weakness may recur.

preop: Ask about family history: a silent porphyria can present for the first time after a triggering drug.
Examine and record any neuropathy and autonomic instability, especially before a regional block.
Keep fasting short; if a long fast is unavoidable, give a glucose-containing infusion, because caloric restriction can precipitate an attack.
Decide before surgery which drug in each class you may need (antibiotics, antihypertensives, antiarrhythmics and others) is safe. The American Porphyria Foundation keeps a drug database.
intraop: Regional anesthesia is not contraindicated, and no local anesthetic is known to have triggered an attack; watch for hypotension with autonomic neuropathy or hypovolemia.

Propofol is well tolerated for induction. Nitrous oxide, isoflurane, sevoflurane and desflurane are considered safe, as are most IV opioids, depolarizing and nondepolarizing relaxants and their reversal drugs.
Benzodiazepines, proton pump indicators and H2 blockers can be used before surgery.
Expect blood pressure lability from autonomic dysfunction.
Several possible triggers together are more dangerous than any single drug.
avoid: Barbiturates (thiopental, methohexital), etomidate and ketamine.
Ketorolac, amiodarone and many calcium channel blockers (check each one before giving it).
postop: If an attack is suspected, watch skeletal muscle strength and cranial nerve function: weakness warns of respiratory failure and aspiration. Postoperative ventilation is rarely needed.
Ondansetron or scopolamine for PONV; codeine, oxycodone, hydrocodone, acetaminophen and many NSAIDs for pain. Tramadol has insufficient evidence.
Treating a crisis: remove triggers, hydrate, give carbohydrate, correct electrolytes including magnesium, and give IV heme early in a severe attack.

preop: X-linked deficiency of hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HPRT) with hyperuricemia, choreoathetosis, spasticity, and compulsive self-mutilation.
Evaluate renal function: uric acid nephrolithiasis and obstructive uropathy are common complications.
Assess severe involuntary athetoid movements, spastic contractures, and missing teeth or oral trauma from chronic self-biting.
Continue allopurinol or febuxostat to suppress uric acid formation; maintain generous hydration before induction.
intraop: Aspiration prophylaxis is indicated due to pharyngeal incoordination, dysphagia, and poor airway protection.
Prone to autonomic instability with exaggerated swings in blood pressure and heart rate during surgical stimulation.
Positioning requires meticulous padding given joint contractures, skeletal deformities, and involuntary athetoid spasms.
Normal response to succinylcholine and nondepolarizing neuromuscular blockers, but monitor with train-of-four to avoid overdosing.
Maintain liberal intravenous hydration to ensure high urinary flow and prevent uric acid precipitation in renal tubules.
avoid: Dehydration and metabolic acidosis: both strongly promote uric acid crystallization and acute obstructive renal failure.
Traumatic airway instrumentation: dentition may be fragile or damaged, and oral mucosa is easily lacerated.
Prolonged physical restraint without adequate pharmacological sedation: triggers severe distress, autonomic surges, and self-harm behavior.
postop: Ensure smooth emergence with adequate sedation and analgesia to prevent acute agitation and self-injurious biting behaviors.
Apply protective mouthguard or padded arm restraints during recovery in accordance with established patient protocol.
Continue generous intravenous hydration until oral fluid intake is fully established.
Multimodal analgesia with antiemetics to prevent distress and retching.

preop: Autosomal recessive disorder of iron overload causing parenchymal iron deposition in liver, heart, pancreas, and endocrine glands.
Screen for iron-overload cardiomyopathy: restrictive or dilated cardiomyopathy, diastolic dysfunction, conduction blocks, and arrhythmias.
Assess liver involvement: transaminases, bilirubin, albumin, INR, and evaluate for cirrhosis and portal hypertension.
Screen for diabetes mellitus ("bronze diabetes") from pancreatic islet damage, as well as hypopituitarism and adrenal insufficiency.
Review therapeutic phlebotomy history, serum ferritin levels, and echocardiographic ventricular function.
intraop: Titrate anesthetic agents cautiously in patients with cardiac dysfunction; avoid myocardial depressants and large drops in systemic vascular resistance.
Invasive arterial pressure monitoring is indicated if significant cardiomyopathy or advanced cirrhosis is present.
Maintain cardiac preload and sinus rhythm: restrictive cardiomyopathy tolerates tachycardia and loss of atrial contribution poorly.
Account for altered drug clearance in hepatic cirrhosis: use neuromuscular blockers with organ-independent elimination (cisatracurium).
Monitor blood glucose closely during prolonged cases because of impaired islet function and erratic glycogen stores.
avoid: Myocardial depressants and excessive vasodilators in patients with restrictive or dilated cardiomyopathy.
Hepatotoxic medications and high doses of acetaminophen in patients with hepatic cirrhosis.
Excessive fluid administration in patients with restrictive ventricular physiology and diastolic heart failure.
postop: Continuous telemetry monitoring for conduction disturbances, supraventricular arrhythmias, and ventricular dysrhythmias.
Monitor blood glucose closely with insulin sliding scale; avoid severe hyperglycemia or hypoglycemia.
Optimize fluid balance to prevent pulmonary edema or hepatorenal syndrome.

preop: Autosomal recessive defect in ATP7B copper transport leading to toxic copper accumulation in liver, basal ganglia, and cornea.
Assess hepatic function: degree of fibrosis or cirrhosis, portal hypertension, ascites, and coagulopathy (platelets, INR, fibrinogen).
Evaluate neurological and bulbar involvement: dysarthria, dysphagia, saliva pooling, tremor, choreiform movements, and dystonia.
Continue copper-chelating agents (penicillamine, trientine) or zinc therapy; check for penicillamine-induced bone marrow suppression or myasthenia-like weakness.
Review baseline renal function: copper deposition can produce renal tubular acidosis and aminoaciduria.
intraop: High aspiration risk due to pharyngeal dystonia and impaired protective airway reflexes: consider rapid sequence induction or cuffed tube.
Titrate anesthetic agents cautiously considering reduced hepatic clearance and altered protein binding.
Nondepolarizing neuromuscular blockers: use quantitative train-of-four monitoring; prefer cisatracurium or rocuronium with sugammadex readiness.
Maintain hepatic perfusion: avoid severe systemic hypotension, hypovolemia, or excessive positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP).
avoid: Hepatotoxic medications and drugs extensively cleared by hepatic microsomal enzymes in patients with liver decompensation.
Dopamine receptor antagonists (droperidol, metoclopramide, phenothiazines): strongly exacerbate extrapyramidal symptoms and dystonia.
Hypothermia and shivering: severely worsens tremor, rigidity, and basal ganglia movement disorders.
postop: Assess airway reflexes, vocal cord function, and swallowing ability before extubation and oral intake.
Monitor for postoperative hepatic decompensation, encephalopathy, and coagulopathy in the surgical intensive care unit.
Provide antiemetics that do not block dopamine receptors (5-HT3 antagonists such as ondansetron).

preop: Start alpha blockade first (phenoxybenzamine most often; prazosin or doxazosin are alternatives). Aim for normal blood pressure, relief of symptoms and resolution of ST-T changes and arrhythmias. The best duration is unknown: 3 days to 2 weeks or longer.
Add a beta blocker only after alpha blockade, for heart rate above 120 or arrhythmias.
Phenoxybenzamine has been stopped 24 to 48 hours before surgery to avoid vascular unresponsiveness after the tumor is removed.
Correct hypovolemia. A calcium channel blocker or metyrosine can be added in resistant cases.
intraop: Place an arterial line before induction. A central venous line is usually enough; a PA catheter or TEE helps with very active tumors or cardiac involvement.

Expect systolic pressure above 200 mmHg during pneumoperitoneum and tumor handling even after alpha blockade. Have nitroprusside (the agent of choice), phentolamine, nitroglycerin, labetalol, esmolol and magnesium ready.
Expect hypotension after the tumor veins are ligated: a large positive fluid balance and vasopressors are usually needed, and the response to vasopressors may be blunted. Lightening anesthesia helps.
Treat ventricular arrhythmias with lidocaine or a beta blocker such as esmolol.
Minimize fear, stress, pain, shivering, hypoxia and hypercarbia: all release catecholamines.
avoid: A nonselective beta blocker before alpha blockade: unopposed alpha vasoconstriction can cause a hypertensive crisis.
Histamine releasers (morphine, atracurium).
Vagolytic or sympathomimetic drugs: atropine, ketamine, pancuronium, succinylcholine.
postop: Check blood glucose: insulin rises after resection and hypoglycemia can occur.
Give glucocorticoids after bilateral adrenalectomy or when hypoadrenalism is possible.

About half of patients stay hypertensive for several days, because catecholamines take 7 to 10 days to normalize. If hypertension persists, consider a missed tumor, renal ischemia or essential hypertension.

preop: Neuroendocrine tumor of pancreatic beta cells producing unregulated insulin secretion: presents with fasting hypoglycemia and neuroglycopenic symptoms.
Maintain continuous intravenous dextrose infusion (5% or 10% dextrose) to keep blood glucose between 80 and 120 mg/dL prior to surgery.
Review medical therapy: diazoxide suppresses insulin release but causes fluid retention; octreotide may be used preoperatively.
Assess cardiovascular status: recurrent hypoglycemia triggers intense adrenergic surges that can cause myocardial ischemia or arrhythmias.
intraop: Place an arterial line for frequent serial arterial blood glucose measurements (every 15 to 30 minutes throughout the case).
Maintain continuous dextrose infusion and titrate based on serial glucose readings; general anesthesia completely masks neurovegetative signs of hypoglycemia.
Anticipate a rapid rebound increase in blood glucose (often exceeding 150 mg/dL) within 30 to 60 minutes after successful tumor resection or vein ligation.
If glucose fails to rise after presumed tumor removal, suspect incomplete resection or multiple ectopic adenomas.
avoid: Unchecked hypoglycemia: general anesthesia masks all clinical warning signs (sweating, tachycardia, tremors, pupillary dilation).
Beta-adrenergic antagonists if possible: blunts autonomic counter-regulatory tachycardia and glucose mobilization during hypoglycemia.
Abrupt discontinuation of dextrose infusion prior to tumor resection.
postop: Rebound hyperglycemia is common following tumor excision due to chronic suppression of normal beta cells; manage conservatively with small insulin doses.
Continue serial blood glucose monitoring every 1 to 2 hours until normal glycemic regulation is firmly established.
Monitor for surgical complications including pancreatic leak, acute pancreatitis, and intra-abdominal hemorrhage.

preop: Excess glucocorticoids resulting in central obesity, systemic hypertension, hypokalemic alkalosis, hyperglycemia, muscle wasting, and capillary fragility.
Airway evaluation: anticipate difficult mask ventilation and intubation from short thick neck, prominent fat pads, obesity, and obstructive sleep apnea.
Control hypertension and correct hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis preoperatively using spironolactone, potassium supplements, or steroid synthesis inhibitors.
Assess bone and skin fragility: high risk of pathological fractures, severe bruising, and skin avulsion from minor trauma.
intraop: Anticipate difficult airway: have video laryngoscopy, ramped positioning, and advanced airway equipment readily available.
Meticulous positioning and padding: protect all bony prominences and nerve sites to avoid fractures and pressure ulcers.
Careful handling of skin and veins: gentle tape removal, soft dressings, and careful blood pressure cuff application to avoid hematomas and tears.
Skeletal muscle weakness and hypokalemia increase sensitivity to neuromuscular blockers: titrate nondepolarizing agents with train-of-four monitoring.
Strict aseptic technique: hypercortisolism causes significant immunosuppression and high surgical site infection risk.
avoid: Rough positioning or excessive torque on extremities and spine: high risk of osteoporotic fractures.
Aggressive adhesives or adhesive tapes directly on thin, fragile skin.
Uncorrected hypokalemia before induction: increases risk of cardiac arrhythmias and prolonged neuromuscular block.
postop: Postoperative adrenal insufficiency occurs immediately after curative resection (hypophysectomy or adrenalectomy): initiate stress-dose steroid coverage.
Monitor closely for upper airway obstruction and respiratory failure; nurse in semi-upright position with CPAP support if indicated for OSA.
High incidence of deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism: implement early mechanical and chemical thromboprophylaxis.

preop: Autonomous aldosterone hypersecretion from adrenal adenoma or bilateral hyperplasia causing sodium retention, potassium wasting, and hypertension.
Control hypertension and normalize serum potassium preoperatively: spironolactone or eplerenone with oral potassium supplementation.
Check ECG for hypokalemic manifestations: flattened T waves, prominent U waves, ST depression, prolonged QT interval, and ventricular arrhythmias.
Assess intravascular volume: hypervolemia with diastolic hypertension is characteristic; evaluate for end-organ hypertensive damage.
intraop: Monitor serum potassium and acid-base status intraoperatively with serial arterial blood gas analyses.
Avoid hyperventilation: respiratory alkalosis drives potassium into cells, sharply exacerbating hypokalemia and precipitating arrhythmias.
Hypokalemia potentiates nondepolarizing neuromuscular blockade: titrate relaxants carefully with quantitative train-of-four monitoring.
Expect hemodynamic swings during laparoscopic adrenalectomy during pneumoperitoneum and tumor manipulation.
avoid: Hyperventilation and respiratory alkalosis: acute hypocapnia dangerously drops serum potassium levels.
Potassium-free intravenous fluids when uncorrected hypokalemia persists.
Nephrotoxic agents, particularly if chronic hypertension has impaired baseline renal function.
postop: Monitor serum potassium and blood pressure closely: transient hyperkalemia can occur post-adrenalectomy due to chronic suppression of contralateral adrenal cortex.
Discontinue spironolactone and potassium supplementation immediately following unilateral adrenalectomy.
Temporary mineralocorticoid replacement (fludrocortisone) is rarely needed unless bilateral adrenalectomy was performed.

preop: Growth hormone excess causing skeletal overgrowth, macroglossia, laryngeal soft tissue hypertrophy, glottic narrowing, and obstructive sleep apnea.
Airway evaluation: major predictor of difficult mask ventilation and difficult intubation; hypertrophied epiglottis and thickened vocal cords narrow glottis.
Screen for severe obstructive sleep apnea and daytime hypersomnolence; evaluate baseline arterial blood gases if hypoventilation is suspected.
Cardiovascular evaluation: concentric biventricular hypertrophy, diastolic and systolic heart failure, hypertension, and conduction disturbances.
Check endocrine status: secondary diabetes mellitus, thyroid dysfunction, and anterior pituitary hormone deficiencies.
Evaluate for peripheral nerve entrapment (carpal tunnel syndrome): may compromise radial artery catheterization.
intraop: Prepare for difficult airway: video laryngoscopy, flexible fiberoptic bronchoscope, and smaller-than-predicted endotracheal tubes (subglottic aperture is narrowed).
Preoxygenate meticulously; preserve spontaneous ventilation until the airway is secured if anatomical difficulty is suspected.
Place an arterial line for invasive pressure monitoring during transsphenoidal resection: test collateral ulnar flow before radial artery cannulation.
Position carefully with generous padding: peripheral nerves are unusually susceptible to compression injury.
avoid: Selecting oversized endotracheal tubes: hypertrophy of vocal cords and subglottic mucosa necessitates smaller tube sizes (e.g., 6.5 to 7.0 mm).
Blind nasal intubation or aggressive nasal instrumentation: enlarged turbinates bleed easily; nasal route is contraindicated if transsphenoidal surgery is planned.
Administering full doses of neuromuscular blockers before verifying ability to mask ventilate.
postop: High risk of acute postoperative airway obstruction: extubate fully awake, in upright position, after complete neuromuscular reversal.
Continuous pulse oximetry and CPAP support for patients with underlying obstructive sleep apnea; avoid excessive opioid sedation.
Monitor fluid balance, urine output, and serum sodium for diabetes insipidus or SIADH following transsphenoidal pituitary surgery.
Provide glucocorticoid replacement if anterior pituitary insufficiency or hypophysectomy occurs.

preop: Inherited defect in globin chain synthesis causing microcytic hemolytic anemia, ineffective erythropoiesis, and iron overload.
Distinguish minor (mild microcytic anemia, usually asymptomatic) from major or intermedia (transfusion-dependent with severe anemia and hemochromatosis).
Airway assessment: severe beta-thalassemia major causes maxillary hypertrophy, malocclusion, and prominent malar bones leading to difficult mask ventilation and intubation.
Cardiovascular evaluation: screen for iron-overload cardiomyopathy, arrhythmias, and pulmonary hypertension; check serum ferritin and echocardiogram.
Target preoperative hemoglobin: optimize to 9 to 10 g/dL for major surgery with packed red blood cell transfusion.
intraop: Anticipate difficult airway: have video laryngoscopy and fiberoptic equipment prepared.
Maintain cardiac output and oxygen delivery: patients tolerate tachycardia and myocardial depression poorly if iron cardiomyopathy is present.
Gentle positioning and padding: chronic marrow expansion causes significant osteopenia and risk of pathological fractures.
Minimize surgical blood loss; have crossmatched blood readily available in the operating room.
avoid: Severe hypoxemia, acidosis, and hypothermia: impairs oxygen-carrying capacity and shifts oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve unfavorably.
Forceful airway manipulation or excessive pressure on fragile maxillary structures and dentition.
Unmonitored fluid overload in patients with iron-induced ventricular dysfunction.
postop: Monitor hematocrit and tissue oxygenation; transfuse packed red blood cells to maintain target hemoglobin levels.
Provide continuous pulse oximetry and supplemental oxygen during early recovery.
Resume iron chelation therapy once renal function and oral intake normalize.

preop: Autosomal dominant red cell membrane defect (spectrin, ankyrin) causing spherical, fragile erythrocytes trapped and destroyed in the spleen.
Clinical presentation includes hemolytic anemia, unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia, splenomegaly, and pigmented gallstones.
Check baseline hemoglobin, reticulocyte count, unconjugated bilirubin, and spleen size (often presenting for splenectomy or cholecystectomy).
Verify post-splenectomy immunization status (Pneumococcus, Meningococcus, Hib) at least 2 weeks before elective splenectomy.
Screen for aplastic crisis history (often provoked by parvovirus B19 infection) or folate deficiency.
intraop: Avoid hypothermia, severe acidosis, and circulatory stasis that worsen red cell fragility and accelerate splenic destruction.
Maintain generous intravenous hydration and renal perfusion to prevent pigment nephropathy from acute hemolysis.
Splenectomy carries significant bleeding risk: establish large-bore intravenous access and verify blood product availability.
Monitor for platelet count rebound and surgical hemostasis following splenic vein ligation.
avoid: Hypothermia and profound metabolic acidosis: exacerbates erythrocyte fragility and splenic sequestration.
Hypovolemia or inadequate diuresis if acute hemolysis occurs (risk of renal tubular damage from free hemoglobin).
postop: Monitor hemoglobin, bilirubin, and platelet count: reactive thrombocytosis is common post-splenectomy; initiate VTE prophylaxis.
Educate on overwhelming post-splenectomy infection (OPSI) risk and emergency fever protocols.
Maintain intravenous hydration to flush hemoglobin breakdown products and ensure robust urine output.

preop: X-linked recessive enzymatic defect impairing NADPH generation, leaving erythrocytes vulnerable to oxidative stress and acute hemolytic anemia.
Screen for history of acute hemolytic crises, dark urine, or favism after oxidative drug exposures or infections.
Check baseline CBC, reticulocyte count, renal function, and bilirubin levels.
Strict review of perioperative medications to exclude known oxidative triggers.
intraop: Maintain normothermia, adequate oxygenation, and normocarbia; treat surgical stress and infections aggressively.
Safe anesthetic agents: propofol, volatile anesthetics, fentanyl, remifentanil, rocuronium, and cisatracurium are clinically safe.
If acute hemolysis occurs (dark tea-colored urine, sudden hematocrit drop), maintain brisk alkaline diuresis to protect renal tubules.
Active patient warming with forced-air blankets and fluid warmers to avoid hypothermic shivering and metabolic stress.
avoid: Known oxidative triggers: methylene blue, rasburicase, primaquine, sulfonamides, dapsone, and nitrofurantoin.
High-dose acetaminophen, prilocaine, and topical benzocaine sprays (induce oxidative stress and methemoglobinemia).
Hypothermia, severe acidosis, and unmanaged surgical infection or stress.
postop: Inspect urine color closely: dark reddish-brown urine indicates free hemoglobinuria and acute intravascular hemolysis.
Monitor serial hemoglobin, hematocrit, and renal function if clinical signs of hemolysis emerge.
Provide clear discharge counseling and medication lists excluding oxidative pharmaceuticals.

preop: Homozygous HbSS causing deoxygenated erythrocyte polymerization, vaso-occlusion, acute chest syndrome, stroke, and chronic organ damage.
Review baseline hemoglobin, reticulocyte count, baseline oxygen saturation, and HbS percentage.
Transfusion strategy: target hemoglobin 10 g/dL with simple transfusion for moderate-risk surgery; exchange transfusion for high-risk procedures or HbS reduction < 30%.
Evaluate end-organ injury: pulmonary hypertension, restrictive lung disease, renal dysfunction, and history of stroke.
Prevent preoperative dehydration: avoid prolonged fasting; start intravenous fluids prior to surgery.
intraop: Meticulously prevent the sickling tetrad: hypoxemia, acidosis, hypothermia, and hypovolemia or vascular stasis.
Administer high FiO2 (maintain SpO2 at baseline or >= 96%); use active warming with forced-air blankets and warmed fluids.
Provide deep anesthesia and effective analgesia to prevent sympathetic vasoconstriction and microvascular stasis.
Regional anesthesia is acceptable and reduces opioid-induced hypoventilation, but avoid hypotension or prolonged tourniquet ischemia.
avoid: Hypoxemia: even brief desaturations trigger rapid HbS polymerization and vaso-occlusion.
Hypothermia and shivering: produces intense peripheral vasoconstriction and erythrocyte sickling.
Dehydration and metabolic acidosis: worsens sickling and sludging in microcirculation.
Prolonged tourniquet times: localized hypoxia and acidemia in ischemic limb provoke sickling upon reperfusion.
postop: High risk of acute chest syndrome (ACS) within 48 to 72 hours postop: use incentive spirometry every 2 hours and early ambulation.
Continue supplemental oxygen to maintain SpO2 >= 96% and IV hydration at maintenance or 1.5x maintenance.
Aggressively manage postoperative pain with multimodal analgesia while avoiding excessive sedation and hypoventilation.

preop: Oxidation of ferrous iron to ferric iron in hemoglobin, unable to bind oxygen and shifting dissociation curve left, producing cellular hypoxia.
Screen for congenital cytochrome b5 reductase deficiency or hemoglobin M variants, or history of drug-induced methemoglobinemia.
Identify exposure to oxidizing triggers: benzocaine sprays, prilocaine, lidocaine (in massive doses), nitrates/nitrites, and dapsone.
intraop: Standard pulse oximetry is unreliable: absorption at 660 nm and 940 nm equalizes, causing SpO2 to plateau around 85% regardless of true arterial oxygenation.
Obtain co-oximetry blood gas analysis to directly measure methemoglobin percentage and true oxyhemoglobin saturation.
Administer 100% inspired oxygen.

In symptomatic patients or methemoglobin levels > 20% to 30%, administer intravenous methylene blue (1% solution over 5 minutes); note that methylene blue requires functional G6PD to reduce ferric iron.
avoid: Topical benzocaine sprays (Hurricaine, Cetacaine) for airway topicalization: major cause of severe iatrogenic methemoglobinemia.
Prilocaine and excessive doses of local anesthetics or nitrates.
Methylene blue in patients with known or suspected G6PD deficiency: can trigger massive acute hemolytic anemia; use ascorbic acid or exchange transfusion instead.
postop: Serial co-oximetry measurements: rebound methemoglobinemia can occur several hours later as lipophilic drugs continue to leach from tissue stores.
Continuous hemodynamic monitoring and supplemental oxygen until methemoglobin level drops below 5%.
Document triggering oxidizing agent clearly in patient allergy and electronic medical record.

preop: Myeloproliferative neoplasm (JAK2 mutation) causing autonomous erythrocyte overproduction, hyperviscosity, and high risk of thrombosis and hemorrhage.
Optimize hematocrit before elective surgery: phlebotomy or cytoreduction to target hematocrit < 45% (men) or < 42% (women) to normalize blood viscosity.
Check platelet count and coagulation profile: extreme thrombocytosis can paradoxically cause acquired von Willebrand disease and bleeding.
Screen for history of thrombosis (DVT, PE, stroke, Budd-Chiari) or mucosal bleeding.
intraop: Maintain liberal hydration to prevent hemoconcentration and severe microvascular stasis.
High risk of perioperative thromboembolism: apply sequential compression devices throughout surgery and avoid venous stasis.
Careful arterial and venous cannulation: increased risk of both vascular thrombosis and hematoma formation.
Maintain strict normothermia; cold temperatures substantially increase blood viscosity.
avoid: Proceeding with elective surgery when hematocrit > 45%: massive increase in perioperative stroke and myocardial infarction risk.
Dehydration and prolonged fasting without intravenous fluid maintenance.
Venous pooling, prolonged immobilization, or extreme lithotomy positioning that promotes venous thrombosis.
postop: Early mobilization and aggressive venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis (mechanical and pharmacological as soon as surgical hemostasis permits).
Continue intravenous hydration until oral fluid intake is robust.
Monitor CBC, hematocrit, and clinical signs of thrombotic or hemorrhagic complications.

preop: X-linked bleeding disorder caused by deficiency of factor VIII (Hemophilia A) or factor IX (Hemophilia B); high risk of hemarthroses and severe surgical bleeding.
Hematology consultation and inhibitor testing (Bethesda assay) are mandatory before elective surgery.
Factor replacement target: raise factor VIII or IX levels to 80% to 100% of normal immediately before major surgery (50% for minor surgery).
In mild Hemophilia A, desmopressin (DDAVP) may be used to release endogenous factor VIII and vWF; test dose preoperatively.
Factor IX requires larger replacement doses due to extensive extravascular distribution.
intraop: Neuraxial anesthesia (spinal, epidural) and deep peripheral nerve blocks are strictly contraindicated unless factor levels are 100% normalized and cleared by hematology.
Gentle airway instrumentation: intubation and suctioning must be atraumatic to prevent retropharyngeal or glottic hematomas that cause fatal airway obstruction.
Coordinate intraoperative continuous factor infusions or boluses to maintain target trough levels (>50% for major surgery).
Meticulous surgical hemostasis; antifibrinolytic agents (tranexamic acid or aminocaproic acid) are valuable adjuncts.
avoid: Intramuscular injections and blind deep regional nerve blocks.
NSAIDs and antiplatelet agents (aspirin) that impair platelet plug formation.
Traumatic airway manipulation, vigorous nasogastric tube insertion, or nasal intubation (severe mucosal bleeding).
postop: Maintain factor levels: keep trough levels > 50% for 7 to 14 days after major surgery, tapering per hematology protocol.
Daily factor level assays to ensure adequate replacement and detect emergence of inhibitors.
Monitor surgical drains, wound sites, and neuro checks for occult compartment syndromes or internal bleeding.

preop: Most common inherited bleeding disorder, characterized by quantitative or qualitative deficiency in von Willebrand factor (vWF), impairing platelet adhesion and factor VIII stabilization.
Identify vWD type (Type 1 mild quantitative, Type 2 qualitative, Type 3 severe absent) and review hematology treatment plan.
Type 1: DDAVP (desmopressin) trial induces release of stored vWF and factor VIII; useful for minor to moderate surgical procedures.
Types 2 and 3, or major surgery: vWF-containing factor VIII concentrates (or recombinant vWF) administered before surgery to achieve vWF activity > 80% to 100%.
intraop: Neuraxial anesthesia is contraindicated unless vWF and factor VIII levels are verified normal and hematology approves.
Gentle airway management to avoid pharyngeal or mucosal lacerations and hemorrhage.
Antifibrinolytic therapy (tranexamic acid or aminocaproic acid) is a highly effective adjunct, particularly for mucosal surgery (ENT, dental, gynecologic).
Monitor blood loss meticulously; have factor concentrates available in the operating theater.
avoid: NSAIDs, aspirin, and other antiplatelet drugs that further destabilize primary platelet hemostasis.
Intramuscular injections and blind regional nerve blocks.
Excessive fluid administration when repeated doses of DDAVP are used (risk of water retention and severe hyponatremia).
postop: Maintain vWF and factor VIII levels > 50% for 3 to 7 days postoperatively (longer for major orthopedic or vascular surgery).
If DDAVP is used, restrict free water intake and monitor serum sodium closely to prevent hyponatremic seizures.
Continue antifibrinolytic therapy until wound healing and mucosal recovery are complete.

preop: Autoimmune hypercoagulable state with antibodies against phospholipid-binding plasma proteins, causing paradoxical in vitro prolonged PTT but severe in vivo thrombosis risk.
Coordinate perioperative anticoagulation bridging: patients are typically on therapeutic warfarin or DOACs; bridge with LMWH or unfractionated heparin.
Screen for end-organ vascular injury: history of stroke, pulmonary hypertension, coronary thrombosis, renal microangiopathy, and Catastrophic Antiphospholipid Syndrome (CAPS).
Check baseline platelet count (mild to moderate autoimmune thrombocytopenia is common).
intraop: Timing of regional anesthesia: neuraxial blocks require strict adherence to ASRA guidelines regarding heparin/LMWH timing; artifactually prolonged PTT cannot be used to assess bleeding safety.
Prevent vascular stasis and hemoconcentration: ensure liberal hydration and intraoperative sequential compression devices.
Arterial line placement: radial catheterization must be done atraumatically; high risk of catheter-related arterial thrombosis.
Maintain strict normothermia; hypothermia promotes microvascular thrombosis.
avoid: Withholding anticoagulation longer than strictly necessary: rebound thrombosis risk is exceptionally high.
Interpreting a prolonged PTT as a bleeding diathesis or contraindication to thromboprophylaxis without understanding the lupus anticoagulant artifact.
Dehydration, venous stasis, and prolonged unpadded tourniquet use.
postop: Resume therapeutic anticoagulation as soon as surgical hemostasis is confirmed by the surgical team.

High vigilance for Catastrophic Antiphospholipid Syndrome (CAPS): acute multi-organ microvascular thrombosis, thrombocytopenia, and systemic inflammatory response; treated with steroids, plasmapheresis, and anticoagulation.
Monitor platelet counts and clinical signs of DVT, pulmonary embolism, or graft thrombosis.

preop: Benign hereditary unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia from reduced UDP-glucuronosyltransferase (UGT1A1) activity.
Jaundice is typically mild and triggered by fasting, dehydration, emotional stress, infection, or fatigue.
Liver architecture, transaminases, and synthetic hepatic function are completely normal.
Reassure patient; minimize preoperative fasting duration and avoid hypocaloric dehydration.
intraop: Avoid prolonged dehydration or starvation during surgery; administer intravenous glucose-containing fluids if fasting is extended.
Standard anesthetic drugs are well tolerated; volatile agents and intravenous anesthetics can be used safely.
Acetaminophen clearance may be modestly reduced, but standard therapeutic doses remain safe.
Maintain normothermia and hemodynamic stability throughout the perioperative period.
avoid: Prolonged starvation, dehydration, and fasting without intravenous fluids (markedly elevates serum bilirubin).
Unnecessary extensive hepatic testing or delaying surgery for asymptomatic mild jaundice.
postop: Anticipate that mild scleral icterus and jaundice may transiently worsen due to surgical stress and fasting.
Reassure the surgical team and patient that postoperative jaundice reflects benign unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia and not liver injury.
Resume oral intake promptly to normalize bilirubin clearance.

preop: Severe inherited deficiency of UGT1A1 enzyme with life-threatening unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia and high kernicterus risk.
Type 1 has absent enzyme activity (transfusion and phototherapy dependent, requiring liver transplantation); Type 2 has partial activity and responds to phenobarbital.
Review baseline total and unconjugated bilirubin, neurological status, and regular phototherapy schedule.
Ensure serum albumin is within normal limits to provide sufficient bilirubin-binding capacity.
intraop: Maintain continuous phototherapy in the operating room whenever feasible; ensure protective eye shielding.
Preserve normal albumin levels: administer human albumin if necessary to bind free unconjugated bilirubin and prevent central nervous system entry.
Use anesthetic agents with minimal albumin-displacement effects.
Maintain strict normothermia, normocarbia, and normal pH: acidemia and hypothermia promote bilirubin penetration through the blood-brain barrier.
avoid: Medications that displace bilirubin from albumin binding sites: sulfonamides, ceftriaxone, furosemide, salicylates, and diazepam.
Metabolic acidosis, hypothermia, and hypoalbuminemia: all markedly increase the fraction of free toxic bilirubin.
postop: Resume intensive phototherapy and liberal hydration immediately in the post-anesthesia care unit.
Perform serial unconjugated bilirubin measurements and close neurological evaluations for signs of acute bilirubin encephalopathy.
Maintain normothermia and physiological acid-base balance.

preop: Failure of lower esophageal sphincter relaxation with esophageal aperistalsis, resulting in megaesophagus and retained food secretions.
Extreme aspiration risk: treat as a full stomach regardless of fasting duration or NPO interval.
Screen for chronic pulmonary aspiration, nocturnal coughing, recurrent pneumonia, and esophageal dilation on imaging.
Preoperative clear liquid diet for 48 hours is often advised prior to elective surgery.
intraop: Treat as full stomach: perform esophageal decompression via large-bore suction tube prior to induction in semi-upright position if massive dilation is present.
Rapid sequence induction (RSI) with cricoid pressure and cuffed endotracheal tube, or awake fiberoptic intubation with head elevated.
Maintain smooth depth of anesthesia; avoid coughing, bucking, or straining during airway instrumentation.
Coordinate carefully with surgeons during esophageal myotomy or endoscopic procedures to avoid esophageal perforation.
avoid: Induction of general anesthesia in a flat supine position without securing the airway.
Light planes of anesthesia that provoke vomiting, retching, or active regurgitation during induction.
Blind forceful insertion of esophageal dilators or temperature probes (high risk of esophageal wall perforation).
postop: Extubate only when patient is fully conscious, upright, with complete recovery of protective airway reflexes.
Observe for signs of intraoperative esophageal perforation (mediastinitis, surgical emphysema, pleural effusion, unexplained tachycardia, fever).
Provide effective multimodal analgesia and chest physiotherapy.

preop: Gastrin-secreting neuroendocrine tumor (gastrinoma) causing massive gastric acid hypersecretion, peptic ulcers, and secretory diarrhea.
Patients often present with dehydration, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis from high-volume gastric output.
Continue high-dose proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) without interruption up to the time of surgery; switch to IV pantoprazole.
Assess fluid balance and correct electrolyte abnormalities (hypokalemia, hypochloremia) before induction.
intraop: Extreme aspiration risk: massive volume of highly acidic gastric secretions.
Administer intravenous H2-receptor antagonists and high-dose PPIs; consider preoperative nasogastric decompression.
Perform rapid sequence induction (RSI) with cricoid pressure and a cuffed endotracheal tube.
Monitor arterial blood gases and potassium levels during long procedures.
avoid: Omitting acid-suppressive therapy on the morning of surgery.
Unprotected airway instrumentation or mask ventilation without cricoid pressure before intubation.
postop: Continue parenteral proton pump inhibitor therapy around the clock to prevent acute rebound acid hypersecretion and stress ulceration.
Maintain continuous gastric decompression if postoperative ileus or abdominal distension occurs.
Monitor serum electrolytes, renal function, and fluid balance in the recovery unit.

preop: Give octreotide 24 to 48 hours before surgery and continue it through the procedure: somatostatin analogues can prevent a carcinoid crisis.
Look for right-sided heart disease (fibrosis of the tricuspid and pulmonary valves), dehydration and electrolyte loss from diarrhea, and wheezing.
intraop: Use invasive arterial pressure monitoring: blood pressure can change rapidly.
Give octreotide again before the tumor is handled; it attenuates most adverse hemodynamic responses.
Carcinoid crisis: intense flushing, diarrhea, tachycardia, and hypertension or hypotension, sometimes with bronchospasm.
Bronchospasm is often resistant to treatment, and beta agonists can worsen it through mediator release; octreotide and antihistamines with ipratropium have been used.

Drugs not known to release mediators: propofol, etomidate, vecuronium, cisatracurium, rocuronium, fentanyl, sufentanil, alfentanil, remifentanil and all inhalation agents (desflurane may suit liver metastases).
Epidural analgesia is safe after adequate octreotide treatment if the local anesthetic is given gradually with careful hemodynamic monitoring.
avoid: Histamine-releasing drugs.
Drugs that may provoke mediator release: succinylcholine, mivacurium, atracurium, epinephrine, norepinephrine, dopamine, isoproterenol and thiopental.
postop: Delayed awakening has been described; plan ICU monitoring when needed.
Symptoms can persist after palliative surgery or with metastases.
Ondansetron is a good antiemetic for these patients.

preop: Autoimmune anti-glomerular basement membrane (anti-GBM) antibody disease causing glomerulonephritis and necrotizing pulmonary alveolar hemorrhage.
Screen for active alveolar bleeding: hemoptysis, dyspnea, bilateral pulmonary infiltrates, and acute drop in hematocrit.
Evaluate renal impairment, severe oliguria, and electrolyte imbalances; coordinate preoperative hemodialysis or plasmapheresis.
Review immunosuppressive therapy (cyclophosphamide, high-dose corticosteroids) and infection vulnerability.
intraop: High risk of sudden intraoperative pulmonary hemorrhage and refractory hypoxemia.
Prepare for lung isolation (double-lumen tube or bronchial blocker) to protect the unaffected lung if unilateral bleeding occurs.
Employ gentle lung-protective ventilation: low tidal volumes, moderate PEEP, and avoid high peak airway pressures.
Avoid nephrotoxic medications; titrate fluid administration strictly according to volume status.
avoid: Fluid overload in oliguric or anuric renal failure: dangerously worsens alveolar hemorrhage and pulmonary edema.
Excessive ventilatory airway pressures that provoke capillary barotrauma and fresh pulmonary hemorrhage.
Nephrotoxic drugs (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides).
postop: Admit to intensive care with continuous arterial line and pulse oximetry monitoring.
Perform serial chest radiographs and arterial blood gas measurements to detect occult or recurrent alveolar bleeding.
Continue post-procedure hemodialysis and immunosuppressive therapy as directed by nephrology.

preop: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) with enlarged cystic kidneys, hypertension, hepatic cysts, and intracranial berry aneurysms.
Intracranial berry aneurysms occur in 10% to 15% of patients: screen for severe headaches or family history of subarachnoid hemorrhage.
Assess renal function, chronic hypertension, and hepatic cyst burden (hepatomegaly may reduce diaphragm mobility and functional residual capacity).
Screen for cardiac valvular abnormalities: mitral valve prolapse and aortic regurgitation occur with increased frequency.
intraop: Strict blood pressure control: prevent intraoperative hypertension during induction, intubation, and emergence to minimize berry aneurysm rupture risk.
Full-stomach precautions: massively enlarged kidneys and liver compress the stomach and raise intra-abdominal pressure, increasing aspiration risk.
Careful positioning to protect protruding flanks and polycystic organs from external pressure.
Titrate fluid administration carefully and avoid nephrotoxic agents.
avoid: Severe hypertension or sympathetic surges during intubation and emergence (risk of intracranial berry aneurysm rupture).
Nephrotoxic medications (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides).
Direct abdominal pressure on large, fragile renal cysts.
postop: Maintain tight blood pressure control in recovery to avoid hemorrhagic complications.
Continuous cardiac telemetry for patients with mitral valve prolapse or conduction defects.
Urgent neurosurgical consultation and imaging for any acute postoperative headache, vomiting, or neurological changes.

preop: Inherited renal tubular defects (Bartter: thick ascending loop of Henle; Gitelman: distal convoluted tubule) causing renal salt wasting and hypokalemic alkalosis.
Key laboratory abnormalities: hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, metabolic alkalosis, and hyperreninemic hyperaldosteronism with normal or low blood pressure.
Check potassium, magnesium, calcium, and intravascular volume status; aggressive preoperative electrolyte replenishment is required.
Review chronic spironolactone, ACE inhibitors, or oral potassium/magnesium supplementation.
intraop: Severe hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia predispose to cardiac arrhythmias (prolonged QT interval, torsades de pointes, ventricular ectopy).
Hypokalemia potentiates nondepolarizing neuromuscular blockade: monitor train-of-four and titrate relaxants with caution.
Monitor arterial blood gases, potassium, and magnesium during long procedures.
Maintain normal intravascular volume with balanced electrolyte crystalloids.
avoid: Hyperventilation and respiratory alkalosis: acutely shifts extracellular potassium into cells, precipitating life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias.
Potassium-free intravenous fluids.
Loop or thiazide diuretics.
postop: Continue intravenous potassium and magnesium supplementation with serial laboratory verification until oral intake resumes.
Continuous ECG telemetry monitoring for arrhythmias and QT prolongation in the recovery unit.
Monitor neuromuscular function closely for signs of residual weakness.

preop: Generalized proximal tubular dysfunction causing renal loss of glucose, amino acids, phosphate, bicarbonate (type 2 proximal RTA), and potassium.
Patients exhibit chronic metabolic acidosis, hypokalemia, hypophosphatemia, dehydration, and osteomalacia or rickets with bone fragility.
Check baseline arterial blood gases, serum bicarbonate, electrolytes, phosphate, and volume status.
Review chronic bicarbonate, potassium, and phosphate supplementation therapy.
intraop: Maintain intravenous hydration using balanced crystalloids with bicarbonate supplementation if severe acidosis persists.
Hypophosphatemia and hypokalemia cause diaphragmatic and skeletal muscle weakness and prolong neuromuscular block: monitor train-of-four.
Handle extremities with extreme gentleness: osteomalacia and demineralized bones fracture easily under minimal stress.
Maintain normothermia and normal ventilatory parameters to avoid worsening acidosis.
avoid: Large infusions of unbuffered normal saline: worsens hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis.
Rough handling, aggressive limb manipulation, or excessive pressure on osteomalacic bones (fracture risk).
Dehydration and hypovolemia.
postop: Serial monitoring of serum electrolytes, bicarbonate, and phosphate.
Continue replacement infusions until oral intake is established.
Assess respiratory muscle strength and ventilatory mechanics before extubation.

preop: Inherited mechano-bullous disorder where minor friction or shearing forces produce intraepidermal or subepidermal blisters and skin denudation.
Airway involvement: microstomia, ankyloglossia, pharyngeal scarring, esophageal strictures, and laryngeal narrowing.
Strictly avoid adhesive tape, standard identification bands, and shearing skin contact on arrival in the operating suite.
Plan airway technique: prepare video laryngoscopy, fiberoptic equipment, and smaller endotracheal tubes.
intraop: Strictly NO adhesive tape: secure lines, eyes, and tubes with soft silicone wraps, petrolatum gauze, or rolled gauze bandages.
Generously lubricate face masks, oral airways, and laryngoscope blades with hydrocortisone ointment or water-soluble lubricant.
Select a smaller endotracheal tube than predicted; gently insert without twisting or shearing mucous membranes.
Pad all pressure points, operating table surfaces, and positioning aids with non-adherent silicone gel pads.
Place blood pressure cuff over soft cotton padding and cycle manually or at extended intervals.
avoid: Any friction, shear, or rubbing force on skin or mucous membranes.
Standard adhesive tapes, adhesive monitoring electrodes, and sticky dressings.
Forceful or repetitive airway instrumentation.
postop: Protect all blisters: aspirate large bullae with sterile fine-needle decompression without stripping the epidermal blister roof.
Transfer patient with wide sliding sheets; never drag or pull on limbs.
Multimodal analgesia with antiemetics to prevent distress, thrashing, and oral retching.

preop: Autoimmune intraepidermal blistering disease (anti-desmoglein antibodies) producing flaccid bullae, mucosal ulcerations, and a positive Nikolsky sign.
Patients are chronically immunosuppressed with high-dose corticosteroids, azathioprine, mycophenolate, or rituximab.
Evaluate mucosal involvement of lips, tongue, pharynx, and larynx; determine stress-dose corticosteroid requirements.
Examine skin lesions and plan atraumatic positioning and line placement.
intraop: Avoid frictional trauma and shear forces on skin and mucous membranes.
Use generously lubricated face masks and non-adhesive silicone dressings; avoid standard adhesive tapes on skin.
Atraumatic airway management: inspect oropharynx carefully and perform gentle intubation to avoid denuding friable mucosal lesions.
Administer intravenous stress-dose hydrocortisone before surgical incision.
Strict aseptic technique: extensive skin breakdown and chronic immunosuppression create high risk for systemic infection.
avoid: Adhesive tapes and abrasive monitoring adhesives directly on skin.
Forceful suctioning or traumatic direct laryngoscopy that shears oral or pharyngeal mucosa.
postop: Continue stress-dose corticosteroid coverage and taper according to surgical stress protocol.
Meticulous skin and wound care with non-adherent sterile dressings.
Monitor closely for secondary surgical site or systemic bacterial infections.

preop: Abnormal proliferation and accumulation of mast cells in skin (urticaria pigmentosa) and visceral organs (systemic mastocytosis).
Predisposed to sudden, massive mast cell degranulation with histamine, prostaglandin, and leukotriene release causing profound shock.
Premedicate with H1-receptor antagonists (diphenhydramine) and H2-receptor antagonists (famotidine), plus oral corticosteroids or cromolyn.
Identify and document patient-specific triggers (temperature changes, stress, mechanical friction, specific medications).
intraop: Maintain strict normothermia: avoid rapid temperature changes, shivering, cold intravenous fluids, and mechanical skin friction.
Have emergency resuscitation drugs immediately available: epinephrine, vasopressin, antihistamines, and large-volume crystalloids.
Safe anesthetic agents: propofol, etomidate, volatile agents, fentanyl, vecuronium, and cisatracurium are clinically well tolerated.
Invasive arterial pressure monitoring is recommended for major surgical procedures.
avoid: Histamine-releasing drugs: morphine, codeine, meperidine, atracurium, mivacurium, and succinylcholine.
Physical and mechanical triggers: hypothermia, hyperthermia, shivering, mechanical skin rubbing, and cold IV fluid boluses.
Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) if patient has a history of aspirin/NSAID-induced degranulation.
postop: Observe in PACU or ICU for delayed mast cell degranulation and hemodynamic collapse.
Continue scheduled H1 and H2 antihistamine therapy into the recovery period.
Treat acute hypotensive episodes promptly with epinephrine and intravenous fluid resuscitation.

preop: Multisystem autoimmune disease characterized by vascular damage, fibrosis of skin, lungs, gastrointestinal tract, heart, and kidneys.
Airway evaluation: microstomia, tight facial skin, reduced mandibular excursion, and stiff neck tissues predict difficult intubation.
Severe gastrointestinal dysmotility and lower esophageal incompetence: high aspiration risk.
Cardiopulmonary assessment: screen for restrictive interstitial lung disease, pulmonary arterial hypertension, and Raynaud phenomenon.
intraop: Anticipate difficult airway: prepare video laryngoscopy or flexible fiberoptic bronchoscope.
Full-stomach precautions: perform rapid sequence induction with cricoid pressure and cuffed endotracheal tube.
Keep the operating room warm; use fluid warmers and padded extremity wraps to prevent severe Raynaud digital vasospasm and necrosis.
Invasive arterial monitoring is recommended for major cases; avoid radial lines if severe digital ischemia or Raynaud disease is present.
Use lung-protective ventilation with low tidal volumes in patients with restrictive pulmonary fibrosis.
