avoid: Hypothermia, cold operating rooms, and cold intravenous infusions (precipitates severe Raynaud vasospasm and tissue ischemia).
High ventilatory airway pressures in patients with stiff, fibrotic lungs.
Peripheral vasoconstrictors unless absolutely necessary.
postop: Maintain warm room temperature and adequate analgesia to prevent sympathetic Raynaud flare-ups.
Monitor blood pressure and renal function closely: acute hypertension warns of scleroderma renal crisis, requiring immediate ACE inhibitor therapy.
High vigilance for post-extubation aspiration and respiratory failure.

preop: Inherited fragmentation and calcification of elastic fibers (ABCC6 mutation) affecting skin, eyes (angioid streaks), and arteries.
Cardiovascular risks: premature coronary artery disease, calcified peripheral arteries, renovascular hypertension, and cardiac ischemia.
Gastrointestinal risks: fragile mucosal vessels cause spontaneous and traumatic upper gastrointestinal bleeding.
Screen for angina, exercise intolerance, claudication, and history of GI hemorrhage.
intraop: Arterial cannulation may be difficult due to calcified, occluded peripheral arteries; verify collateral circulation before cannulation.
Fragile mucosal vasculature: gentle intubation and suctioning; avoid aggressive nasogastric tube insertion (risk of massive mucosal bleeding).
Maintain stable hemodynamics: avoid tachycardia and hypotension to prevent myocardial ischemia in premature coronary disease.
Careful patient positioning with generous padding on all bony points.
avoid: Traumatic instrumentation of mucous membranes (high risk of mucosal and upper gastrointestinal hemorrhage).
Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and antiplatelet agents.
Severe hemodynamic fluctuations that compromise coronary or cerebral perfusion.
postop: Continuous ECG telemetry monitoring for myocardial ischemia and arrhythmias.
Monitor serial hematocrit and inspect for signs of gastrointestinal hemorrhage.
Maintain stable blood pressure control to protect fragile, calcified arterial vasculature.

preop: Heterogeneous connective tissue disorder of collagen synthesis; vascular type (Type IV) carries extreme risk of arterial, bowel, and uterine rupture.
Classical and hypermobility types feature severe joint laxity, skin hyperextensibility, tissue fragility, and easy bruising.
Screen for aortic root dilation, mitral valve prolapse, spontaneous pneumothorax history, and vascular type diagnosis.
Evaluate coagulation: bleeding time may be prolonged despite normal standard coagulation assays.
intraop: Vascular access precautions: invasive arterial and central venous cannulation carries catastrophic vessel dissection/rupture risk in vascular EDS; avoid unless life-saving.
Employ low ventilatory airway pressures to prevent spontaneous alveolar rupture and tension pneumothorax.
Meticulous positioning and padding: joints subluxate and dislocate easily during transfer and positioning.
Gentle airway instrumentation to prevent pharyngeal lacerations, vocal cord hematomas, and temporomandibular joint dislocation.
avoid: Invasive arterial and central venous lines in vascular EDS unless mandatory (high arterial dissection and rupture risk).
High peak inspiratory airway pressures (pneumothorax risk).
Rough joint manipulation or extreme hyperextension during positioning.
Intramuscular injections and blind regional nerve blocks.
postop: Monitor closely for occult vascular hemorrhage, retroperitoneal bleeding, pneumothorax, and hematoma expansion.
Avoid vigorous physical therapy or aggressive joint mobilization in early recovery.
Provide multimodal analgesia with antiemetics to prevent straining and retching.

preop: Autosomal dominant fibrillin-1 mutation causing aortic root dilation, aortic dissection, mitral valve prolapse, and skeletal deformities.
Pulmonary risk: spontaneous pneumothorax from apical bullae, pectus excavatum, and scoliosis.
Airway evaluation: high-arched palate, retrognathia, and temporomandibular joint laxity may complicate airway management.
Review recent echocardiogram (aortic root diameter, valvular regurgitation) and continue beta-blocker therapy up to induction.
intraop: Strict hemodynamic control: prevent hypertension, tachycardia, and increased myocardial contractility (dP/dt) to protect the fragile aortic root.
Continue beta-blockers; treat acute hypertensive episodes promptly with esmolol, labetalol, or nitroprusside.
Gentle airway instrumentation: avoid trauma to high-arched palate and loose dentition.
Employ protective lung ventilation with low tidal volumes and low peak pressures to prevent rupture of apical pulmonary blebs.
avoid: Intraoperative hypertension and tachycardia: sharply increases aortic wall shear stress and dissection risk.
High airway pressures and vigorous positive-pressure ventilation (spontaneous pneumothorax risk).
postop: Maintain tight blood pressure and heart rate control with intravenous beta-blockers in PACU and ICU.
Continuous cardiac telemetry monitoring for arrhythmias.
Urgent diagnostic evaluation (CT angiogram or TEE) for any acute chest, back, or abdominal pain.

preop: Severe spinal deformity producing restrictive lung defect, reduced vital capacity, ventilation-perfusion mismatch, and pulmonary hypertension.
Curvature Cobb angle > 100 degrees carries substantial risk of chronic cor pulmonale and postoperative respiratory failure.
Review pulmonary function tests, baseline arterial blood gases, echocardiogram, and spinal imaging.
Assess airway and cervical mobility: associated cervical deformities may complicate intubation.
intraop: Anticipate difficult mask ventilation, positioning challenges, and reduced chest wall compliance.
Intraoperative neuromonitoring (SSEP/MEP) during corrective spinal surgery: use total intravenous anesthesia (TIVA) without muscle relaxants after induction.
Blood loss can be extensive: employ cell salvage, tranexamic acid, and have crossmatched blood available.
Use lung-protective ventilation; monitor for elevated peak airway pressures.
avoid: Prolonged neuromuscular blockade during motor evoked potential monitoring.
Nitrous oxide in patients with underlying pulmonary arterial hypertension.
Excessive crystalloid resuscitation causing pulmonary edema in low-capacity lungs.
postop: High risk of postoperative respiratory failure, atelectasis, and prolonged mechanical ventilation.
Admit to ICU; implement aggressive pulmonary toilet, incentive spirometry, and noninvasive respiratory support.
Multimodal analgesia with neuraxial or regional techniques (epidural or erector spinae blocks) to avoid opioid-induced hypoventilation.

preop: Chronic inflammatory spondyloarthropathy causing spinal fusion ("bamboo spine"), fixed cervical kyphosis, and restricted chest expansion.
Airway warning: severe restriction of cervical spine mobility, reduced mouth opening (TMJ involvement), and rigid thoracic cage.
Cardiac evaluation: screen for aortic insufficiency, cardiac conduction defects, and bundle branch blocks.
Plan awake fiberoptic intubation or video laryngoscopy in the pre-formed neutral position.
intraop: Anticipate impossible direct laryngoscopy and impossible neck extension: perform awake fiberoptic intubation.
Brittle, rigid spine: handle patient with extreme care; minor trauma or neck manipulation can cause cervical spine fracture and quadriplegia.
Neuraxial anesthesia is technically difficult or impossible due to ossified interspinous ligaments and fused vertebrae.
Pad all pressure points carefully to conform to the patient's fixed posture.
avoid: Any attempt to forcefully extend the cervical spine: high risk of catastrophic cervical spine fracture and spinal cord transection.
Forceful direct laryngoscopy with rigid blades.
Blind attempts at neuraxial anesthesia without imaging guidance.
postop: Maintain strict cervical spine immobilization in neutral position until patient is fully conscious and cooperative.
Monitor for restrictive hypoventilation, atelectasis, and airway compromise.
Perform detailed neurological checks of all four extremities postoperatively.

preop: Disorganized bone remodeling causing enlarged, structurally weak, highly vascular bones, skull deformities, and platybasia.
Extensive skeletal involvement acts as an arteriovenous shunt, producing high-output cardiac failure.
Evaluate cranial nerve function, cervical spine involvement, and cardiac function on echocardiography.
Review baseline serum alkaline phosphatase, calcium levels, and bisphosphonate or calcitonin therapy.
intraop: Examine airway for restricted cervical motion, platybasia, and basilar invagination.
Anticipate massive intraoperative surgical hemorrhage during orthopedic bone surgery due to intense bone hypervascularity.
Have large-bore intravenous access, cell salvage, and crossmatched blood products prepared.
Manage high-output cardiac state carefully; avoid myocardial depressants and large swings in systemic vascular resistance.
avoid: Extreme cervical neck flexion or extension in patients with platybasia or basilar invagination.
Underestimating surgical blood loss during bone reaming or osteotomy.
postop: Monitor closely for postoperative hemorrhage, hematoma expansion, and high-output heart failure decompensation.
Check serum calcium levels: hypocalcemia can develop following bisphosphonate administration or extensive remodeling.
Continue cardiac telemetry monitoring.

preop: Most common skeletal dysplasia (FGFR3 mutation) causing disproportionate dwarfism, macrocephaly, and midface hypoplasia.
Neurological and skeletal risks: foramen magnum stenosis, craniocervical instability, spinal stenosis, and kyphoscoliosis.
Respiratory risks: severe obstructive sleep apnea, restrictive pulmonary mechanics, and pulmonary hypertension.
Airway assessment: large tongue, small mouth, midface retrusion, and limited neck extension.
intraop: Difficult airway: avoid neck hyperextension during laryngoscopy due to foramen magnum stenosis and cervicomedullary compression.
Use video laryngoscopy or flexible fiberoptic intubation with in-line cervical stabilization.
Neuraxial anesthesia is technically challenging (narrow epidural space, spinal stenosis); drastically reduce local anesthetic dosing due to diminished CSF volume.
Position carefully with generous padding; protect large head and neck.
avoid: Neck hyperextension or extreme flexion during airway management and positioning (causes acute brainstem or spinal cord compression).
Standard adult local anesthetic dosing for spinal anesthesia (causes dangerously high or total spinal block).
postop: High risk of postoperative upper airway obstruction, sleep apnea, and respiratory depression: extubate fully awake in upright position.
Continuous pulse oximetry and respiratory monitoring in PACU or step-down unit.
Avoid heavy opioid sedation; utilize multimodal non-opioid analgesics.

preop: Congenital growth disorder with prenatal and postnatal dwarfism, characteristic triangular facies, micrognathia, and body asymmetry.
High vulnerability to fasting hypoglycemia due to scarce muscle mass and depleted hepatic glycogen stores.
Assess airway: micrognathia and small mouth predict difficult laryngoscopy.
Check baseline blood glucose; avoid prolonged fasting and start intravenous dextrose infusion prior to surgery.
intraop: Anticipate difficult airway: have video laryngoscopy and fiberoptic equipment prepared; select smaller endotracheal tubes.
Maintain continuous intravenous dextrose infusion; perform frequent intraoperative blood glucose checks.
Precarious thermoregulation: utilize forced-air warming blankets and warmed fluids to prevent rapid hypothermia.
Careful positioning to protect asymmetric limbs and fragile skeletal structures.
avoid: Prolonged preoperative fasting without intravenous dextrose supplementation.
Hypothermia: small body mass leads to rapid thermal loss.
Using oversized endotracheal tubes: larynx and subglottis are proportionately small.
postop: Continue serial blood glucose monitoring until regular oral intake is established.
Close respiratory monitoring for post-extubation airway edema or croup.
Maintain active warming until normal body temperature is secured.

preop: Marked congenital dilation of trachea and main bronchi from muscular and elastic tissue atrophy (Mounier-Kuhn syndrome).
Presents with recurrent lower respiratory tract infections, bronchiectasis, copious sputum, and dynamic tracheobronchial collapse.
Review chest CT imaging to evaluate the exact internal tracheal diameter and sites of dynamic collapse.
Optimize pulmonary status with preoperative chest physiotherapy and bronchodilators.
intraop: Standard endotracheal tube cuffs may fail to seal the abnormally dilated trachea, producing massive ventilatory leaks and aspiration risk.
Prepare specialized large-diameter tubes, tubes with extra-large cuffs, or place the tube distal to the tracheal enlargement.
High risk of dynamic airway collapse during exhalation: apply positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) to stent airways open.
Avoid high inspiratory peak pressures that cause tracheal overdistension or diverticular rupture.
avoid: High peak inspiratory airway pressures that risk rupture of fragile, dilated tracheal diverticula.
Overinflating standard ETT cuffs to extreme pressures to seal leaks (causes tracheal mucosal ischemia and necrosis).
postop: High risk of dynamic tracheobronchial collapse upon extubation: extubate with CPAP and have noninvasive positive pressure ventilation ready.
Aggressive chest physiotherapy, humidified oxygen, and clearance of thick retained secretions.
Observe closely in PACU or ICU for signs of acute respiratory compromise.

preop: Neurodevelopmental disorder (chromosome 15q deletion) with morbid hyperphagic obesity, hypotonia, and severe obstructive sleep apnea.
Associated conditions: daytime hypersomnolence, pulmonary hypertension, cor pulmonale, type 2 diabetes, and altered pain threshold.
High aspiration risk: chronic food gorging and delayed gastric emptying mean full stomach must be assumed regardless of stated fasting history.
Screen for difficult airway from obesity and short thick neck.
intraop: Perform rapid sequence induction (RSI) with cricoid pressure and cuffed endotracheal tube.
Difficult mask ventilation and intubation: prepare ramped positioning, video laryngoscopy, and supraglottic airways.
Prone to severe temperature instability (hypothermia or unexplained hyperthermia): monitor temperature continuously.
Extreme sensitivity to central respiratory depressants: titrate opioids sparingly.
avoid: Relying on patient or family fasting history (secret binge eating and hoarding are characteristic features).
Excessive opioid administration: prolonged postoperative apnea and hypoventilation are common.
postop: Continuous pulse oximetry and respiratory monitoring in ICU or monitored step-down unit.
High risk of postoperative obstructive apnea, hypoventilation, and atelectasis: use CPAP/BiPAP support.
Implement early mobilization and aggressive mechanical and chemical venous thromboembolism prophylaxis.

preop: Triad of congenital absence or hypoplasia of abdominal wall muscles, urinary tract dilation with renal dysplasia, and cryptorchidism.
Pulmonary hypoplasia and absent abdominal expulsive muscles produce severe cough impairment and chronic respiratory compromise.
Evaluate baseline renal function, electrolytes, and urinary tract anatomy.
Assess respiratory status: screen for recurrent pulmonary infections and baseline oxygen saturation.
intraop: Absent abdominal musculature severely impairs ability to generate cough and clear secretions postoperatively.
Response to nondepolarizing neuromuscular blockers is unpredictable: titrate carefully using quantitative train-of-four monitoring.
Maintain renal perfusion with balanced crystalloids; avoid nephrotoxic drugs.
Handle extremities and position gently: associated skeletal deformities are common.
avoid: Overdosing neuromuscular blockers in the presence of weak abdominal and respiratory musculature.
Nephrotoxic medications in patients with baseline renal dysplasia.
postop: Aggressive pulmonary toilet, suctioning, and assisted cough maneuvers are essential for secretion clearance.
Close monitoring of renal function, electrolytes, and urine output.
Observe for postoperative atelectasis and respiratory fatigue in a monitored unit.

preop: Focal cranial dystonia characterized by blepharospasm and oromandibular dystonia (jaw clenching, involuntary tongue protrusion, and grimacing).
Involvement of laryngeal and pharyngeal musculature can cause spasmodic dysphonia and upper airway obstruction.
Review current medications: anticholinergics, baclofen, and botulinum toxin injections.
Assess speech, swallowing, and airway patency prior to induction.
intraop: Oromandibular spasms or laryngeal adductor dystonia can cause acute airway obstruction during induction or emergence.
Ensure smooth induction with adequate anesthetic depth and complete neuromuscular blockade before laryngoscopy.
Avoid dopamine antagonists which provoke acute dystonic crises.
Ensure complete reversal of neuromuscular blockade before attempting extubation.
avoid: Dopamine receptor antagonists: metoclopramide, droperidol, haloperidol, and phenothiazines.
Light planes of anesthesia during airway instrumentation that precipitate reflex laryngeal spasm.
postop: Extubate only when patient is fully conscious with intact bulbar reflexes and complete neuromuscular recovery.
Observe closely in PACU for acute oromandibular dystonic spasms or tongue retraction.
Have anticholinergic agents (diphenhydramine, benztropine) available to treat acute dystonic flare-ups.

preop: Task-specific focal laryngeal dystonia causing involuntary spasms of vocal cord muscles during phonation.
Adductor type (most common) causes strained, strangled voice; abductor type causes breathy, whispering voice.
Patients often receive regular laryngeal botulinum toxin injections; determine interval since last injection.
Evaluate airway for residual vocal cord paresis, aspiration history, or stridor.
intraop: Examine vocal cords during laryngoscopy for spasms or asymmetry; select appropriately sized endotracheal tubes.
Ensure deep anesthesia and adequate muscle relaxation before intubation to prevent traumatic laryngospasm.
Atraumatic airway management: avoid mucosal trauma or edema that worsens baseline vocal cord dysfunction.
Monitor neuromuscular blockade with train-of-four.
avoid: Light anesthesia or premature airway manipulation that triggers reflex vocal cord adduction and severe laryngospasm.
Traumatic intubation that damages delicate vocal cord tissues.
postop: Perform smooth extubation to prevent coughing, bucking, or post-extubation laryngospasm.
Observe in PACU for upper airway patency, stridor, and swallowing safety.
Provide humidified oxygen and voice rest in the immediate recovery period.

preop: Rare congenital skeletal dysplasia (Conradi-Hünermann syndrome) with punctate epiphyseal calcifications, asymmetric limb shortening, and cataracts.
Craniofacial and spinal dysmorphism: midface hypoplasia, micrognathia, saddle nose, kyphoscoliosis, and cervical vertebral instability.
Assess airway, cervical spine mobility, and restrictive pulmonary defect.
Check for associated cardiac septal defects and renal anomalies.
intraop: Difficult airway: anticipate challenging bag-mask ventilation and direct laryngoscopy; have video laryngoscopy and fiberoptic bronchoscope ready.
Select smaller endotracheal tubes due to tracheal and subglottic hypoplasia.
Gentle positioning with meticulous padding: contractures, asymmetric limb shortening, and scoliosis make positioning precarious.
Avoid forceful neck manipulation during intubation.
avoid: Neck hyperextension during laryngoscopy in the presence of cervical vertebral instability or spinal stenosis.
Forceful airway instrumentation.
postop: Close airway observation in PACU for post-extubation croup, stridor, and subglottic narrowing.
Monitor respiratory mechanics and pulse oximetry.
Provide multimodal analgesia with careful attention to positioning comfort.

preop: Rare neurovascular disorder (voltage-gated sodium channel SCN9A mutation) causing episodic burning pain, erythema, and increased warmth in extremities.
Episodes are triggered by warmth, exercise, or dependency and relieved by elevation and cold exposure.
Identify patient-specific triggers, successful cooling strategies, and chronic neuropathic analgesics.
Screen for underlying myeloproliferative disorders in secondary erythromelalgia.
intraop: Maintain cool or neutral ambient operating room temperature: avoid warming affected extremities (warmth triggers excruciating flare-ups).
Regional anesthesia (epidural, peripheral nerve blocks) provides sympathetic blockade and exceptional perioperative pain relief.
If general anesthesia is used, employ multimodal analgesia (lidocaine infusion, ketamine) to suppress neuropathic pain cascades.
Avoid prolonged extremity dependency.
avoid: Direct heat, forced-air warming blankets placed directly over affected limbs, and high ambient OR temperatures.
Prolonged immersion of limbs in ice water (risks severe frostbite, tissue necrosis, and ulceration).
postop: Continue regional nerve blocks or epidural infusions for postoperative pain management.
Maintain comfortable, cool ambient room temperatures; avoid placing heavy warm blankets over feet and hands.
Monitor for rebound vasodilation and burning pain upon resolution of regional anesthesia.

preop: Congenital fusion of cervical vertebrae: classic triad of short neck, low posterior hairline, and severely limited cervical range of motion.
Major airway alert: impossible neck extension, craniocervical instability, and high risk of spinal cord injury during airway management.
Associated anomalies: scoliosis, cardiac septal defects, renal agenesis, and Sprengel deformity of the scapula.
Review cervical spine imaging and perform comprehensive preoperative neurological examination.
intraop: Severe limitation of cervical flexion and extension makes direct laryngoscopy hazardous or impossible: perform awake fiberoptic intubation.
Maintain strict in-line cervical spine stabilization; absolutely avoid neck extension or rotation during intubation and positioning.
Position patient with generous padding tailored to their fixed cervical anatomy.
Neuraxial techniques are generally contraindicated or technically challenging due to extensive spinal anomalies.
avoid: Any forceful cervical extension, flexion, or manipulation (carries high risk of spinal cord compression and permanent quadriplegia).
Blind direct laryngoscopy.
postop: Maintain neutral cervical alignment until patient is fully conscious and cooperative.
Perform detailed neurological examinations of all four extremities immediately upon emergence and in PACU.
Observe closely for airway edema or respiratory insufficiency.

preop: Inherited defect in type I collagen synthesis causing extreme bone fragility, recurrent fractures, blue sclerae, and dentinogenesis imperfecta.
Associated features: kyphoscoliosis, restrictive lung defect, platelet dysfunction, and hypermetabolic state mimicking malignant hyperthermia.
Airway evaluation: brittle teeth, fragile mandible, short neck, and basilar invagination.
Plan atraumatic transfer and positioning; prepare video laryngoscopy.
intraop: Extreme fragility: minimal trauma causes fractures; pad all operating surfaces and avoid aggressive manipulation.
Cycle blood pressure cuff manually or at extended intervals; avoid overinflation (cuff inflation can fracture the humerus).
Atraumatic airway management: gentle mask application and video laryngoscopy to protect fragile teeth and cervical spine.
Hyperthermia and hypermetabolism can occur intraoperatively; monitor temperature and EtCO2 closely (differentiate from MH; volatile agents are not contraindicated).
avoid: Succinylcholine: violent muscle fasciculations can produce multiple bone fractures.
Automated high-pressure cycling of blood pressure cuffs (causes humerus and arm fractures).
Forceful jaw thrust, tight mask straps, or aggressive direct laryngoscopy (fractures mandible or cervical spine).
postop: Meticulous nursing transfer: lift patient using wide support draw-sheets; never pull or lift by limbs.
Monitor for postoperative bleeding and hematoma formation due to capillary fragility and platelet dysfunction.
Provide effective multimodal analgesia.

preop: Catastrophic genetic disorder (ACVR1 mutation) with progressive heterotopic ossification of skeletal muscle, tendons, ligaments, and fascia.
Minor trauma, intramuscular injections, biopsies, and muscle stretching trigger explosive new bone formation and permanent joint ankylosis.
Temporomandibular joint is typically completely ankylosed (zero mouth opening); severe thoracic insufficiency from fused chest wall.
Plan awake fiberoptic nasotracheal intubation; assess nasal airway patency.
intraop: Complete TMJ ankylosis makes oral intubation impossible: awake fiberoptic nasotracheal intubation is mandatory.
Never attempt to force the jaw open or use oral airways (causes irreversible jaw ossification and complete airway obstruction).
Position patient strictly in their pre-existing fixed posture using customized pillows, gel pads, and foam supports.
Strictly avoid all intramuscular injections: administer all medications intravenously.
avoid: ANY intramuscular injection, muscle stretching, or surgical biopsy (triggers catastrophic heterotopic ossification).
Forcible opening of the mouth, jaw thrust, or direct oral laryngoscopy.
Attempting to straighten or force rigid limbs into conventional surgical positions.
postop: Maintain patient in their custom fixed posture without manipulating limbs.
Continue strictly atraumatic care and intravenous medication delivery.
High vigilance for respiratory failure due to rigid thoracic cage and restrictive lung disease.

preop: Plan a trigger-free anesthetic: any combination of sedation, TIVA or regional anesthesia.
Have the MH cart with dantrolene immediately available.
Treat central core disease and King-Denborough syndrome as MH susceptible unless proven otherwise; Duchenne and Becker muscular dystrophies are also highly associated.
intraop: Prepare the machine: remove the vaporizers, change the CO2 absorbent and the breathing circuit, and fit activated charcoal filters on the inspiratory and expiratory limbs.
Flush with fresh gas at 10 to 15 L/min for 10 to 15 minutes (some authors suggest up to 60 minutes for modern machines), then confirm the gas analyzer reads zero volatile agent in both limbs.

Early signs of a crisis: rising EtCO2, tachycardia, tachypnea, masseter or generalized rigidity, mixed acidosis, sweating, mottled skin, arrhythmias and labile blood pressure. A rising temperature is a later sign.
avoid: All halogenated volatile anesthetics: sevoflurane, desflurane, isoflurane, halothane, enflurane and methoxyflurane.
Succinylcholine.
postop: After masseter rigidity from succinylcholine, observe for 12 to 24 hours (EtCO2, urine, creatine kinase, potassium and blood gases). MHAUS advises creatine kinase and urine myoglobin every 6 hours for 36 hours.
After a crisis, admit to ICU for at least 24 hours and continue dantrolene, because recurrence is common. Crisis steps and dantrolene doses are in SOS › MH.

preop: Deficiency or dysfunction of C1 esterase inhibitor producing unregulated bradykinin release, causing severe episodic angioedema.
Surgical trauma, dental work, and airway manipulation are potent triggers of life-threatening laryngeal edema.
Administer preoperative prophylaxis: C1-esterase inhibitor concentrate (plasma-derived or recombinant), or fresh frozen plasma if concentrate is unavailable.
Examine airway and have emergency rescue medications in the operating room prior to induction.
intraop: Have targeted rescue medications immediately at hand: C1-esterase inhibitor concentrate, icatibant (bradykinin B2 antagonist), or ecallantide.
Standard anaphylaxis treatments (epinephrine, antihistamines, corticosteroids) are ineffective because HAE is mediated by bradykinin, not histamine.
Perform gentle, atraumatic airway instrumentation; minimize pharyngeal and laryngeal friction.
Maintain hemodynamic stability and minimize surgical stress.
avoid: Relying on epinephrine, antihistamines, or corticosteroids to treat an acute HAE attack (ineffective against bradykinin).
Traumatic or repetitive airway manipulation.
Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors: strictly contraindicated (blocks bradykinin breakdown and precipitates fatal attacks).
postop: High risk of delayed laryngeal edema: swelling can develop up to 24 to 72 hours postoperatively.
Observe in PACU or ICU with immediate fiberoptic airway rescue and tracheostomy capability ready at bedside.
Continue prophylactic therapy until tissue inflammation and surgical wounds have stabilized.

conditions.name: Superior vena cava / superior mediastinal syndrome

preop: Obstruction of superior vena cava and tracheobronchial tree by anterior mediastinal mass (lymphoma, thymoma, germ cell tumor).
Presents with facial, neck, and airway edema, venous engorgement, elevated intracranial pressure, orthopnea, and stridor.
Review CT imaging: evaluate cross-sectional tracheal area, carinal compression, and cardiac or pulmonary artery involvement.
Assess symptoms in supine position: severe orthopnea or dyspnea predicts catastrophic complete airway collapse under general anesthesia.
intraop: Induction of general anesthesia and muscle relaxation eliminates spontaneous negative-pressure breathing, causing fatal, irreversible airway collapse and RV outflow obstruction.
Prefer local anesthesia with ketamine sedation preserving spontaneous ventilation, or awake fiberoptic intubation in semi-Fowler position.
Establish lower-extremity intravenous access (femoral or saphenous): upper extremity venous return is obstructed and drugs are delayed.
Have rigid bronchoscope, repositioning plan (prone/lateral), and ECMO/cardiopulmonary bypass backup immediately on standby.
avoid: Neuromuscular blockers and general anesthesia with loss of spontaneous ventilation before establishing airway safety and bypass standby.
Upper-extremity intravenous access for emergency resuscitation drugs and fluid administration.
Supine positioning: compresses tracheobronchial tree and heart under the tumor.
postop: Extubate only when patient is fully awake, spontaneous ventilation is robust, and in sitting or head-up position.
Nurse in head-elevated position to reduce facial, cerebral, and laryngeal venous edema.
Maintain immediate access to rigid bronchoscopy and emergency airway equipment.

preop: Life-threatening idiosyncratic reaction to dopamine receptor antagonists (antipsychotics, metoclopramide) or withdrawal of dopaminergic agents.
Manifests with hyperthermia, generalized "lead-pipe" muscle rigidity, altered mental status, autonomic lability, and marked creatine kinase elevation.
Evaluate renal function, electrolytes, urine myoglobin, and arterial blood gases; coordinate ICU stabilization.
Differentiate from malignant hyperthermia: NMS involves central dopamine depletion, not a primary ryanodine receptor channelopathy.
intraop: Emergency management: active external cooling, generous intravenous fluid hydration, and dantrolene or bromocriptine administration.
Administer balanced crystalloids to maintain brisk urine output and prevent acute renal failure from rhabdomyolysis and myoglobinuria.
Invasive arterial pressure monitoring is indicated to manage profound blood pressure lability and autonomic storms.
Continuous core temperature monitoring with esophageal or bladder probes.
avoid: Dopamine receptor antagonists: haloperidol, droperidol, metoclopramide, and phenothiazines.
Succinylcholine: high risk of catastrophic hyperkalemic cardiac arrest secondary to extensive rhabdomyolysis.
postop: Admit to intensive care for continuous hemodynamic monitoring, active cooling, and renal protection.
Maintain forced alkaline diuresis to prevent myoglobin-induced acute tubular necrosis.
Continue bromocriptine or dantrolene until muscle rigidity and hyperthermia resolve.

preop: Herniation of abdominal viscera into the thoracic cavity causing bilateral pulmonary hypoplasia, pulmonary hypertension, and persistent fetal circulation.
Decompress stomach immediately with a continuous-suction Replogle or nasogastric tube to prevent gut distension.
Assess preoperative echocardiogram for pulmonary artery pressures, ductal shunting, and associated cardiac defects.
Avoid emergency surgery: postpone operative repair until pulmonary vascular resistance and hemodynamics stabilize.
intraop: Avoid bag-mask ventilation prior to intubation: forces gas into the herniated stomach and bowel, worsening pulmonary compression.
Immediate gentle intubation by experienced provider; employ gentle lung-protective ventilation.
Maintain low peak inspiratory pressures (< 25 cmH2O) and accept permissive hypercapnia to avoid barotrauma to the fragile hypoplastic contralateral lung.
Have inhaled nitric oxide (iNO) and inotropes immediately available for acute pulmonary hypertensive crises.
avoid: Bag-valve-mask positive pressure ventilation before intubation (inflates intrathoracic bowel and causes respiratory arrest).
High peak inspiratory pressures (causes contralateral pneumothorax, pulmonary hemorrhage, and death).
Nitrous oxide: diffuses rapidly into herniated bowel loops, causing massive mediastinal shift.
postop: Transport directly to neonatal intensive care unit intubated; continue lung-protective ventilation and pulmonary vasodilator therapy.
High vigilance for sudden desaturation: immediately suspect contralateral tension pneumothorax or acute pulmonary hypertensive crisis.
Delayed extubation until pulmonary vascular remodeling allows adequate oxygenation.

preop: Congenital esophageal discontinuity with fistula connecting trachea to lower esophagus (Type C most common).
High risk of gastric distension, aspiration of acidic secretions, and chemical pneumonitis.
Maintain continuous suctioning of blind proximal pouch with a Replogle catheter; nurse in semi-upright position.
Screen for VACTERL association (vertebral, anal, cardiac, TEF, renal, limb anomalies); perform echocardiogram to rule out right-sided aortic arch.
intraop: Perform gentle awake or inhalational induction preserving spontaneous breathing until airway is intubated.
Position endotracheal tube carefully so the tip lies distal to the tracheal fistula but proximal to the carina.
Avoid positive pressure mask ventilation prior to intubation: air enters the fistula, causing massive gastric distension and impaired diaphragmatic excursion.
If gastric distension prevents ventilation, surgical gastrostomy or emergency fistula occlusion may be necessary.
avoid: Positive pressure mask ventilation before intubation (inflates stomach, elevates diaphragm, and risks gastric rupture).
Placing the endotracheal tube bevel or tip proximal to the fistula opening.
postop: Transport intubated to neonatal ICU; avoid neck hyperextension which places tension on the fresh esophageal anastomosis.
Maintain low airway pressures to prevent anastomotic leak or tracheal disruption.
Avoid blind suctioning of the esophagus: mark suction catheters to prevent catheter tip from disrupting surgical repair.

preop: Neural tube defect with herniation of meninges and spinal cord; strongly associated with Chiari II malformation and hydrocephalus.
Latex allergy alert: patients have extremely high rates of latex sensitization; enforce strict 100% latex-free precautions from birth.
Assess for signs of brainstem compression from Chiari II malformation: stridor, central sleep apnea, dysphagia, and weak cry.
Protect the open neural placode with sterile saline dressings; prevent hypothermia.
intraop: Strict latex-free environment throughout the surgical suite, including gloves, catheters, and equipment.
Induction and intubation in supine position with the open defect supported in a padded sterile donut ring, or in lateral position.
Prone positioning requires careful chest and pelvic rolls to ensure free abdominal excursion and prevent elevated airway pressures.
Maintain aggressive thermoregulation: neonates lose heat rapidly through exposed neural tissue.
avoid: ANY latex-containing medical equipment, gloves, or materials.
Direct pressure or trauma to the unprotected neural placode during induction, positioning, or surgery.
postop: Nurse in prone or lateral position to prevent tension on the spinal surgical incision.
Continuous monitoring for central apnea, stridor, and vocal cord dysfunction secondary to Chiari II malformation.
Maintain latex-free precautions indefinitely across all hospital units.

preop: Autosomal recessive motor neuron degeneration (SMN1 mutation) causing progressive symmetrical muscle weakness, hypotonia, and bulbar paralysis.
Severe restrictive pulmonary impairment, weak cough, inability to clear secretions, and recurrent aspiration pneumonias.
Review pulmonary function, baseline oxygen saturation, scoliosis, and recent nusinersen or gene therapy history.
Assess cardiac function: cardiomyopathy and conduction abnormalities can occur.
intraop: Extreme sensitivity to nondepolarizing neuromuscular blockers: if used, drastically reduce dosing under quantitative train-of-four monitoring.
Prefer total intravenous anesthesia (TIVA) without muscle relaxants whenever feasible.
Absolute contraindication to succinylcholine: denervated skeletal muscles release massive, fatal amounts of potassium.
Full-stomach precautions: bulbar dysfunction and gastric hypomotility increase aspiration risk.
avoid: Succinylcholine: causes catastrophic hyperkalemic cardiac arrest.
Standard doses of nondepolarizing neuromuscular blockers: leads to prolonged postoperative paralysis.
postop: High risk of postoperative respiratory failure, atelectasis, and extubation failure: prepare noninvasive positive pressure ventilation (BiPAP).
Aggressive airway suctioning, cough assistance, and chest physiotherapy.
Observe in pediatric intensive care unit with close monitoring of ventilatory mechanics.

preop: Congenital triad of micrognathia, glossoptosis, and cleft palate resulting in severe neonatal upper airway obstruction.
Prone or lateral positioning often relieves airway obstruction by allowing the posterior tongue to fall forward.
Assess severity of airway obstruction, feeding difficulties, chronic hypoxemia, and secondary pulmonary hypertension.
Plan primary difficult airway strategy: assemble specialized pediatric airway equipment.
intraop: Major difficult airway: bag-mask ventilation and direct laryngoscopy are exceptionally difficult due to micrognathia and tongue displacement.
Prepare video laryngoscopy, paraglossal straight-blade approach, supraglottic airway devices, and flexible fiberoptic bronchoscope.
Preserve spontaneous ventilation during inhalational induction until the airway is secured; avoid muscle relaxants before intubation.
Position patient prone or lateral if supine ventilation becomes impossible.
avoid: Administering neuromuscular blockers prior to confirming ability to ventilate and intubate.
Supine induction without airway adjuncts or position modification.
postop: High risk of severe upper airway obstruction upon extubation.
Extubate only when fully awake, in prone or lateral position, with immediate availability of airway rescue gear.
Continuous pulse oximetry and respiratory monitoring in neonatal intensive care.

preop: Asymmetric hypoplasia of structures derived from 1st and 2nd branchial arches: unilateral mandibular and maxillary hypoplasia and microtia.
Goldenhar variant includes epibulbar dermoids, vertebral anomalies (cervical spine fusion/hemivertebrae), and congenital heart disease.
Airway evaluation: marked facial asymmetry, limited mouth opening, and deviated laryngeal anatomy.
Screen for cervical spine instability and congenital cardiac defects on echocardiography.
intraop: Anticipate severe unilateral difficult airway: laryngoscopy is complicated by asymmetric mandibular hypoplasia and a deviated larynx.
Use video laryngoscopy or flexible fiberoptic intubation; introduce blade from the less affected, larger side of the mouth.
Avoid forceful neck manipulation during airway instrumentation in patients with uncharacterized cervical vertebral anomalies.
Protect epibulbar dermoids and eyes with sterile lubricant and protective shields.
avoid: Assuming symmetrical airway anatomy during mask ventilation and laryngoscopy.
Forceful neck extension or rotation in patients with cervical spine hemivertebrae.
postop: Close observation in recovery for stridor, unilateral soft tissue obstruction, and airway compromise.
Position head to optimize airway patency toward the unaffected side.
Provide humidified oxygen and multimodal analgesia.

preop: Mandibulofacial dysostosis (TCOF1 mutation) with severe bilateral micrognathia, malar hypoplasia, cleft palate, and choanal atresia.
Airway difficulty is severe and worsens progressively with age as facial structures grow disproportionately.
Screen for obstructive sleep apnea, choanal atresia/stenosis, and associated hearing loss.
Formulate primary and secondary difficult airway management plans with pediatric ENT support.
intraop: Major difficult airway alert: direct laryngoscopy is frequently impossible (grade 4 view in majority of patients).
Use video laryngoscopy, optical stylets, or fiberoptic intubation through a supraglottic airway device.
Maintain spontaneous ventilation during inhalational induction until the airway is definitively secured.
Nasal intubation may be impossible due to choanal stenosis or atresia; evaluate nasal patency before attempting nasal passage.
avoid: Administering neuromuscular blockers before the trachea is successfully intubated.
Blind nasal intubation or aggressive nasal instrumentation without confirming choanal patency.
postop: High risk of catastrophic post-extubation airway obstruction: extubate fully awake, in upright or prone position.
Tracheostomy equipment and advanced airway rescue carts must remain at bedside.
Admit to pediatric intensive care unit for continuous respiratory and oxygenation monitoring.

preop: Craniosynostosis syndrome with midface hypoplasia, high-arched palate, choanal stenosis, complex hand/foot syndactyly, and elevated ICP.
High incidence of cervical spine anomalies (C5-C6 fusion present in up to 70% of patients).
Assess for severe obstructive sleep apnea, elevated intracranial pressure, and restricted cervical motion.
Plan for massive blood loss and brain relaxation during cranial vault remodeling procedures.
intraop: Difficult mask ventilation and intubation due to midface retrusion, narrow nasopharynx, and high-arched constricted palate.
Handle cervical spine with extreme care: maintain in-line stabilization during laryngoscopy and positioning.
Blood loss during craniosynostosis repair can be rapid and massive: ensure large-bore venous access, arterial line, and crossmatched blood.
Avoid hypercapnia and maintain brain relaxation to prevent acute herniation.
avoid: Neck hyperextension during airway management and positioning (risk of cervical cord compression).
Hypoventilation causing hypercapnia and acute intracranial pressure spikes.
postop: High risk of postoperative upper airway obstruction from facial edema and underlying sleep apnea: nurse in head-elevated position.
Admit to pediatric intensive care unit following craniofacial surgery.
Monitor neurological status, hematocrit, and coagulation parameters closely.

preop: Craniosynostosis syndrome with bicoronal synostosis, midface hypoplasia, shallow orbits with severe proptosis, and elevated ICP.
Unlike Apert syndrome, extremities are normal (no complex syndactyly) and cervical spine fusion is less frequent.
Screen for obstructive sleep apnea, elevated intracranial pressure, and chronic airway compromise.
Evaluate degree of proptosis: extreme eye prominence requires meticulous corneal protection.
intraop: Difficult mask ventilation and intubation from midface hypoplasia and narrow pharyngeal dimensions; prepare video laryngoscopy.
Protect protruding eyes with lubricating ointment, moisture chambers, and careful tape application (high risk of corneal ulceration).
Manage intraoperative blood loss and brain relaxation during cranial vault remodeling surgery.
Maintain tight control of EtCO2 and hemodynamics to preserve cerebral perfusion pressure.
avoid: Direct pressure on protruding globes during mask ventilation or positioning (causes corneal abrasion or globe subluxation).
Hypercapnia and venous hypertension that elevate intracranial pressure.
postop: Close respiratory monitoring in PICU for stridor, upper airway obstruction, and sleep apnea.
Maintain continuous eye protection and lubrication into the recovery period.
Serial neurological evaluations for signs of elevated intracranial pressure.

preop: Human papillomavirus (HPV 6 and 11) infection causing recurrent exophytic papillomas of the larynx, vocal cords, and subglottis.
Presents with progressive hoarseness, stridor, and life-threatening upper airway obstruction.
Review operative laryngoscopy records and imaging to assess extent of glottic obstruction.
Plan shared airway management with the ENT surgical team: discuss tubeless anesthesia, laser precautions, and jet ventilation.
intraop: Shared airway: close communication between anesthesiologist and surgeon is essential throughout the procedure.
Techniques include inhalational induction preserving spontaneous breathing, intermittent apnea with small endotracheal tube, or jet ventilation.
If laser surgery is performed, strictly adhere to airway fire protocol: FiO2 <= 30%, laser-safe endotracheal tube with saline-filled cuff.
Gentle instrumentation to prevent dislodging papilloma clusters into distal tracheobronchial tree.
avoid: Laser ablation in high FiO2 environments (catastrophic airway fire hazard).
Dislodging friable papilloma fragments into distal airways during instrumentation (causes pulmonary dissemination).
postop: High risk of acute postoperative laryngeal edema, vocal cord spasm, and stridor.
Administer intravenous dexamethasone and humidified oxygen.
Observe in PACU with emergency re-intubation and tracheostomy equipment immediately available at bedside.

preop: Trisomy 21 with high prevalence of congenital heart disease (AV canal defects, VSD, ASD, ToF), atlantoaxial instability, and sleep apnea.
Atlantoaxial instability occurs in 15% to 20%: review cervical spine flexion/extension radiographs and screen for neurological signs.
Airway evaluation: macroglossia, tonsillar hypertrophy, small mouth, and subglottic stenosis.
Review echocardiogram for residual shunts, pulmonary hypertension, or ventricular dysfunction.
intraop: Cervical spine precautions: maintain neutral neck alignment; avoid extreme flexion or extension during intubation and positioning.
Airway sizing: macroglossia and subglottic stenosis are common; select an endotracheal tube 0.5 to 1.0 mm smaller than expected for age.
Profound bradycardia during inhalational induction is common; treat with glycopyrrolate or atropine.
Venous access may be difficult due to obesity and small peripheral vessels: prepare ultrasound guidance.
avoid: Extreme neck flexion or extension during laryngoscopy, intubation, and positioning (risk of atlantoaxial subluxation and spinal cord injury).
Using oversized endotracheal tubes: high risk of mucosal injury and severe post-extubation subglottic edema.
postop: High risk of post-extubation croup, subglottic stridor, and airway obstruction: nurse in head-up position with humidified oxygen.
Continuous pulse oximetry and ECG monitoring for bradycardia and desaturations in recovery.
Careful airway observation before discharge from PACU.

preop: Identify high-risk procedures within the fire triangle zone (head, neck, and laser airway surgery).
Use laser-resistant tubes when indicated, minimize inspired oxygen concentration, and avoid nitrous oxide.
Allow alcohol-based skin preparations to dry completely and exclude pooled vapors before draping.
intraop: Recognize flames, smoke, foul odor, or sudden loss of circuit pressure and immediately shout "Airway fire!".
Simultaneously remove the burning tracheal tube and halt fresh gas flow by disconnecting the breathing circuit.
Flood the surgical field with sterile saline and extinguish any burning debris in water.
Re-establish mask ventilation with air or minimal oxygen once the fire is out and assess the airway.
avoid: Avoid ventilating with high inspired oxygen or nitrous oxide while fire or smoldering debris remains.
Do not attempt blind reintubation prior to direct visual inspection of the laryngeal lumen.
postop: Perform urgent rigid/flexible bronchoscopy to assess tracheobronchial mucosal burn injury and clear debris.
Admit the patient intubated to the intensive care unit to monitor and manage progressive airway edema.

preop: Screen for previous adverse drug reactions, multiple surgical exposures, and latex allergy in high-risk groups.
Verify immediate availability of resuscitation drugs, 100% oxygen, and difficult-airway equipment.
intraop: Detect sudden cardiovascular collapse, refractory hypotension, tachycardia, or acute bronchospasm with high airway pressures.
Immediately discontinue all suspected triggers (antibiotics, NMBDs, colloids, chlorhexidine, blood products).
Administer 100% oxygen, rapidly expand intravascular volume with crystalloids, and titrate IV epinephrine early.
Elevate the legs if hypotensive and start CPR promptly for severe systolic collapse or cardiac arrest.
avoid: Avoid relying solely on fluid boluses or pure alpha-1 vasoconstrictors without administering epinephrine early.
Do not continue infusing colloids, blood products, or antibiotics initiated shortly before hemodynamic collapse.
postop: Obtain serial serum tryptase samples immediately, at 1 to 2 hours, and at 24 hours post-event.
Monitor in the intensive care unit for biphasic reactions and arrange formal outpatient allergy testing.

preop: Identify full-stomach or delayed gastric emptying risk (trauma, pregnancy, bowel obstruction, GLP-1 therapy, emergency cases).
Enforce fasting intervals when elective and prepare rapid sequence induction with a cuffed tracheal tube.
intraop: Recognize gastric contents in the pharynx, sudden hypoxemia, wheezing, or acute loss of lung compliance.
Immediately place the patient in Trendelenburg and lateral position if feasible, suction the oropharynx, and secure the airway.
Ventilate with 100% oxygen and positive end-expiratory pressure; suction the trachea prior to positive-pressure breaths when possible.
avoid: Avoid routine large-volume bronchial lavage or alkaline washes that drive aspirated acid deeper into distal alveoli.
Avoid empirical prophylactic antibiotics or high-dose corticosteroids unless bacterial superinfection is later proven.
postop: Obtain a chest radiograph to inspect for dependent infiltrates (classically right lower lobe).
Monitor the patient in a high-dependency or ICU setting for 12 to 24 hours for chemical pneumonitis or ARDS.

preop: Screen for hyperreactive airways, active asthma, COPD, smoking, or recent viral upper respiratory tract infection.
Optimize baseline bronchodilator therapy before surgery and defer purely elective cases during acute exacerbations.
intraop: Recognize rising peak inspiratory pressures, an upsloping shark-fin capnograph, and expiratory wheezing or silent chest.
Switch to 100% oxygen, halt airway/surgical stimulation, and deepen anesthesia using non-pungent volatile or IV agents.
Rule out mechanical mimics (kinked ETT, endobronchial intubation, secretions, tension pneumothorax) and deliver inhaled or IV bronchodilators.
avoid: Avoid rapidly escalating pungent volatile agents such as desflurane during reactive airway constriction.
Avoid histamine-releasing neuromuscular blockers and high ventilator respiratory rates that worsen auto-PEEP.
postop: Confirm complete normalization of expiratory flow and gas exchange prior to deep or awake extubation.
Recover the patient with continuous pulse oximetry and humidified supplemental oxygen.

preop: Identify high-risk injuries (tibial/forearm fractures) and prolonged surgical positioning such as steep lithotomy.
Ensure meticulous padding and avoid tight circumferential wraps around high-risk extremities.
intraop: Suspect acute compromise when observing tense woody limb swelling, severe out-of-proportion pain, or pain on passive stretch.
Immediately remove all constrictive dressings, splints, or casts and notify the surgical team.
Position the affected extremity strictly at heart level and maintain adequate systemic arterial perfusion pressure.
avoid: Avoid elevating the affected limb above heart level, which further lowers local arteriovenous perfusion gradient.
Avoid relying on palpable distal pulses to rule out compartment syndrome, as pulses persist until irreversible ischemia.
postop: Measure intracompartmental pressures promptly if clinical exam is equivocal or in sedated patients.
Coordinate emergent orthopedic or vascular surgical fasciotomy without delay to prevent myonecrosis and rhabdomyolysis.

preop: Screen for baseline hepatic or renal impairment, cognitive decline, hypothermia risk, and chronic sedative use.
Select short-acting agents and titrate anesthesia using processed EEG and quantitative neuromuscular monitoring.
intraop: Confirm volatile agent clearance and verify adequate minute ventilation to exclude severe hypercapnia or hypoxemia.
Assess train-of-four neuromuscular recovery, core temperature, and point-of-care blood glucose immediately.
Check pupillary symmetry and consider targeted reversal (naloxone or flumazenil) only after airway and metabolic checks.
avoid: Avoid administering broad pharmacologic antagonists blindly without ruling out residual neuromuscular blockade.
Do not extubate or discharge an unresponsive patient to recovery without excluding hypothermia or hypercapnia.
postop: Obtain an emergent non-contrast head CT and neurology consult if pharmacologic and metabolic causes are excluded.
Admit the patient to the intensive care unit for ongoing airway protection and serial neurologic exams.

preop: Inspect dentition carefully before induction and document loose teeth, crowns, veneers, bridges, or partial dentures.
Counsel high-risk patients on dental injury risk and plan gentle laryngoscopy or non-laryngoscopic airway techniques when feasible.
intraop: Inspect the oral cavity immediately if dental fracture or avulsion is noted during intubation or airway removal.
Locate and retrieve every missing tooth fragment to prevent tracheobronchial aspiration or esophageal ingestion.
Store an avulsed permanent tooth by the crown in normal saline or cold milk and avoid scrubbing the root.
avoid: Avoid blind oropharyngeal suctioning that can dislodge loose teeth further down the airway.
Never reimplant an avulsed primary (deciduous) tooth in pediatric patients or store a permanent tooth dry.
postop: Obtain a chest or neck radiograph immediately if any tooth fragment remains unaccounted for.
Inform the patient honestly upon full emergence, document thoroughly, and arrange urgent dental consultation.

preop: Verify central venous access or reliable large-bore proximal peripheral catheters before infusing vesicants or concentrated vasopressors.
Ensure peripheral infusion sites remain visible or accessible for periodic inspection during prolonged procedures.
intraop: Suspect extravasation upon unexplained loss of drug effect, swelling, blanching, coolness, or rising pump occlusion pressure.
Stop the infusion immediately while leaving the cannula briefly in place to gently aspirate residual drug from the tissue pocket.
Remove the catheter, mark the border of induration, elevate the limb, and administer specific local antidote (e.g., subcutaneous phentolamine for catecholamines).
avoid: Avoid flushing the infiltrated catheter with saline, which forces concentrated vesicant deeper into surrounding tissue.
Avoid running concentrated norepinephrine or calcium chloride continuously through distal hand or foot veins.
postop: Apply appropriate thermal therapy (warm compresses for vasopressors; cold for most non-vasoconstrictor vesicants per local protocol).
Perform serial neurovascular checks and request early plastic or wound surgery consultation for skin blistering or necrosis.

preop: Identify patients with acute long-bone or pelvic fractures, particularly prior to intramedullary reaming or arthroplasty.
Coordinate early orthopedic fracture immobilization to reduce marrow fat intravasation.
intraop: Recognize unexplained acute hypoxemia, tachycardia, fever, petechial rash, or acute right ventricular strain during bone instrumentation.
Alert the surgical team during medullary reaming/cementing, deliver 100% oxygen, and support intravascular volume and right ventricular perfusion.
avoid: Avoid high airway pressures or aggressive PEEP swings that further impair right ventricular afterload in acute cor pulmonale.
Do not delay supportive oxygenation or rely on high-dose corticosteroids, which lack established mortality benefit.
postop: Monitor closely in the intensive care unit for the classic triad of respiratory failure, neurologic dysfunction, and petechiae.
Provide lung-protective mechanical ventilation if ARDS develops and evaluate for concurrent venous thromboembolism.

preop: Review baseline blood pressure, antihypertensive adherence, and screen for secondary causes such as pheochromocytoma or renal artery disease.
Continue baseline beta-blockers and clonidine preoperatively to prevent severe rebound hypertension.
intraop: Confirm arterial pressure accuracy and exclude reversible triggers first: light anesthesia, surgical pain, hypercapnia, hypoxemia, or bladder distension.
Deepen anesthesia and analgesia appropriately; if hypertension persists, titrate short-acting IV agents (e.g., esmolol, nicardipine, clevidipine, or labetalol).
avoid: Avoid precipitating precipitous hypotension in chronically hypertensive patients whose cerebral autoregulation curve is shifted rightward.
Never treat suspected pheochromocytoma catecholamine surges with unopposed beta-blockade prior to alpha-blockade.
postop: Assess for end-organ ischemia (ECG changes, neurologic deficits, surgical site bleeding) before recovery discharge.
Transition smoothly to scheduled oral antihypertensive therapy and manage postoperative pain and emergence agitation.

preop: Identify insulin-dependent diabetes, sulfonylurea exposure, neonates, severe liver failure, or sepsis prior to fasting.
Adjust basal insulin and withhold oral hypoglycemics on the morning of surgery while checking baseline point-of-care glucose.
intraop: Monitor point-of-care blood glucose hourly during prolonged cases because general anesthesia masks neuroglycopenic symptoms.
Treat confirmed low glucose promptly with IV dextrose bolus, start a dextrose-containing maintenance infusion, and recheck glucose within 15 minutes.
avoid: Avoid attributing unexplained tachycardia, diaphoresis, or delayed emergence solely to anesthesia depth without checking glucose.
Avoid administering insulin infusions without concurrent hourly glucose checks and a reliable dextrose carrier.
postop: Evaluate mental status and serial blood glucose measurements in PACU until stable oral or enteral intake resumes.
Adjust postoperative insulin regimens to prevent recurrent delayed hypoglycemia.

preop: Assess baseline intravascular volume status, cardiac reserve, sepsis, and preoperative renin-angiotensin inhibitor exposure.
Establish adequate venous access and invasive arterial monitoring before induction in high-risk cardiovascular patients.
intraop: Verify NIBP/arterial transducer zeroing and ECG rhythm while simultaneously reducing volatile depth and giving 100% oxygen.
Administer prompt vasopressor boluses and balanced crystalloid challenge while inspecting surgical field for occult hemorrhage.
Systematically rule out obstructive/distributive shock (tension pneumothorax, tamponade, anaphylaxis, VAE, myocardial ischemia).
avoid: Avoid tolerating sustained mean arterial pressure drops that impair renal, myocardial, and cerebral organ perfusion.
Avoid attributing refractory hypotension solely to anesthetic depth when surgical bleeding or anaphylaxis is evolving.
postop: Verify hemoglobin, lactate, acid-base balance, and urine output in PACU or ICU after prolonged hypotensive episodes.
Monitor for acute kidney injury, myocardial injury after noncardiac surgery, or postoperative delirium.

preop: Screen for pre-existing cardiopulmonary disease, morbid obesity, or difficult airway anatomy before induction.
Ensure thorough preoxygenation with a tight-fitting facemask to maximize functional residual capacity oxygen reserve.
intraop: Detect falling pulse oximetry saturation, verify plethysmograph waveform, and immediately switch to 100% inspired oxygen.
Switch to manual bag ventilation to feel lung compliance and confirm circuit integrity, inspired oxygen concentration, and capnography.
Auscultate bilateral breath sounds to exclude mainstem intubation, esophageal displacement, pneumothorax, bronchospasm, or mucus plugging.
avoid: Avoid dismissing desaturation as probe artifact before visually confirming cyanosis, arterial waveform, and ventilation.
Avoid delaying airway inspection or circuit disconnection checks when manual bagging feels abnormal.
postop: Obtain an arterial blood gas and chest radiograph when persistent shunt, atelectasis, or pneumothorax is suspected.
Transfer to PACU or ICU on continuous pulse oximetry and supplemental oxygen until oxygenation normalizes.

preop: Identify reactive airway disease, COPD, morbid obesity, or chest wall deformities and complete full circuit checks.
Optimize bronchodilator therapy prior to induction in patients with reversible bronchoconstriction.
intraop: When high peak or plateau pressure alarms sound, switch immediately to manual bag ventilation to gauge compliance.
Trace systematically from anesthesia machine to patient: check for kinked/bitten ETT, cuff herniation, secretions, bronchospasm, or pneumothorax.
Compare peak minus plateau gradient to distinguish airway resistance issues from reduced lung or chest wall compliance.
avoid: Avoid forcefully bagging against sudden high resistance before ruling out tension pneumothorax or circuit obstruction.
Avoid blindly deepening volatile anesthesia before confirming breathing circuit and tracheal tube patency.
postop: Reassess bilateral breath sounds and obtain a chest radiograph or bronchoscopy if barotrauma or plugging occurred.
Monitor in recovery for recurrent bronchospasm, post-obstructive edema, or subglottic swelling.

preop: Identify intracranial mass lesions, hydrocephalus, or traumatic brain injury prior to anesthetic planning.
Avoid heavy preoperative sedation that causes hypoventilation, hypercapnia, and secondary cerebral vasodilation.
intraop: Recognize Cushing triad (hypertension, bradycardia, irregular respirations) or a tense, bulging dura on surgical exposure.
Deliver 100% oxygen, initiate mild hyperventilation toward mild hypocapnia, elevate the head 30 degrees, and keep the neck midline.
Administer osmotic therapy (mannitol or hypertonic saline) and support mean arterial pressure to preserve cerebral perfusion pressure.
avoid: Avoid hypoxemia, hypercapnia, excessive PEEP, tight ETT ties, and extreme neck rotation that obstruct jugular venous drainage.
Avoid systemic hypotension that drops cerebral perfusion pressure across the injured brain.
postop: Maintain 30-degree head elevation and tight hemodynamic and carbon dioxide control during transfer.
Obtain an emergent non-contrast head CT for sluggish pupils or delayed emergence and admit intubated to the neuro-ICU.

preop: Identify pediatric age, active upper respiratory infection, passive smoke exposure, and airway surgery risk.
Plan smooth deep or fully awake extubation and consider topical or IV lidocaine/opioid blunting when indicated.
intraop: Detect inspiratory stridor or silent complete airway obstruction with paradoxical chest-abdominal rocking.
Clear blood or secretions from the oropharynx, apply 100% oxygen with gentle CPAP, and perform Larson maneuver (jaw thrust with styloid notch pressure).
Deepen anesthesia with IV propofol or administer a small dose of succinylcholine promptly if obstruction does not break and SpO2 falls.
avoid: Avoid aggressive high-pressure mask breaths against closed vocal cords, which insufflate the stomach and worsen regurgitation risk.
Never delay muscle relaxation or airway rescue when severe hypoxemia or bradycardia develops.
postop: Observe in PACU for at least 2 to 4 hours for delayed negative-pressure pulmonary edema.
Maintain humidified oxygen and continuous pulse oximetry until laryngeal reflexes and respiratory effort are normal.

preop: Identify extremes of age, low muscle mass, pregnancy, or cardiac/hepatic/renal disease requiring dose reduction.
Use ultrasound guidance, incremental fractionated injections, and frequent gentle aspiration before every local anesthetic bolus.
intraop: Recognize CNS prodrome (perioral numbness, tinnitus, metallic taste, agitation, seizures) or abrupt arrhythmias and cardiac arrest.
Stop local anesthetic injection immediately, call for the LAST kit, secure oxygenation/ventilation with 100% oxygen, and avoid hypercapnia/acidosis.
Initiate 20% intravenous lipid emulsion therapy using the dedicated SOS LAST dosing calculator without delay.
avoid: Never substitute propofol for 20% lipid emulsion in cardiovascularly unstable LAST patients.
Avoid vasopressin, calcium channel blockers, beta-blockers, local anesthetic antiarrhythmics (lidocaine), and large epinephrine boluses.
postop: Monitor in an intensive care unit for at least 12 to 24 hours for recurrent arrhythmias or delayed lipid rebound.
Evaluate for pancreatitis or hyperlipidemia after large lipid infusions and document the event prominently.

preop: Stratify cardiovascular risk using RCRI and functional capacity guidelines prior to major noncardiac surgery.
Continue baseline beta-blockers and statins through the morning of surgery to avoid rebound myocardial ischemia.
intraop: Recognize new ST-segment elevation/depression, unexplained arrhythmias, hypotension, or regional wall motion changes on echocardiography.
Administer 100% oxygen, correct tachycardia and hypotension to optimize myocardial oxygen supply-demand balance, and correct severe anemia.
Titrate IV nitroglycerin for active ischemia when blood pressure tolerates and notify the surgical team to expedite closure.
avoid: Avoid persistent tachycardia, hypothermia-induced shivering, acute anemia, and prolonged hypotension.
Avoid administering IV beta-blockers when acute decompensated heart failure or cardiogenic shock is present.
postop: Obtain an immediate 12-lead ECG, serial high-sensitivity cardiac troponins, and urgent cardiology consultation.
Admit the patient to a cardiac ICU for telemetry, antiplatelet/anticoagulation risk assessment with surgery, and possible angiography.

preop: Identify prolonged prone spine fusion, cardiac surgery, or procedures expecting substantial blood loss and fluid shifts.
Discuss the rare risk of ischemic optic neuropathy during preoperative consent for high-risk spine surgery.
intraop: Ensure zero external globe compression using padded foam/mirror frames and recheck eye position every 15 to 30 minutes.
Maintain baseline mean arterial pressure, avoid extreme hemodilution, and stage prolonged prone spine cases when blood loss mounts.
Keep the head neutral or slightly elevated (10 degrees reverse Trendelenburg) to minimize orbital venous congestion.
avoid: Avoid horseshoe headrests during prone spine surgery where slight patient shift can compress the globe (central retinal artery occlusion).
Avoid prolonged deliberate hypotension and excessive crystalloid-only resuscitation in lengthy prone procedures.
postop: Perform a bedside visual acuity, visual field, and pupillary light reflex check as soon as the patient is awake.
Obtain an emergent ophthalmology consultation immediately for any visual deficit or sluggish pupil.

preop: Screen for epilepsy, intracranial lesions, alcohol withdrawal, and metabolic disorders; maintain oral antiepileptic drugs on surgery day.
Consider proconvulsant drug interactions and minimize severe sleep deprivation or missed medication doses.
intraop: Recognize rhythmic tonic-clonic activity or unexplained tachycardia, hypertension, pupillary dilation, and surging ETCO2 under paralysis.
Administer 100% oxygen, protect the airway and prevent physical injury, and terminate activity promptly with IV benzodiazepine or propofol.
avoid: Avoid proconvulsant exposures (high-dose local anesthetics, normeperidine, flumazenil in chronic benzodiazepine users).
Never treat seizures with neuromuscular blockers alone, which mask motor convulsions while cerebral status epilepticus persists.
postop: Check point-of-care glucose, serum sodium/electrolytes, and arterial blood gases immediately to rule out metabolic triggers.
Admit to ICU with neurology consultation and continuous EEG monitoring until seizure control is established.

preop: Screen patients with chest trauma, bullous emphysema, COPD, or planned central line placement, supraclavicular blocks, or thoracic/neck surgery.
Review preoperative chest radiographs and verify immediate access to large-bore decompression angiocatheters.
intraop: Recognize acute unilateral absent breath sounds, escalating peak airway pressures, refractory hypoxemia, and shock with tracheal deviation.
Turn off nitrous oxide, give 100% oxygen, alert the surgical team, and perform immediate needle thoracostomy decompression.
Follow emergent needle decompression promptly with formal chest tube thoracostomy connected to water-seal suction.
avoid: Never delay needle decompression in an unstable patient to wait for a confirmatory chest radiograph.
Avoid nitrous oxide whenever pneumothorax is suspected, as it rapidly diffuses into air spaces and expands pleural tension.
postop: Verify full bilateral lung re-expansion with post-insertion chest radiography and monitor water-seal bubbling.
Transfer to ICU with thoracic surgical follow-up before considering extubation.

preop: Verify spinal landmarks carefully and confirm epidural catheter position with a test dose and incremental fractionated dosing.
Avoid excessive intrathecal or unintended subdural local anesthetic volumes, especially in shortened stature or pregnancy.
intraop: Detect rapid ascending sensory block, hand weakness, dysphonia/aphonia, apnea, profound bradycardia, and refractory hypotension.
Reassure the patient if awake, immediately secure the airway with tracheal intubation, and ventilate with 100% oxygen.
Support circulation aggressively with rapid IV fluids, vasopressors, and early IV epinephrine for severe bradycardia or arrest.
avoid: Avoid placing the patient in steep reverse Trendelenburg position to halt block spread, which triggers catastrophic venous pooling and arrest.
Do not delay intubation or epinephrine when aphonia, unconsciousness, or severe hypotension occurs.
postop: Maintain controlled mechanical ventilation and vasopressor infusion until complete motor and respiratory block regression.
Monitor in ICU with continuous arterial pressure tracking and confirm airway reflex recovery prior to extubation.

preop: Perform rigorous two-person clerical verification matching patient identity, blood group, and unit number before spiking any unit.
Review antibody screen results, prior transfusion reactions, and known IgA deficiency preoperatively.
intraop: Suspect acute hemolytic reaction under anesthesia upon sudden unexplained hypotension, diffuse microvascular oozing, hemoglobinuria, bronchospasm, or fever.
Immediately halt the blood transfusion, disconnect the tubing, and infuse 0.9% saline through new tubing to preserve renal perfusion.
Support blood pressure and maintain brisk urine output with crystalloids and diuretics as needed.
avoid: Avoid discarding the implicated blood bag or administration tubing, which the blood bank needs for investigation.
Never infuse additional units from the same donor batch before clerical and serologic crossmatch review completes.
postop: Send the remaining donor unit, tubing, and post-reaction patient blood and urine samples immediately to the blood bank.
Monitor in ICU for disseminated intravascular coagulation, hyperkalemia, and acute kidney injury.

preop: Identify high-risk procedures where non-collapsible veins sit above heart level (sitting craniotomy, laparoscopy, hysteroscopy, CVC insertion).
Place precordial Doppler or transesophageal echocardiography and consider a multi-orifice right-atrial central catheter in high-risk cases.
intraop: Recognize abrupt plummet in ETCO2, rising end-tidal nitrogen, acute desaturation, millwheel murmur, and cardiovascular collapse.
Immediately notify surgery to flood the operative field with saline and wax bone edges; halt nitrous oxide and ventilate with 100% oxygen.
Support hemodynamics with vasopressors and fluids and attempt air aspiration through a central venous catheter when positioned.
avoid: Avoid nitrous oxide in air-entrainment cases, as it rapidly diffuses into intravascular bubbles and expands embolus volume.
Avoid leaving the surgical site elevated above the heart or continuing laparoscopy insufflation during suspected VAE.
postop: Position the patient in Durant maneuver (left lateral decubitus Trendelenburg) to trap air in the right ventricular apex away from the outflow tract.
Transfer to the intensive care unit to monitor for paradoxical arterial/cerebral air embolism and noncardiogenic pulmonary edema.

preop: Assess symptoms (angina, syncope, dyspnea) and review echocardiographic aortic valve area and mean gradient.
Maintain hydration without precipitating overload; fixed left ventricular outflow obstruction cannot raise stroke volume.
intraop: Hemodynamic goals: preserve sinus rhythm (atrial kick provides up to 40% of LV filling), maintain normal-to-low heart rate (60–80 bpm), and maintain normal-to-high SVR.
Treat hypotension immediately with phenylephrine to protect coronary perfusion pressure across the hypertrophied myocardium.
Place external defibrillation pads and invasive arterial monitoring before induction in critical stenosis.
avoid: Tachycardia, which shortens diastolic filling time and precipitates subendocardial myocardial ischemia.
Abrupt SVR drops (single-shot spinal anesthesia or heavy propofol boluses), which cause refractory hypotension.
Loss of sinus rhythm or uncorrected hypovolemia.
postop: Monitor in an ICU or telemetry step-down unit with multimodal, opioid-sparing pain control to prevent postoperative tachycardia.
Avoid rapid fluid boluses once sympathetic tone recovers.

preop: Differentiate acute AR (endocarditis, aortic dissection — surgical emergency) from chronic compensated AR on echocardiography.
Continue vasodilator and heart failure therapy while assessing LV dilation and systolic reserve.
intraop: Hemodynamic goals ("faster, fuller, forward"): keep heart rate normal-to-mildly elevated (80–90 bpm) to shorten diastole and limit regurgitant fraction.
Maintain modest preload and mild afterload reduction (low-normal SVR) to favor forward aortic flow.
Use arterial line and transesophageal echocardiography in moderate-to-severe ventricular dysfunction.
avoid: Bradycardia, which prolongs diastole and increases regurgitant volume overload.
Acute SVR surges (light anesthesia, pain, pure vasoconstrictors) that drive backward regurgitation into the left ventricle.
postop: Monitor for pulmonary edema during emergence and prevent emergence hypertension with smooth analgesia.
Manage acute decompensated AR post-repair with inodilators if LV ejection fraction drops.

preop: Assess mitral valve area, transmitral gradient, pulmonary artery pressures, atrial fibrillation, and anticoagulation bridging status.
Continue rate-controlling medications (beta-blockers, digoxin) up to the morning of surgery.
intraop: Hemodynamic goals: keep heart rate slow-to-normal (60–75 bpm) to preserve diastolic filling across the stenotic mitral orifice, and preserve sinus rhythm when present.
Maintain preload carefully without over-distending the left atrium and avoid factors elevating PVR (maintain normocarbia, normothermia, and high oxygenation).
Treat hypotension primarily with phenylephrine rather than ephedrine (which provokes tachycardia).
avoid: Tachycardia or fast atrial fibrillation, which slashes LV filling and precipitates flash pulmonary edema.
Hypoxia, hypercarbia, acidosis, and nitrous oxide, which spike pulmonary vascular resistance and strain the right ventricle.
postop: Monitor closely in telemetry/ICU for acute atrial fibrillation, pulmonary edema, and right ventricular decompensation.
Provide smooth analgesia avoiding pain-induced tachycardia and hypoventilation.

preop: Identify etiology (ischemic papillary dysfunction vs myxomatous prolapse), LV ejection fraction, and pulmonary hypertension severity.
Optimize baseline vasodilator therapy and note that LVEF can overestimate true systolic function due to low-impedance backward ejection into the left atrium.
intraop: Hemodynamic goals ("faster, fuller, forward"): maintain high-normal heart rate (80–90 bpm), slightly lowered SVR to promote forward systemic output, and adequate preload.
Preserve myocardial contractility and avoid PVR spikes (normocarbia, adequate oxygenation, normothermia).
avoid: Bradycardia, which increases LV end-diastolic volume, dilates the mitral annulus, and worsens regurgitant fraction.
Sudden SVR elevation (sympathetic surge, high-dose phenylephrine) or hypercarbia.
postop: Control emergence pain and blood pressure tightly to prevent acute increases in afterload and pulmonary venous congestion.
Monitor respiratory status and consider telemetry in severe MR.

preop: Evaluate dynamic left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT) gradient, systolic anterior motion (SAM) of the mitral valve, syncope history, and ICD presence.
Continue baseline beta-blockers or verapamil through the morning of surgery and avoid prolonged dehydrating fasts.
intraop: Hemodynamic goals: maintain expanded intravascular preload, keep heart rate slow, preserve/augment SVR, and allow mild anesthetic myocardial depression to minimize dynamic LVOT obstruction.
Treat hypotension aggressively with IV crystalloid boluses and pure alpha-1 agonist (phenylephrine) rather than beta-agonists.
Maintain sinus rhythm to preserve stiff LV filling.
avoid: Beta-adrenergic inotropes and chronotropes (epinephrine, norepinephrine, dopamine, dobutamine, isoproterenol, ephedrine) that worsen dynamic outflow obstruction.
Hypovolemia, vasodilators, and spinal sympathectomy causing decreased preload and afterload.
Tachycardia and loss of atrial kick.
postop: Maintain telemetry monitoring and reactivate ICD if disabled for electrocautery.
Prevent postoperative pain, hypovolemia, and emergence tachycardia.

preop: Recognize Beck triad (hypotension, jugular venous distension, muffled heart sounds), pulsus paradoxus, electrical alternans, and echocardiographic RV/RA diastolic collapse.
Consider awake percutaneous pericardiocentesis under local anesthesia prior to general anesthesia when hemodynamics are unstable.
intraop: Hemodynamic goals ("full, fast, tight"): maintain high preload, elevated heart rate (do not slow compensatory tachycardia), contractility, and SVR.
